CHAPTERS OF THE CATHOLIC EPISTLE OF JAMES

1. On patience and undoubting faith, and on humility, addressed to the rich. In this chapter: on the burning within us and the passions that arise from it, and that their cause is not from God; for if there is any good in us, it is from [?]

2. On meekness and purity and good action that shares with others, leading to blessedness; and on knowledge and due measure in speech.

3. On love toward each person without partiality, according to the law.

4. That a person is justified not by faith alone but also by works, and not by either one on its own, but by both together.

5. That the rash and disorderly tongue kills the one who has it, and that it must be mastered so as to praise and glorify God. In this chapter: on good conduct, free of the strife against one another that comes from vainglory over human wisdom; and on divine wisdom; and that laziness and love of pleasure give rise to strife and disorder, and to enmity toward God; and on repentance unto salvation; and on not judging one's [?]

6. That a man's steps are directed not by man but by God. In this chapter: on the greed of the rich and their luxury in the world, and on the righteous judgment of God.

7. On long-suffering and the endurance of sufferings, and on truth. In this chapter: particular exhortations suited to each person, together with faith; and that one must serve the salvation of one's neighbor.

THE CATHOLIC EPISTLE OF JAMES THE APOSTLE

1. On patience and undoubting faith, and on humility, addressed to the rich. In this chapter: on the burning within us and the passions that arise from it, and that their cause [?] is from God. For if there is any good in us, it is from [?]

"James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion: greetings. Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials." Of God, that is, the Father, and of the Lord, that is, the Son. So if he is equally a servant of the Father and of the Son, the Son is of equal honor with the Father, both in essence and in operation. The apostles of the Lord prided themselves on being servants of Christ above every worldly rank, and wished to make this their distinguishing mark, whether speaking, writing letters, or teaching. "All joy." He knows that sorrow according to God and these trials are both praiseworthy and worthy of joy, for they are an unbreakable bond and an increase of love and compunction. Hence it is also said, "Child, if you come forward to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for trial." And Christ says, "In the world you will have tribulation; but take courage." And, "Narrow and afflicted is the way that leads to life." For without training no one can be found worthy of crowns, whether worldly [?] crowns or those according to God. In his humility he calls them brothers, not children. To the earnest, trials are a cause of all joy, because through them their tested quality becomes evident; and that testing leads on to perfect work. But someone will say: if this is what trials accomplish, how is it that Christ [?] not to be brought into trial in the [?]

[?] when their eagerness has been quenched, and it has ended in no good for those who underwent them. Others are brought on because of sin, as destruction was brought on the Sodomites. These trials we must flee as far as we can, by living without sin. But those that come from God, as to Job and to Abraham, we must not only not flee, but, if it is at all possible, even draw them to ourselves through endurance and thanksgiving. For when God tests, he knows how to do it for our benefit and to proclaim us victors. He said "various trials" because some, as we said, come from God and others from ourselves. "Knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance. And let endurance have its perfect work, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing." [?] the pure. As also in the saying, "Silver refined by fire, tested in the [?]." But how does testing produce endurance? Because that faith is proved pure which persists in endurance and steadfastness under the trials that come upon it. For it is truly the work of a believer to accept such onslaughts with long-suffering and thanksgiving, just as Job did, giving thanks in all things. "Let it have its perfect work." Notice that he did not say of endurance, as a statement, "It has perfect work," but as a command, "Let it have." For he is not announcing a virtue already present, but one now coming into being, and he lays down how it ought to come about. "If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all simply and without reproach, and it will be given him. But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing. For the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind. That man must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord. A double-minded man, unstable in all

He says that wisdom is the cause of the perfect work. "Let him ask of God." Since he knows that the testing of faith and endurance in trials are the achievement not of ordinary people but of those who are wise according to God, he therefore urges those who long to achieve these things to ask for wisdom. "Doubting nothing." If he believes, let him ask; but if he doubts, let him not even ask. For one who disbelieves that he will receive will not receive. "Like a wave of the sea." The one who doubts, being uncertain about his own requests, perseveres a little and then immediately withdraws. He suffers this out of pride, giving up quickly because what he asked for did not follow on the spot, as one who thinks great things of himself and supposes he does not deserve to miss what he asks for. The humble-minded man is the opposite of this. "That man must not suppose." That is, the one who asks with arrogance and careless-

ness. "Remove double-mindedness from yourself, and do not be double-minded at all about asking from God, saying within yourself, 'How can I ask anything from the Lord and receive it, when I have sinned against him so much?' Do not reason this way, but turn to the Lord with your whole heart and ask of him without hesitation, and you will know his great compassion: that he will never forsake you, but will fulfill your soul's request. For God is not like human beings, who bear grudges against one another; he bears no grudge, and he has compassion on what he has made." "A double-minded man." By a double-minded man he means one who has no support and no footing, settled neither firmly toward the things to come nor securely toward the things present, but led and carried about this way and that, clinging now to the future, now to the present. Such a man he likened both to a wave of the sea, which has nothing settled or stable, and to the flower of grass, which does not even last itself, but withers away as soon as the sun rises. Notice that he did not say such a man is like grass, but like the flower of grass, showing by the flower how utterly short-lived he is. And since he knows that humility is the midwife of all good things, and that without it nothing worthwhile is accomplished, he therefore adds, "Let the lowly brother boast," and what follows. How is he called double-minded, and why? Because he is settled neither toward the present life nor toward the life to come. For life too is called "soul," as in the saying, "All that a man has he will give for his soul." "In all his ways." By ways he means the movements of the soul, on which hopes hang, whether good ones or not, as David also says, "And you foresaw all my ways." "Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation, because like the flower of grass he will pass away. For the sun rises with its scorching heat and withers the grass, and its flower falls, and the beauty of its appearance perishes. So also the rich man will fade away in his pursuits." He likens the one who doubts to a wave stirred by the wind, which is lifted high, swollen by the gusts, but sooner than it has risen is laid flat and lulled to rest. The doubter suffers this very thing: out of pride and arrogance he rests his requests on nothing of what is needful. Therefore he adds, "Let the lowly brother boast," saying in effect: let whoever wishes to ask for something first ask for what is needful, and in this he will not fail to obtain what he asks. These things are the kingdom of God and his righteousness. Then let him persevere in asking for such things, and not pray for a little while and immediately withdraw (for that is the mark of a braggart), but let him wait to receive, persevering in humility. "The lowly, in his exaltation." From what is according to [?]

And the rich [?] "And the beauty of its [appearance] [?]." He has used the word "face" loosely. For this is said of man alone, and not of the other animals. But in the case of [?] it is not called a face; and in the case of birds, a beak [?]. "In his pursuits." By the pursuits of the rich man he means his courses in prosperity, or his affairs, in the midst of which he is unexpectedly carried off [?]

"[Let no one, when tempted, say,] 'I am tempted by God.' For God cannot be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one. Rather, each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire. Then desire, having conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, brings forth death. Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers." This blessed man seems to have treated the subject of trials rather boldly when he said, "Count it all joy when you fall into trials." Then, remembering the Lord's [?] that we not fall into [trial], propitiating [him], he urges the better course [?]; and so he takes up the argument again in the present passage, making clear which trial comes from God, and is even a source of great joy, and which comes from ourselves by our own choice. Yet it was right that the Lord and God Jesus Christ, looking to the greater weakness of human nature, should counsel us to pray against the onset of trials, since the disciples were still in a more imperfect state. He did the same in many other matters, putting off the more perfect things for the time being. But when, through the knowledge [that came] by his resurrection [?] and his ascension into heaven, the weak [?] was strengthened

[?] his [?] according to the flesh, he introduces [this teaching], since [our nature] was thenceforth able, strengthened [?] by the Lord's sufferings, to wrestle down every assault that came upon it. Since trials are twofold, as we said, endurance is profitable in each case. In those from God, because after them we win public acclaim, as Abraham did; in those from ourselves, because by enduring them with thanksgiving we offer this as a kind of compensation for our sins [?]. For the righteous man who acknowledges [his faults] is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech. "Let no one, when tempted, say." If trials are twofold, why does he now remove every trial from having its cause in God [?]?

[?] But consider [?] "when tempted." [?] the trials that bring about licentiousness [?] [?] to be in continual turmoil: this one, he says, is not tempted by God [?]. For having overcome the trial that came upon him, and having made himself more secure, he becomes thereafter hard for trials to capture, especially those stirred up from within himself. For having turned to a more philosophical way of life, he has blocked up the spring from which trials flow, and from then on he continues at rest from trials. God cannot be tempted by evil, according to the one who said (even if he is [?] to us), "[?] has [no] troubles [?]"

[?] in which alteration and change are seen, which are the first beginnings [?] of our nature. Desire and sin, and the death that grows from it upon the soul, are as it were steps in human ruin. For desire, once it has found room to be received and a place to dwell, produced sin, which gave birth to death, unless we uproot it from our mind and so find the beginning of a second life. He has now sufficiently shown that the divine nature can neither itself be tempted nor bring this upon others. Here he calls trials the thoughts that disturb and confound the soul's stability; for those from God above all give the soul a settled state, making it radiant and displaying to the many the soul's ineffable beauty. Therefore he now adds: "Every good gift and every perfect present is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning. Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, so that we might be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures." "From above, from the Father of lights." For the things that come from us neither have perfection, but rather much imperfection, nor make the soul radiant. How could anything be perfect that comes from those who receive by gradual progress, who with difficulty and much toil wash away the shame that comes from birth, and only then attain the divine radiance? "With whom there is no variation." For he himself cries out through the prophet, "I am, and I do not change." And "shadow of turning" means not even so much as a hint of it reaching to suspicion. "Of his own will he brought forth." He said "of his own will" to silence those who babble that this universe came into being by chance. For since he said above, "with whom there is no variation," and showed by this that the divine is unchangeable, he adds, "Of his own will he brought us forth." For if we are begotten, clearly we are also changeable. How could that be unchangeable which proceeds by change from non-being into being? Then, since he said, "He brought us forth," lest anyone

suppose that he begot the Son in the same way as us, and that the Son too was born along with us, he adds, "by the word of truth." For according to the divine John, all things came into being through the Son. So if our coming forth is through the Word of truth, we who have our being from the Word are not of the same kind as the one by whom we came into being. "So that we might be firstfruits." That is, the first and most honored. By "creatures" he means the visible creation itself.

"Swift" [to hear] does not lead to bare listening, but to an active listening, a hearing that sets out toward putting into practice what has been heard. For he knows that whoever lends his ear eagerly to what is said will also make himself ready to carry it out; just as, conversely, whoever approaches something slowly is held back by the delay, and is sometimes prevented altogether from undertaking it. That is why, for the teaching of divine things, he commands swiftness, but for things that are dangerous to handle, slowness. These are speaking and becoming angry. For both thoughtless talk and unconsidered [anger] often fail to end in good. That is why a certain divine man says, "He who has spoken has often regretted it, but he who kept silent never." And again the blessed David says, "Be angry, and do not sin": that is, when you are angry, do not at once bring on the madness that anger prompts. The present words agree with these. For slowness to speak and sluggishness to anger, by delaying in these matters, bring the one who handles them back to what is needful and right. Through judicious reflection it either dissolves the impulse toward these things altogether, or leads him to conduct his affairs as is fitting, especially in the case of anger, which, when it bursts forth without reason, robs a person of the righteousness of God. That is why he adds this reason too: "For the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God." For if righteousness is a disposition in the soul that gives to each according to his deserts, and anger, as the one who said it puts it, destroys even the prudent, how could anger, which darkens the mind through excessive passion so as to destroy even the prudent, establish that which judiciously gives to each according to his deserts? "Slow to anger." He wants us to practice slowness in two respects, in speaking and in becoming angry. For delay knows how to bring about restraint of impulse.

On meekness and purity and good action that shares with others, leading to blessedness; and on knowledge and due measure in speech.

"Therefore, putting away all filthiness and the over-

To "filthiness" he also adds "overflow of wickedness," wishing to make this point: even if some filthiness often befalls a person, he should quickly withdraw from it, and not, by persisting and lingering in it, make the evil firmer and harder to wash out through habit. For the things we do more continually and more abundantly naturally turn what is done into nature, or give it the settled character of nature. "In meekness." For it is in meekness, not in tumult and confusion, that teaching is received. "The implanted word." He calls the implanted word that which distinguishes the better from the worse, by which we are also rational, and

"But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves. For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks at the face of his birth in a mirror. For he looked at himself and went away, and at once forgot what he was like. But the one who looks into the perfect law, the law of liberty, and remains in it, being not a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, will be blessed in his doing." Since he knows that even those who listen eagerly to the word often quench their warmth in the very act of listening, he now adds these words, in effect urging: show your eagerness not in listening only, but much more in doing. "Deceiving yourselves" means "misleading yourselves." "Deceiving yourselves." By "the face of birth" he means coming to know oneself through the law. That is why he added "of birth" to "face." For by learning through the law what we have become, we perceive what kind of people the spiritual law makes us through the washing of regeneration. Then, if we do not abide in this vision through our conduct, we forget the gift as well. For one who has given himself over to evil deeds does not even remember that he has been blessed by God. If he remembered that he had been adopted as a son, justified and sanctified, which are spiritual gifts, he would not give himself over to works that set grace at nought. "In a mirror." From this ordinary mirror he carries the argument over to the mirror of the mind, without adding any of the words that would mark what he says as an illustration. It is as if he were to say: "If anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks at the face of his birth in a mirror. For just as that man looked at himself and went away, and at once forgot what he was like, so too this one has perceived through the law of Moses why he came into being, namely for the glory of God, and that he was made in the image of the God who made him; yet after perceiving it, he did none of the things he perceived, but, like the first man, in the matter of perceiving, con-

…was placed. So he did not use the word that ought to have been used. Yet James, the Lord's disciple, does not do this without reason. He says everything concisely, as a disciple of the "concise Word", and at the same time he draws the hearer in and urges him not to listen to these things carelessly. "But the one who looks into": notice that he said "looks into", not "enters". For the spiritual law, which is everywhere desirable and magnificent, knows how to draw a person in and perfect him even from a brief encounter. Since it is perfect and lacks nothing in any respect, it frees the one who meets it from doubting any of the things it contains, and persuades him to remain with what he has seen. "Into the perfect law": the Jews prided themselves on their observances of the law and thought that by these they fully achieved piety toward God. Busying themselves with these alone, they reckoned that they had gained perfection for themselves, while they treated other people with arrogance and contempt. This is clear from the Pharisee in the Gospel and his insolence against the tax collector. To check this conceit blessed James says what precedes. Having mentioned a doer of works and called him blessed, he at once corrects the evil that grows up in many people's doing, and says: Do not suppose, you who have obtained blessedness by doing the law, that doing alone is acceptable to God. It is not so. The one accepted is he who, besides doing, does not treat others with contempt and is not unkind toward his own kin. "The law of liberty": having said "perfect law", he added "of liberty", making liberty its distinguishing mark. For the law according to Christ frees from slavery to everything fleshly: sabbath-keeping, circumcision, and worship concerned with the other purifications. It sets the one who comes to it in freedom and relief from these things. Through its liberality, and the sweetness that comes from freedom, it has made him attentive and freed him from forgetfulness, which ruins every good thing. For nothing so persuades a person to cling to something as the ease and freedom he sees in it. Moreover, it has declared such a person blessed. "A forgetful hearer": he joined forgetfulness to hearing, since if hearing lacks doing, nothing prevents forgetfulness from following as well, as when one hears in passing and not actively [?]

"If anyone among you thinks he is religious and does not bridle his tongue, but deceives his heart, that man's religion is worthless. Religion that is pure and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans [?] in their affliction, [?] from the world." "Religion" seems to mean something more than faith. For the word implies knowledge of hidden things

and certainty about the things perceived in faith. That is why blessed James now used this word. In saying "religious" it is as though he said: You think you know the secret things in the law and keep them exactly. How can that be, when you do not know how to bridle your tongue but slander your neighbour, and when you live arrogantly and pity none of the needy? The law does not admit the slanderer. It even commands us to pity our enemies, and to help an enemy lift his beast when we find it fallen under its load [?]. So if you wish to be religious, show your religion not in knowing the law but in doing it, and that means having compassion on your neighbours. For compassion toward one's neighbour makes one like God: "Be compassionate," he says, "as your heavenly Father is compassionate." But compassion must not be shown with partiality either. God does not divide out his benefits, but does good to all without distinction, rich and poor, wicked and good. "Bridling" means, as it were, choking it, and not deceiving one's conscience by the conceit of being a doer of the law. For that is what "heart" means here, as in "a broken and humbled heart." "Pure religion": perhaps someone will say: If James is a teacher of the covenant according to Christ, how is it that he does not now abolish the things of the law, but rather exalts them, accepting those who practise its religion,

…the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory. For if a man with gold rings and fine clothes comes into your assembly, and a poor man in filthy clothes also comes in, and you pay attention to the one wearing the fine clothes and say to him, 'You sit here in a good place,' and say to the poor man, 'You stand over there,' or 'Sit here under my footstool,' have you not made distinctions among yourselves? And you have become judges with evil thoughts." "Not with partiality": whoever does anything with partiality fills himself with much stain and much blemish. He dishonours those of his own kind, and before them himself, since what is shown toward one's fellow also comes back upon oneself. "And have you not made distinctions": the conjunction "and" is superfluous [?]. "Et non dijudicastis" [?]. This means: You have corrupted your discernment. You made no inquiry whether you should honour the poor but earnest man or the rich but slothful one, but so without discernment and with partiality you honoured the one for his wealth and dishonoured the other for his poverty. "And you have become judges with evil thoughts": that is, unjust judges who have added wickedness through partiality. The conjunction "and" is redundant here, as has been said, in an archaic manner of expression. Since this is the conclusion of what was said above, the conjunction is superfluous. The sense is: For if a man with gold rings and fine clothes comes into your synagogue, and a poor man in filthy clothes also comes in, and so on, you have not made distinctions among yourselves and have become judges with evil thoughts. That is, having corrupted your discernment, you have come to choose evil thoughts, honouring the one and dishonouring the other, even though the same nature is present in both. "Listen, my beloved brothers. Has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom which he promised to those who love him? But you have dishonoured the poor man. Is it not the rich who oppress you, and are they not the ones who drag you into court? Are they not the ones who blaspheme the good name that was invoked over you? If you really fulfil the royal law according to the Scripture, 'You shall love your neighbour as yourself,' you do well. But if you show partiality, you commit sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors." Many people find poverty hard even to hear about. That is why, having said "the poor of the world", he at once added "rich". Rich in what? In faith. And so it is: because the poor are not distracted by the world, they become more energetic and more active than the wealthy once they come to faith. That is why the Lord chose such men as his disciples, and he also made them heirs of the king-

-dom [?]. "They blaspheme the good name": the good name is a new name, as the prophet says: "But those who serve me shall be called by a new name, which shall be blessed over all the face of the earth." "According to the Scripture": Deuteronomy says it. "For whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all. For he who said, 'Do not commit adultery,' also said, 'Do not murder.' If you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law. So speak and so act as those who are to be judged by the law of liberty. For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment." "But stumbles in one": he said this about love. All of his argument before this was aimed at establishing love. He mentioned "You shall not commit adultery, you shall not murder" as examples. Notice that the examples, too, come from the part of the law that serves love. Whoever loves his neighbour perfectly will neither commit adultery nor murder, for these are the acts of someone who treats his neighbour as an enemy. If it did not mean this, no human being would be saved, since no one is flawless in all the commandments. Someone who has achieved chastity, say, is sometimes overcome by anger. And someone who blossoms with almsgiving may perhaps be [overcome] by envy [?]. So this is not said about complete flawlessness in all the virtues. It is said about love: that they should practise it not with partiality and deficiently, but wholly. We say the same about the other virtues. Whoever does not hold to the works of temperance, say, or of justice to the end, but practises them deficiently, limps in his practice and damages the whole body of virtue. So "the whole law" must be understood as the law of love, which is his principal aim. By "the law of liberty" he means the impartial law, which is Christ's. For the man who shows partiality is not free but a slave: "For by whatever a person is overcome, to that he is also enslaved." "For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy": if we forgive our neighbours their sins against us, and share what we have with the needy, God's mercy toward us will receive us in the examination of what has been established [?]. Great is the achievement, just as, conversely, great is the condemnation of those who do not deal conscientiously with their own kind. Upon those who have been unsympathetic toward their neighbours' offences against them, the condemnation of the wicked servant will close in, along with the requital in the [prayer] [?]. For there we ask God to forgive us, as we also forgive those who have offended against us. And those who are merciless, that is, unsharing and harsh toward people who need bodily comfort, will meet a judgment without mercy, as the present saying states. "But mercy triumphs over judgment": for the merciful will obtain mercy, according to the Lord's

declaration. Besides, if compassion toward the poor can blot out the sins of idolaters, as we heard in Daniel, what would it not accomplish for believers? This mercy seems to me to work like the oil from trees that athletes rub on themselves, which lets them slip out of their opponents' grips. So too at the universal judgment, the mercy we have shown our neighbours will let us escape the attacks of the demons who accuse us. Another interpretation: "For judgment is without mercy." This reason is aimed at those whose great harshness leads them to show contempt for the lowly through partiality. He softens their harshness and hardness by frightening them with this declaration, saying in effect: The law commands you to love your neighbour as yourself. Just as no one shows partiality against himself, for that would be madness, so you should not show partiality either. But if folly and hardness lead you into partiality, fear that you too may meet the same treatment from the just Judge and shut yourself out from his mercy. "For judgment is without mercy." "But it triumphs": that is, it conquers, overcomes, blunts.

That a person is justified not by faith alone but also by works; not by either one separately, but by both together. "What use is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him? If a brother or sister is naked and lacks daily food, and one of you says to them, 'Go in peace, be warmed and filled,' but you do not give them what the body needs, what use is that? So also faith by itself, if it has no works, is dead. But someone will say, 'You have faith, and I have works.' Show me your faith, and I will show you my faith by my works. You believe that God is one? You do well. Even the demons believe, and shudder." Notice the spiritual understanding. He did not say only "If you have faith," but "What use is it?" It is as though he said: Show me the thing for which I may credit you with this name. That is what faith is for. "So also faith by itself, if it has no works, is dead": this does not contradict blessed Paul, because the word "faith" is used in two senses. We usually call simple assent to what is evident "faith" [?], and we know that the demons believe that [he is] the Son of God. Again, we also use the word "faith" for adherence that comes from the disposition of the heart together with firm assent. James calls the [mere]

assent dead faith, lacking the works that rekindle it. But Paul speaks of the faith that comes from the heart's disposition, which is by no means deprived of works. Such faith could not arise empty of holy works. Not even Abraham obtained it without first struggling against the godlessness of his fathers, and faith was awarded to him as the prize of that contest. But Paul preferred faith to works, meaning the works of the law: sabbath-keeping, circumcision, and the other sanctifications. For "works" also has two senses. Works are the things that confirm faith, and without them faith is dead. Works are also the works of the law, without which both Abraham and all who belong to Christ are justified. And who does not know that faith, I mean true faith, would not come to an impure person? No one would store myrrh in a vessel full of mud, and faith in God would not arise in an impure person. So the divine apostles do not disagree. Each turns on a different sense of the word, and each carries through and completes the task set before him according to the sense he needs. "Do you want to know, you empty man, that faith without works is dead? Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered his son Isaac on the altar? You see that faith worked together with his works, and by works faith was made perfect. And the Scripture was fulfilled which says, 'Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness,' and he was called the friend of God. You see, then, that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. Likewise, was not Rahab the prostitute also justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out another way? For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead." He called the one who boasts of bare faith an "empty man", because he has nothing of the substance of works to make it full. "Abraham our father": both Paul and James take the same Abraham as an example in their teaching on faith. The one uses Abraham's example to show that faith is better than works. The other shows that the same Abraham is an image of both kinds of faith. One is the faith before baptism, which requires no works but only faith, the confession of salvation, and the word by which we are justified when we believe in Christ. The other is the faith after baptism, which is yoked with works. So the Spirit who spoke in the

apostles is not shown to contradict himself. The first faith justifies the one who comes to it by confession alone, if he should depart this life at once. Such a person has no works, but the cleansing of baptism is sufficient provision for his journey. The second faith requires the one already baptized to show good works as well. Paul agrees with this elsewhere, teaching that the faith after baptism demands to be perfected through works, when he says, "Neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love." And love requires much discipline to be fulfilled. Another interpretation: Abraham was an image of justification by faith alone when he believed and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and of justification by works when he offered his son on the altar. For he not only did the work, but also did not abandon his faith that his seed would multiply like the stars through Isaac, reckoning that God is able to raise even the dead. Yet Paul brings forward David as a witness, wisely arranging his argument. For the divine Spirit knew of the faith in Christ that would come in due time. So he says: "Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not reckon sin." "Faith without works is dead": he means the faith after baptism. For faith bereft of works is of no benefit. Indeed, it makes us liable to a greater sin, since we have received the talent but have not traded with it. That is why the Lord too, giving us a pattern to show that after baptism we also need works, went into the wilderness after he was baptized by John and took up the contests against the devil. And Paul exhorts those already counted worthy of the mysteries, saying, "Let us strive to enter that rest." He means that faith is not enough: purity of life must be added, and we must be very zealous about this. "Do not many of you become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we will receive a greater judgment. For we all stumble in many ways." Having spoken above and taught that believers must not hold a faith empty of earnest works, he moves on to another precept, a sister to that one. (For some people try to teach what they have not achieved themselves [?].) He says that such people incur a greater judgment and gain nothing besides. Whoever teaches things he does not have as though he had them [?] is accursed, because he slips through his own tongue. He confirms this with an argument from the greater. For the tongue is naturally apt to slip through inattention anyway, and even then its owner does not escape judgment, as Solomon says: "Through the sin of his lips the sinner falls into a snare." How much more, then, the one who sins deliberately, teaching with his tongue what he does not

That the rash and unruly tongue kills its owner, and must be controlled so that it speaks well and gives glory to God. Also on good conduct and avoiding strife with one another out of love of glory for human wisdom; on divine wisdom; that strife, disorder, and enmity toward God arise from sloth and love of pleasure; on repentance leading to salvation; and on not judging one's neighbour. "If anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect man, able to bridle his whole body as well. If we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we guide their whole body too. Look at ships as well: though they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are steered by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs."

He proves from how easily the tongue slips that no human being can possibly live without sin. From this he also shows that no one possesses perfection. For who has not sinned with his tongue? But if someone has mastered his tongue's tendency to slip, why should he not also be able to steer his whole body well? Whoever has mastered what is quickest to stumble will hardly fail to master what is slower. "If we put bits into the mouths of horses": the construction is "We put the bits into the mouths of horses." Unless it is construed this way, the sentence makes no sense. These words support what was said about the tongue, again arguing from the greater: whoever masters what is easily moved will also prevail over what is hard to manage. At the same point he answers an objection. Someone might well say: What effort does it take to steer so small a member? Or what [harm] can come from so small a thing [?]? He shows that this too is answered by the bit, the rudder, and the spark, which are small but achieve great things. Another interpretation: these words also teach that we must not move the tongue at random, but turn it toward better things, as the bit turns a horse's boldness and the rudder a ship's momentum. So we too ought to steer the tongue toward what is good by right reason. That is the meaning of "So also the tongue": the tongue too ought to be steered by right reason, and not do what it does. For though it is small it does great things, and so it kindles a great fire for us, since it too is a fire. And what does it do? It dresses up injustice through the eloquent skill of orators. It stains the body by seducing women with flattery. It brings about murders through deceit. It reaps other people's goods through perjury. And above all, it sets on fire the wheel [?] of Gehenna. That is, it kindles and stirs up Gehenna against us, as if to overrun us

…[?] the fire. "But it too," he says, "is set on fire by Gehenna." This is clear from the rich man whose tongue was being scorched. For it was his tongue and nothing else that was punished, because the tongue is ready for pleasure and idle talk. If, then, the text reads "of Gehenna," as some of the copies have it, the saying is to be explained this way. But if it reads "the wheel of generation," it has the following explanation. By "the wheel of generation" he means our life. So by setting the wheel of generation on fire, the tongue stains our life. And how? By moving rashly. This is what makes our life rough, that is, the span of our life. The Psalmist too means this when he speaks of "the crown of the year." A crown and a wheel do not differ, since both are circular and wheel-shaped. And life is a wheel because it rolls back upon itself. How then does the tongue stain life? By moving in the way we described above, which makes life both filthy and full of groaning. So then, let the tongue be guided by right reason. It is a world of iniquity when it is, as it were, carried out toward the vulgar rabble of the common crowd and looks to them; for "world" here must be understood as the multitude. Or else it is a "kosmos," an adornment, in the sense that it adorns human nature, for by it we share our thoughts with one another, since some also want to take the word "kosmos" in this sense. Either way, when it is carried toward the vulgar crowd it does wrong: it stains the whole body, sets on fire the wheel of generation, and is set on fire by Gehenna. Yet it is not hard to manage it so that it moves reasonably, and as the one who manages it would wish. For if every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, is tamed and has been tamed by human nature, can no one tame the tongue just because it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison? I would not say so. For if it were untameable and never turned toward the better, how could we bless God and the Father with it, and with it curse men? See, it is led by the will of the one who uses it. "But, my brothers, these things ought not to be so." For if we bless by means of it, is it not shameful, then, to curse men who have been made in the likeness of God? Or is it right that blessing and cursing should come out of the same mouth? No [?]…

"So also the tongue is a small member, and boasts of great things. See how great a forest a little fire kindles. And the tongue is a fire, the world of iniquity. So the tongue is set among our members, staining the whole body, setting on fire the wheel of generation, and set on fire by Gehenna. For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, is tamed and has been tamed by human

nature; but [?] the tongue no one among men can tame. It is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison. With it we bless God and the Father, and with it we curse men who have been made in the likeness of God." "So also the tongue." That is: in the same way the tongue too ought to move well, since, although it is a small member, it accomplishes great things, both good, that is, and bad. He has not spelled this out, because the one who writes these words is a disciple of the concise Word. "The world of iniquity." Some take "world" here to mean the multitude, as also in "The world did not know him," meaning the common multitude. So the tongue too is a world, that is, a multitude of iniquity; and how great a multitude is indicated by his words "how great a forest." "For every kind." This objection must be understood in relation to what was said above. Having said and shown, by the bridle and the rudder, that these things are small yet achieve great things when they are moved well, and having added that the tongue too ought to be guided by right reason, he now shows, by the examples set before us, that he is not commanding impossibilities. It is as if he were saying: "But someone will say that, although the tongue is a small member, yet, since it accomplishes great things both good and bad, it is neither obedient nor easy for us to lead where we wish." That is no defence. For if man tames beasts foreign to his own nature, fearsome to look at and still more fearsome to handle, will he not much more readily manage his own member? This is why the words "But the tongue no one among men can tame" are to be read not as a statement but as a question, so that it runs: "If man domesticates wild beasts and makes them manageable, will he not tame his own tongue?" That is how it must be read. For if it were read as a statement, you would not find him, as he goes on, making proper use of his admonition, I mean, "These things, my brothers, ought not to be so." For if it were impossible to reform the tongue, then one who urged people to attempt the impossible would not be giving sound counsel. Someone might say that "an unruly evil, full of deadly poison" must be taken as a statement. For these words magnify how hard the tongue is to manage [?]. But "From the same mouth come blessing and cursing" must also be read as a question. For the words are meant to shame the hearers, since we are commanded to bless all, for revilers will not inherit the kingdom of God. Is it not shameful, then, to use the same instrument as a servant of vice and of virtue? No one in his right mind would stir mud and perfume with the same implement. Are you praying? Do not curse your enemy. For prayer and cursing are far apart. If you do not forgive the one who has hurt you, neither will you be forgiven; rather, you will be caught cursing yourself when you pray that your debts be forgiven you as you forgive your own debtors. But, for the sake

of easy understanding, it is good to set out the whole passage as well, arranged in the proper order of its wording, adding some of what is left unsaid. It runs like this: "See, we put bridles into the mouths of horses so that they obey us, and we guide their whole body. See, the ships too, though they are so large and are driven by fierce winds, are guided by a very small rudder wherever the impulse of the helmsman wishes. So then, let the tongue too be guided by right reason. And this is not hard. For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, is tamed and has been tamed by human nature. If this is so, can no one tame the tongue?" I would not say so. "From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. These things, my brothers, ought not to be so. [?] Does a spring pour forth sweet and bitter water from the same opening? Can a fig tree, my brothers, bear olives, or a vine figs? So no spring can yield both salt and sweet water. [?] Who among you is wise and understanding? Let him show his works by his good conduct, in the meekness of wisdom. But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and lie against the truth. This wisdom does not come down from above; it is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. For where there is jealousy and selfish ambition, there is disorder and every evil practice. But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and without hypocrisy. And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace." "From the same mouth." From one who has been counted worthy of such initiation into the mysteries, let nothing bitter be uttered, nothing unpleasant. "Who among you is wise?" There were men who loved to rule and boasted in the wisdom of this world, and they preached out of strife and jealousy against the true teachers, simply courting the crowd and harbouring envy besides, and mixing human things with divine, so as to draw the hearers to themselves by the novelty of what they said. This is how heresies arose. Having finished, then, his discourse on rashness and lack of control of the tongue, he passes next to the envy that arises in men from a similar folly. And he says that these teachings are not those of steady men [?], since they come not from divine wisdom but from demonic. He said this after first praising the good teacher, saying that his wisdom shows itself in meekness through good works. And since the word "zeal" is seen to stand midway between good and bad (for zeal is an ardent movement of the soul toward something, with some imitation of the object it is eager for), for this reason

he added "bitter," to show what the zeal was directed toward. And selfish ambition is blameworthy contentiousness. "First pure." Pure, clean and unsoiled, clinging to nothing of the flesh. "Impartial." Not making distinctions over the observance of foods and various washings. Paul discusses these matters precisely in the Letter to the Colossians. "Where do wars and fights among you come from? Do they not come from this, from your pleasures that are at war in your members? You desire and do not have; you murder and are jealous, and cannot obtain; you fight and wage war, and you do not have because you do not ask. You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your pleasures. Adulterers and adulteresses, do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God." He shows that, even though they put on the appearance of teaching, they are all fleshly and do the most grievous things, procuring pleasures for themselves. Some seek a more luxurious table (Paul too condemns them for this, saying: "For such people do not serve the Lord but their own belly"); others reach out to acquire splendid estates or houses; others to surround themselves with servants or rented houses; and each for some other thing. These are the things the evil one suggests to them, scheming to lead them away from their own salvation. "You desire and do not have." He proceeds by positing something and then removing it, the proposition being removed because of its absurdity. It is absurd because the things contemplated in the proposition would become kindling for pleasure. For if desire ends in the fulfilment of pleasures, then murder and jealousy, and indeed fighting and war, are not good. That is why they do not even obtain the things for whose sake they pursue these practices. It should be noted that he is not speaking here of murder and war in the fleshly sense; that would be grievous to imagine even of robbers, let alone of believers who come to the Lord. Rather, as it seems to me, he says that those commit murder who kill their own souls by these reckless undertakings, through which they also wage war against piety. And just as, further on, he will call them adulterers and adulteresses, not that they were all such, but because they prostitute [?] the divine and good commandments by turning aside to other, spurious things (for no one would put up with a fornicating teacher, even if he were filthier than swine), so too by murders and wars he means not bodily but spiritual ones. "You ask and do not receive." Like the Pharisee in the Gospel according to Luke. For the more of his own achievements he listed, the more he stopped up the divine hearing; and the empty bulk of his words flowed over his lips and dissolved into foam, like a seething wave. But someone will say: if

the promise of the Lord Jesus, the teacher who cannot lie, is true, namely, "Everyone who asks receives," how is it that the present apostle now says this? We answer that whoever proceeds to ask in the proper way keeps the promise intact as well, and misses none of the things he asks for. But if someone goes outside the purpose of the prayer that has been handed down to us and only appears to ask, then, since he does not ask in the way he should, he does not truly ask at all, and so he will not receive. Suppose a teacher, say a grammarian, promises to teach the science of grammar to everyone who comes to him. If the would-be pupil comes carelessly and does not exert himself to take in what has been promised, and then proves to be just as careless as before, would anyone justly charge the teacher with falsehood? Not if he were sensible. For the one who was to learn did not come in the way the teacher urged. But someone might ask how one should ask, or for what. Listen to the very one who made the promise: "Seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness." It is clear, then, that whoever asks in this way, and for such things above all, will not miss the other things either, and in receiving them he will not fall short of his own salvation. But whoever asks for harmful and damaging things will not find the one from whom every good gift comes willing to grant them. Indeed, even one who asks for divine knowledge, or some spiritual gift, and does not receive it, fails to receive because he asks out of love of pleasure. For he asks wrongly, and asks for an evil that leads to his own destruction; and God is surely not a supplier of evils. "Adulterers and adulteresses. Do you not know that friendship with the world…" A little above he refuted certain falsely wise men who prostitute the divine Scripture and twist it to suit their own will, so as to draw from it provision for their pleasure-loving life; and this springs from nothing other than boastfulness and arrogance. For this reason he now goes on more forcefully and, in a manner foreign to his usual meekness, uses words of reproach, calling such people adulterers and adulteresses and putting them to shame by his reproof, using roughly such rebukes as these: "Tell me, foolish man: you want to show yourself wise, and [?] to live with strife and in constant warfare, and always to cling to present things? To chase after the things of the present life without ever turning back? This is not the way of the wise but of vulgar men, of those who lean toward friendship with the world. And it shows you to be adulterers against the beauty laid up in store, divine and chaste, since you prefer what is passionate, profane and shameful, and through your attachment to the present take upon yourselves enmity with God. Or do you not know that friendship with the world estranges us from friendship with God and makes us enemies of God?" By "world" here he means the whole of material life, as the mother of corruption. Whoever hastens to share in it becomes an enemy of God. For because of his zeal for useless things he is careless of divine things [?] and disdainful of them, which is how we behave only toward those we hate and toward our enemies. Since, then, there are two

objects that men pursue, God and the world, and two attitudes turn upon each of them, friendship and hatred, whichever of the two we are found pursuing, we are certainly seen to disregard the other. Zeal produces friendship, neglect produces hatred. So whoever holds fast to divine things both is and is called a friend of God; but whoever neglects God and is caught clinging tightly to the things of the world would be counted among God's foremost enemies. And since it has been shown that these things, and all the evil of such people, spring from the boastfulness and arrogance of the falsely wise teachers, he uses a second rebuke, wishing to sober them from the drunkenness of such things and free them from their stupor, and he says: "Or do you think that Scripture speaks in vain? Does the spirit that he made to dwell in us long enviously? But he gives greater grace." Through these words he indicates something like the following, speaking elliptically, again because of his habit of concise speech. He says, then: "By my own words I have directed you toward the upright and blameless use of your wisdom, so that you may not misuse it out of arrogance and so adulterate and falsify the word of teaching. And if you are looking for this in Scripture as well, listen. For it says: 'The Lord opposes the arrogant.' So I did not speak idly when I said that contempt for the Lord's teachings, born of arrogance, together with eager pursuit of the world, produces enmity toward God. For if he opposes the arrogant, and it is our enemies that we are accustomed to oppose, then surely the arrogant too must be counted among his enemies. For Scripture does not issue commands that are impossible for us and exceed our strength in vain, that is, to no purpose, or out of envy. Rather, it longs for, that is, seeks, the grace that is made to dwell in us through its exhortation; and finding this grace at work in us through spiritual humility, it gives greater grace. So if you are obedient to Scripture, humble yourselves before God, and you will find the grace that comes through his exalting you." Arrogance is vice exalted to the uttermost. It differs from conceit in that arrogance exalts itself over things it actually possesses, whereas conceit does so over things that do not exist at all. Diametrically opposed to it is freedom from pride, that is, humility, which is a great good. And since both arise in us by our own choice, everyone who exalts himself in boastfulness is not only condemned by the Lord but also humbled by him, while the one who has humbled himself through freedom from pride is exalted in due time, since the prizes it wins lead the one who practises it to spiritual heights. "Or do you think that Scripture speaks in vain, or out of envy?" Neither of these. Rather, it longs for, that is, seeks, the grace that has been made to dwell in you through its exhortation. The answer "no" is left unspoken here, just as in the passage

in Job: "Do you think I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be shown to be righteous?" For there too the answer "No" is left unspoken for this reason. "The spirit longs." By "spirit" he means good choice, as David too says: "With a governing spirit," that is, with a choice that masters the passions; and "a right spirit," that is, a right choice. "Submit yourselves, therefore, to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded. Be wretched, mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom. Humble yourselves before the Lord, [and he will exalt] you. Do not speak against one another, brothers. Whoever speaks against a brother and judges his brother speaks against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge. There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy. Who are you to judge another?" "Purify your hearts, you double-minded." Both earlier and here he calls "double-minded" those who do not make their choices in a single way, but are led and carried about by human trickery. For they are not of one way of life, like those whom the Lord makes to dwell in a house. That "soul" also means life, the passage in Job will teach us well enough: "Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his soul." "Do not speak against one another." He knows that arrogance, through disdain and slander against decent people, drives those given to it on toward utter contempt for them. To lead them away from this, he wishes to bring them to their senses by what follows, saying: "He speaks against the law and judges the law," that is, he condemns it, he despises it. For whoever condemns does so out of contempt. And which law? First, the one that declares: "Do not judge, so that you may not be judged." Then also the one in the Psalms: "Whoever slandered his neighbour in secret, him I drove away." And to show that this comes from contempt, he adds: "But if you condemn the law, you are not a doer of the law." For how will anyone bear to go on living under what he despises? "So do not," he says, "take an attitude of contempt, as though you were making laws against the law. That is not permitted to you, since there is only one lawgiver, God, who is able to save and to destroy those who transgress his law. For it belongs to the law and the lawgiver to make its transgressors liable to punishment, not to you. Besides having nothing more to offer than idle chatter, you also trip yourself up and bring the verdict down on yourself. For since you do the same things as the one you slander, in condemning him you condemn yourself far sooner." "Who are you to judge another?" This is said with contempt, meaning: "Being what you are, how do you dare to judge one who is subject to the same passions as you?"

"Come now, you who say, 'Today and tomorrow let us go into such and such a city, and spend a year there, and trade and make a profit' — you who do not know what tomorrow will bring. For what is your life? It will be a vapor that appears for a little while. Instead you ought to say, 'If the Lord wills, we shall live and do this or that.' But now you boast in your arrogance. All such boasting is evil. So for one who knows how to do good and does not do it, it is sin."

"You who say, 'Today.'" He does not take away free will. Rather, he shows that the whole matter is not in a person's own power, but also needs grace from above. It is permitted to work, to run, to trade, and to do everything that belongs to living, but one must not credit this to one's own labors. It must be credited to God's love for humankind. For Jeremiah says, "Lord, a man's way is not in himself." And the author of Proverbs says, "Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what the coming day will bring forth." "For what is your life?" He points to how vain and worthless our life is, and he shames us for wearing out our whole life on such things. He means that our toil is spent once and for all on passing evils that vanish as soon as they come into being. David mocks this too, saying, "Surely man walks about as an image; yet he is troubled in vain": that is, troubled about what has no being and exists only as a phantom, for that is what an image is. Or else: about what does not exist in its own right, but only as a likeness and semblance of the life that truly goes on. "For it is a vapor." A vapor is an airy substance that rises from moisture when fire warms it, and it has very little substance. Because it is so extremely fine, it quickly vanishes into the surrounding air, passing into it and dissolving, as a little dampness does in water. He likened our life to such a thing, and very aptly. He interrupted his discourse with this illustration, and then turned back and supplied what follows from it. For the whole passage runs like this: "Come now, you who say, 'Today and tomorrow let us go into such and such a city, and spend a year there, and trade and make a profit,' instead of saying, 'If the Lord wills, we shall live and do this or that.' But now you boast in your arrogance." That would be the natural order, but he does not keep it. He broke the flow of the discourse with the illustration and only afterward added what was missing, because he first wanted to show, by an image of the thing itself, how vain it is for us to be

distracted by arrogance about this world. For the sequence is this: "You boast in your arrogance." Who? "You who do not know about tomorrow. For what is your life?" and so on. With "What is your life?" he reduced life to nothing, and in this way he prepared the ground for the illustration of its worthlessness. Then he brings in the illustration itself, at the most fitting moment. "You boast in your arrogance." A boaster, and arrogance, means eagerness for things that have no real existence. That is why a boaster (alazōn) is so called: he "lives with wandering" (meta alēs zōn), that is, with something unstable and without substance. "All such boasting is evil." He takes up again the empty boasting that pride tends to give birth to, and, as if concluding his argument, he adds that it is evil. And if it is evil, it certainly comes from the Evil One as well. Those who have been dedicated to the Lord through holy baptism must not accept what the Evil One sows. He also adds, "So for one who knows how to do good and does not do it, it is sin." With this he again instructs the false teachers: Do not dare to teach what you have not first achieved yourself. "For blessed," it says, "is not the one who teaches, but the one who does and teaches." Deeds must come before words. In the same way the righteous man proclaims a faith that has been shown in practice. "For whoever breaks," says the Lord, "one of the least of these commandments and teaches people so" (that is, emptily, teaching what he has not labored at himself) "will be called least; but great is he who does them and then teaches." For the God-man himself also taught the things he had first begun to do. This, I think, is also the sense of "Let him who boasts, boast in the Lord": it means "according to the Lord." Paul is using the Lord as his model from long before, doing as he did and teaching as he taught. And when David says, "In the Lord my soul shall be praised," he means nothing other than that he would be praised for walking according to the Lord's commandments.

"Come now, you rich, weep and wail over the miseries that are coming upon you. Your wealth has rotted, and your garments have become moth-eaten. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a witness against you and will eat your flesh like fire. Look, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, cry out, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts. You have lived on the earth in luxury and self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts as on a day of slaughter. You have condemned and murdered the righteous one; he does not resist
"Come now." He laments the stinginess and meanness of the rich, urging them to wail, that is, to mourn, because they are storing up their wealth for what has no existence [?] and for decay, and

not spending it on those in need. For only wealth spent on such people is not lost; it is kept whole for the one who spends it. That is why the author of Proverbs says, "Send your bread upon the face of the water." That is, send it upon what seems like dissolution and decay (for that is what naturally happens to bread thrown on water), yet it is not lost. Instead, by being dissolved it gains refreshment for us at the time when, with our tongue scorched in the flame, we will need a drop of water. "Your wealth." The word "which" must be understood [?], so that it reads: "Your wealth, which you stored up [?], will devour your flesh." "Has rotted, and your garments." He means that the rotting of your wealth, the worm-eaten or moth-eaten state of your garments, and the rust on your gold and silver will testify against you and prove your refusal to share. So in the last days (he means the coming of the Lord) you will find that your wealth has been stored up for you like fire, for destruction. This is what happened to the rich man in the Gospel. "You have lived in luxury." This is an attack on the Jewish rulers. They fed on the poor and grew fat on honors from everyone, yet they were being made ready for slaughter by Roman hands. Above all, they condemned and killed the Lord, the only righteous one, who did not quarrel or cry out. "You have murdered the righteous one" beyond question refers to Christ. But by adding "He does not resist you," he extended the statement to the others who suffered similar things at the hands of the Jews. Perhaps he is also hinting prophetically at his own suffering.

On patience and endurance of sufferings, and on truth. Here also are exhortations suited to each person, together with faith, and the teaching that we must serve our neighbor's salvation.

"Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it until it receives the early and the late rain. You too be patient. Strengthen your hearts, for the coming of the Lord has drawn near. Do not grumble against one another, brothers, so that you may not be condemned. See, the judge is standing at the doors. As an example of suffering hardship and of patience, my brothers, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord. See, we call blessed those who endured. You have heard of the endurance of Job, and you have seen the outcome the Lord brought about, that the Lord is full of compassion and mercy."

He has denounced the luxury of the Jewish rulers and their harsh and inhuman treatment of the poor. Now he turns to the faithful and says: Brothers, do not be scandalized when you see these things, and do not lose heart, as if no punishment were stored up for them, or as if it were stored up but slow to come. For punishment is close on their heels. He means the Roman

invasion and the Romans' taking of the Jews into captivity. He calls this the coming of the Lord, as John does too, he who leaned on the Lord's breast. Speaking of his own departure from life, John reports the Lord as saying, "If I want him to remain until I come." And indeed his life was extended until the capture of Jerusalem and a little beyond. That the coming of the Lord, both here and in John's case, means the utter destruction of Jerusalem is also clear from the prophet who says, "Behold, the Lord is coming, and who will endure the day of his entry?" For the coming of the Lord brings punishment on the ungodly. John Chrysostom too, in one of his exegetical works, explains this very phrase, "until I come," and says that the saying means the utter destruction of Jerusalem. He confirms this from the prayer of the three young men, who say, "So let our sacrifice be before you today, and be accomplished behind you." He asks: What does "behind you" mean? After your wrath has passed. And when did that wrath come? When Nebuchadnezzar was laying Jerusalem waste. So much for the coming. Some of the Fathers also say that here he means patience toward one another and endurance toward those outside. For one is patient with those one could retaliate against, but one endures those one cannot retaliate against. That is why endurance is never said of God, only patience; endurance is said of human beings. "Until it receives the early rain." The early rain is repentance with tears in youth; the late rain is repentance in old age. But everything depends on God's love for humankind, which is why he says, "until it receives."

"But above all, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath. Let your 'Yes' be yes and your 'No' be no, so that you may not fall into hypocrisy." But someone will ask: If a person is forced to swear, what should he do? We will answer that the fear of God will be stronger than the pressure of the one forcing him. Someone might press further: The old law held that whoever swore by the name of the Lord deserved praise, so why does grace forbid it? We will answer that the old law commanded the Jews to swear by God in order to lead them away from swearing by idols. In the same way it ordered them to sacrifice to God in order to draw them away from sacrificing to demons. But once it had taught them well enough to worship God, it rejected sacrifices as useless, seeking as sacrifice not the offering of animals but a broken spirit. And what is that? A spirit that, through humility, is wholly consumed in the fire of love, like Paul's, who burned exceedingly when any of the faithful were made to stumble. "Let your 'Yes' be yes." That is: let your affirmation be firm and concern what is firm,

and let your denial concern things that cannot happen. "So that you may not fall into hypocrisy." By hypocrisy he means condemnation, which follows those who swear recklessly and who are carried into perjury by the habit of taking oaths. Or the word here may mean play-acting itself, where a thing is one thing but appears to be another. How, then, does one who swears fall into hypocrisy? Because his oaths make people believe he is truthful, but when he breaks them, he is shown to be a liar instead. Or else it is because he says "yes" about what is not firm, or "no" about what could not have been done. He forbids swearing by God because of perjury. He forbids swearing by heaven and the other things because people do not refer these to the honor of God either. For everyone who swears swears by something greater. [?] Elijah [?] ... And again he prayed

Prayer goes along with suffering hardship, so that the one being tried may pass through his trials more lightly. Then, once prayer has calmed what troubles us and the soul has reached its proper state and tranquility, let him sing psalms, so that his good things may be multiplied and he may delight in spiritual joy. For, as our own great Basil says, the consolations of hymns are granted to a cheerful and untroubled state of soul. Whoever has not advanced in this way and has not reached such a state, which David calls holiness ("Sing psalms to the Lord," he says, "you his holy ones"), only spins out long nonsense, singing idly and emptily, as the proverb puts it. "Anointing with oil." The apostles did this while the Lord was still living among people, anointing the sick with oil and healing them. "The effective prayer." The prayer of a righteous person becomes effective when the one he prays for works together with him through spiritual self-discipline. For if, while others pray for us, we give ourselves to luxury and ease and a dissolute

"Brothers, if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone turns him back, let him know that whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save a soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins."

"And someone turns him back, let him know." We must serve our neighbor's salvation. "That whoever turns a sinner back." Jeremiah says this too: "And if you bring out the precious from the worthless, you shall be as my mouth." For everyone who proclaims God's words becomes God's mouth. "For it is not you," he says, "who speak, but the Spirit of my Father who speaks in you." For this reason too, through David, he forbids the sinner to recite his statutes and to take his covenant on his lips.

The end, with God, of the Catholic Epistle of James.

[ARGUMENT] OF THE FIRST CATHOLIC EPISTLE OF PETER

Peter himself writes this epistle, a letter of teaching, to the Jews who were living in the dispersion and had become Christians. Since they had come to faith from Judaism, he strengthens them. First he explains and shows that faith in Christ was proclaimed beforehand by the prophets, and that through them the redemption by his blood was made known. He shows that [?] all things were preached as good news to the Gentiles too, things into which angels long to look. Then he advises them to live in a way worthy of the one who called them, and he urges them to honor kings as well. He tells wives and husbands to live in harmony. After a few moral exhortations, he indicates that the Lord also brought this proclamation of salvation and resurrection to Hades, so that those who had died earlier might rise and be judged in the body, and might abide by the grace of the resurrection. He adds that the end of all things has now drawn near, and that all must be ready, since they will give an account to the judge. And so he brings the epistle to a close.

CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST [?] CATHOLIC EPISTLE OF PETER

1. On rebirth in Christ, and on

endurance of trials, and on the saving faith proclaimed beforehand by the prophets.
[2.] [?] On hope and sanctification, and on the steadfast way of life we owe because of our adoption.
3. On living in Christ in a way worthy of our adoption, for the benefit of those outside as well, to [God's] glory.
4. On submission to rulers, on brotherly love, and on godliness. Here also: on the submission of slaves and on patient, uncomplaining endurance for Christ's sake. On the obedience of wives and their harmony with their husbands, and on salvation in the spirit after the pattern of Sarah. On how husbands should treat their wives. On gentle forbearance toward everyone. God's love for humankind in Noah's day is a type of this, and for us it is the compassion shown through the baptism of Christ [?].
5. On putting away wicked deeds and taking up the fruits of the Spirit according to the variety of gifts.
6. That through fellowship with Christ we must master the natural passions, and through hope in him bear the injuries others do us.
7. Exhortation to the presbyters on overseeing the flock. Here also: on the humility all owe to one another, for victory over the [?].
8. Prayer for the perfecting of believers.

THE FIRST CATHOLIC EPISTLE OF THE APOSTLE PETER

CHAPTER 1

On rebirth in Christ, and on endurance of trials, and on the saving faith proclaimed beforehand by the prophets.

"Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the chosen sojourners of the dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in sanctification by the Spirit, for obedience and for sprinkling with the blood of Jesus Christ."

The order of thought is: "Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in sanctification by the Spirit, for obedience and for sprinkling with the blood of Jesus Christ." The rest, which comes in between, should be set aside for now, for it shows

to whom the epistle is addressed. He used "according to the foreknowledge of God" to show that he is in no way behind the prophets, who were also sent, except in time. That the prophets too were sent, Isaiah says in the words "He has sent me to bring good news to the poor." But though Peter comes after them in time, he does not come after them in God's foreknowledge. In this respect he shows himself a match for Jeremiah, who was known and sanctified before he was formed in the womb and was appointed a prophet to the nations. And since the prophets, among other things, proclaimed beforehand the coming of Christ (that was why they were sent), Peter adds the purpose of his own mission. He says, in effect, "I was sent in sanctification by the Spirit, for obedience and for sprinkling with the blood of Jesus Christ." By these words he shows that the purpose of his apostleship is to set people apart. He expresses this by the word "sanctification," as in "And you shall be to me a special people, sanctified," which means "set apart from the other nations." So the purpose of his apostleship is to set apart, through spiritual gifts, nations that obey the cross and are sprinkled with Christ's passion. Whenever they needed cleansing from the stain of Gentile defilement, they were to be sprinkled not with the ashes of a heifer but with the blood of Christ's passion. At the same time, by mentioning blood he hints in advance at the martyrdom that those who believe in Christ will bear for his sake. For whoever follows the footsteps of the teacher in obedience would surely not refuse, if need be, to pour out his own blood for the one who poured out his own for the whole world.

"Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ." He writes to those of the circumcision, as blessed James did. But James wrote in general terms to all the Jews living anywhere in the world, while Peter writes specifically to the regions of Pontus and Galatia. He adds "Pontus" to "Galatia" because there is also another Galatia among the Celts. That is the original Galatia, from which these people migrated to this region. So he addresses his words to them and to the other nations named in the greeting, using this as a circular letter. Here is the sequence, filling in what is stated elliptically. This is done for the sake of clarity, and also by paraphrasing and recasting the verbal forms of the text: "Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, sent according to the foreknowledge of God the Father to set apart for him in the Spirit those who are obedient and who have received the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ as their cleansing: to you, the chosen sojourners of the dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, may grace and peace be multiplied. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who in his surpassing riches and mercy, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, has begotten us again, that is, remade us, and brought us over into a living hope,

into an inheritance imperishable and undefiled and unfading, reserved for those who are guarded in power through faith, which faith was revealed for salvation [?] in the last time. In which time, though for a little while now (since the present life is short and brief) you have been grieved (if indeed you had to be grieved through various trials), you rejoice, knowing this: that you are being tested [?], so that the proof of your faith, much more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire, may be found to your praise and honor and glory at the time when Jesus Christ is revealed.
