This Jesus Christ you love, though you have not yet seen him in the body. And believing in him whom you do not see, you rejoice with inexpressible joy, as you receive the end of your faith. And what is this [?]? The salvation of the soul. It was this salvation that the prophets also searched into and sought out. "To the elect sojourners." He said "sojourners" either because of the dispersion, or else because all who live according to God are called sojourners on the earth, as David also says: "I am a stranger with you and a sojourner, as all my fathers were." The word does not mean the same as "proselyte" (for that means one who has come from elsewhere, that is, one who has settled in a place), but something more, and humbler. A by-work is humbler than the work, and a by-path humbler than the road (for "work" and "road" are the principal things, done in the proper sense, while "by-work" and "by-path" are things that exist, as it were, alongside them). In the same way "sojourner" is seen as a kind of secondary existence beside "resident," and means something humbler. "Grace to you and peace be multiplied." "Grace," because we are saved freely, without having contributed anything. "And peace." For those who have offended their own Master and have been ranked among his enemies need this. "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has begotten us again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead." He blesses God, and so gives him thanks in return for the good things he gives. And what are his gifts? A hope: not like the hope of dwelling in Canaan through Moses, which was a mortal hope promising mortal things to mortals, but a living one. And where does it get its life? From Jesus Christ, who rose from the dead. For in the same things in which he rose, he will count worthy those who come to him through faith in him. What is given, then, is a living hope, an inheritance imperishable and undefiled, laid up not on earth, as it was for the fathers, but in the heavens. This is also why it is everlasting, which makes it greater than the inheritance on earth. Besides all this, believers are preserved and guarded, since the Lord also prayed for this when he said, "Holy Father, keep them." And it is "in power." What is this power? That the guarding lasts until the revelation of the Lord. For if the guard were not powerful,

it would not have held out for so long. [?] Since, then, the things given are of such a kind and so great, it is not at all unlikely that exultation also follows for those who receive them. But the Teacher's promise brings in grief, not joy, when he says, "In the world you will have tribulation." So to the exultation he adds "a little"; and since this is grievous, he presses on with "now," in harmony with his own Master. For he too says, "In the world you will have tribulation," but "your sorrow will turn into joy." Either, then, "now" was added because of the exultation, since the exultation that will follow lasts not for a little while but for a long, indeed an endless, time. Or else "a little" should be taken with the grievous thing that comes after it, so that it reads: "If need be, having been grieved a little now by various trials." But since the mention of trials caused alarm, he went on to give the reason for the trials: through them your proof becomes more evident, and more precious than gold. For gold too is prized more highly by people when it has been tested by fire. He also adds "if need be," because not every believer is tested by affliction, nor every sinner; and neither of them prospers forever either. Rather, the righteous who are afflicted suffer so that their crowns may be increased, while sinners suffer to pay the penalty for their sins. Yet not all the righteous are afflicted, lest you think vice praiseworthy and come to hate virtue. Nor are all sinners afflicted, lest the resurrection be disbelieved, as though everyone received their due here. "Into an inheritance imperishable and undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven for you, who are guarded by the power of God through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time. In this you rejoice, though now for a little while, if need be, you have been grieved by various trials, so that the proof of your faith, much more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire, may be found to praise and honor and glory at the revelation of Jesus Christ. You love him though you have not known him; and though you do not see him now, yet believing in him you rejoice with joy inexpressible and glorified, receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of souls." If the inheritance is in the heavens, the thousand-year restoration is a fable. "In which you rejoice, a little now, if need be." The order is: having been grieved a little now, if need be, that is, if this too must happen (for not all the saints are afflicted), you will rejoice in the last time. The present tense has been used for the future. Or it may also be taken as a present, as is noted below. "To praise and honor." With these words he shows why the righteous suffer hardship here. He consoles them by telling them that afflictions make them more illustrious, and at the same time he makes them more zealous

by adding "at the revelation of Jesus Christ," since that time, by displaying their labors, will bring great glory to those who have finished the contest. He also adds something else that draws them toward enduring afflictions. What is it? "Whom you love now, though you have not known him." For if you love him from hearing alone, though you have not known him with the eyes of the flesh, he says, think how great a love you will show when you see him, and see him revealed in glory at that. For if his passion drew you so strongly, how will his appearing in unsurpassable splendor affect you, when he also grants you the prize, the salvation of souls? Since, then, you are about to appear before such a one and to be counted worthy of such glory, if you now show an endurance equal to it, you will have the whole of what has been set before you.

"Concerning this salvation the prophets sought and searched diligently, who prophesied of the grace that was to come to you, searching what time, or what kind of time, the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing to when it testified beforehand to the sufferings of Christ and the glories after them. It was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but us in these things, which have now been announced to you through those who preached the gospel to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, things into which angels long to look." Since he had mentioned the salvation of the soul, and this was obscure and strange to his hearers, he brings in the prophets as having sought and searched concerning it. For they did seek, as Daniel did concerning the things to come; and that is why the angel who brought him revelations called him "a man of desires." And he goes on to say what they sought: "What time, or what kind of time, the Spirit in them was pointing to." "What time" means the time at the consummation; "what kind of time" means the time when the Jews, having been turned toward complete piety by their various captivities, became ready to receive the mystery of Christ. Notice that by saying "Spirit of Christ" he proclaims Christ as God. This Spirit pointed to the sufferings of Christ: through Isaiah, who said, "He was led as a sheep to the slaughter"; through Jeremiah, "Come, let us put wood into his bread"; and to the resurrection through Hosea: "On the third day we shall rise up before him, and we shall press on to know the Lord; we shall find him ready as the dawn." It was revealed to them, he says, not for their own sake but for yours. By these words he accomplishes two things: he shows the forethought of the prophets, and he shows that those now called to faith in Christ were foreknown by God before the foundation of the world. Through the prophets' forethought he leads them not to be disobedient toward what the prophets had taken such care over on their behalf, since sensible sons do not despise their fathers' labors either. For if the prophets, who stood to gain nothing from it, sought and found, and when they had found set it down in books,

we would not be in the right, he says, if we were contemptuous of these things. And for that reason do not make light of us either, who preach these things to you, and so render our gospel void. That, then, is the point of the prophets' forethought. Through their having been foreknown by God, he makes them afraid of showing themselves unworthy of God's foreknowledge or unworthy of his calling, and urges them instead to spur one another on to be counted worthy of God's gift. "Through those who preached the gospel to you." Since both the preachers and the prophets acted in the Holy Spirit, the prophets in prophecy and the preachers in the gospel, there is no difference between these and the prophets. Therefore, he says, you must bring the same zeal as those who listened to the prophets, so that you do not fall [?] into the punishment of those who disobeyed the prophets. It should also be noted that in these words Peter reveals the mystery of the Trinity: the Son and the Spirit by saying "Spirit of Christ," and the Father by saying "from heaven." "From heaven" should be taken not in a local sense but as referring to God's surpassing preeminence. "By the Holy Spirit sent from heaven." He means what happened on the day of Pentecost. "Into which angels long" stands for "which even angels longed for," that is, things whose knowledge and fulfillment even the angels themselves desired. That is why, when these things came to pass, they sang for overflowing joy, "Glory in the highest."

On hope and sanctification, and the steadfast conduct owed in return for adoption. "Therefore, girding up the loins of your mind, be sober and set your hope fully on the grace that is being brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ. As children of obedience, do not be conformed to the desires you had before in your ignorance; but as he who called you is holy, be holy yourselves also in all your conduct, because it is written, 'Be holy, for I am holy.'" The exhortation follows as a consequence of what he has already set out. He had said that the prophets ministered to you the things of your salvation, and that these were so wonderful that they became lovely even to angels; and the angels showed that these things were lovely to them too by singing to God, out of overflowing joy at the birth of Christ, "Glory in the highest." Having said this, he draws the consequence and says: Since, then, the things ministered to you all are of this kind, lovely and greatly longed for not only by men but also by angels, you too must not be careless toward them; rather, brace yourselves and act like men. This is what he means by girding up the loins, which Job too is commanded to do by God. And he made clear which loins he meant, saying that they are those of the mind. [Luke 2:14 [?]. Patrol. Gr. 119.]

"set your hope fully on the joy that is being brought to you." This is the joy he spoke of a little earlier, at the second coming of the Lord. Notice that he did not simply say "be sober," but "fully," since the law had given them only a faint and introductory sobriety. By "being conformed" he means accommodating oneself to present circumstances. This is what some foolish people say even now: "Go along with the times." He commands them, then, to renounce such vanities, whether they had been held by them before this knowingly or in ignorance; but now at least, he says, conform yourselves to him who called you, who is holy, and become holy yourselves. "And if you call on him as Father who judges impartially according to each one's work, conduct yourselves in fear during the time of your sojourning, knowing that you were redeemed from the futile way of life handed down from your fathers not with perishable things, silver or gold, but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot,"

He has built his exhortation on many grounds: first, from the angels who are full of longing for these things; then from Scripture; then from necessity. For since they call on God as Father, those who long for adoption must do things worthy of the Father. And fourth, because they received countless good things through the price paid down for them (this is the blood of Christ, which was given as a ransom for those who had sold themselves to the evil one through sin). He commands them to keep fear as a companion throughout their whole life: not the beginner's fear (for that has punishment as its companion), but the fear that perfects. For the saints who have been perfected are always afraid of falling short in any of the things that ought to belong to the perfected. Now notice that Christ said, "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son," and yet Peter here says that the Father judges. To this we shall reply as follows. Christ also said, "The Son can do nothing of himself unless he sees the Father doing it." This shows that the Holy Trinity is of one nature, and that the operations of the Godhead are not divided among the persons contemplated in it; rather, there all is identity and a peaceful, untroubled harmony. So he said without distinction that the Father judges, since whatever is said of one of the three is accomplished in a manner befitting God, being common to all of them both in fact and in our reckoning. Besides, since the Lord often called the apostles children, and said to the paralytic, "Child, your sins are forgiven you," and to the woman with the flow of blood, "Daughter, your faith has saved you," there is nothing incongruous in his too being called father of those he begot, whom he begot by imparting holiness to them. "In fear during the time of your sojourning." It is of this perfecting

fear that blessed David also spoke: "Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for those who fear him lack nothing." "He was foreknown before the foundation of the world, but was made manifest in the last times for your sake, who through him believe in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope are in God. Having purified your souls by obedience to the truth through the Spirit for unfeigned brotherly love, love one another earnestly from a pure heart, for you have been born again not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and abiding word of God, which endures forever. For all flesh is like grass, and all the glory of man like the flower of grass. The grass has withered and the flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord endures forever. And this is the word that was preached to you." To the death of Christ he joined his resurrection as well. For he is wary that the newly planted may easily turn to unbelief because of the shame of Christ's sufferings. And he shows that the mystery of Christ is not new either, since this too troubles the foolish. It comes from above and from before the foundation of the world, and was providentially stored up by God for the time he saw fit. It was made manifest to the prophets who searched into these things, as he said a little earlier; and now, he says, it is made manifest more plainly, since what was known, to God of course, before the foundation of the world has now been made manifest, that is, accomplished and carried through. And he adds for whose sake it was accomplished: for your sake. For your sake, he says, God raised him from the dead. And why for your sake? So that, he says, having purified yourselves by obedience to the truth through the Spirit, you may have your faith and hope in God. And why purified? Because you have believed in him who first began imperishable life for you through his resurrection from the dead, and so you are obliged yourselves to walk in newness of life, imperishable like him who called you. But if both Peter and Paul say that the Father raised the Lord from the dead, do not be troubled. They are using a more elementary manner of teaching here. Listen to Christ saying that he raises himself, in the words, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." And Luke too says, "To whom he also presented himself alive after his suffering." And again Christ says, "I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again." So it is by way of accommodation that they sometimes attribute the Son's resurrection to the Father, in order to show that the Father and the Son have one operation. The order is: foreknown before the foundation of the world, but made manifest in the last times for your sake, who believe in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, [Ps. 33:10. John 2:19. Acts 1:[?]]

so that, having purified your souls ("so as to" [hōste] has been used for "in order that" [hina]) by obedience to the truth, you may have your faith and hope in God. He also changes "to be" into "to have" because of "in order that." For if "so as to" is kept, the sentence is both ungrammatical and unintelligible. "For brotherly love." The whole reads thus: In order that you may have your faith and hope in God, having purified your souls by obedience to the truth, that is, having prepared yourselves beforehand for obedience to the truth through the Spirit. For there is also an obedience to wicked and false things, which is not through the Spirit, that is, not spiritual. Now the purification for obedience, that is, the preparation, the training, the practice, tends to draw in many other fellow workers as well, if it is to be spiritual and ungrudging. And this is the work of brotherly love: to share with one's neighbor too the good things one has found. That is why he presses on with "for unfeigned brotherly love." He introduces it abruptly, for this is characteristic of the blessed apostles, as we also find in blessed James: "Who is wise and understanding among you?" and "Come now, you who say, 'Today or tomorrow,'" and many other such passages. That spiritual people ought to share with one another, with all zeal, the good things they have found you may learn from what he says elsewhere too: "Let us consider one another so as to provoke love," that is, to sharpen and arouse it. Having said, "Born again not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and abiding word of God, which endures forever," he sets beside it, dismissively, the perishable nature of human glory and, so to speak, its unreality. In this way he entices his hearers to hold fast to the things he has set before them, since these are stable and endure forever, while the others are overtaken by corruption in their very existence. Here "grass" and "the flower of grass," which is even weaker in its existence than grass, are brought in to confirm what he says. David too likens our life to these. Then, having belittled our glory, he resumes and teaches more clearly what it was that regenerated them through the living and abiding word of God, which endures forever, and says: "And this is the word that was preached to you." He affirms that it endures forever, in agreement with the Lord. For the Lord too says, "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." It should be understood that "for unfeigned brotherly love" ought to be read thus: "Love one another earnestly from a pure heart, for unfeigned brotherly love." For the results of things usually follow the actions undertaken for their sake. Since, then, unfeigned brotherly love follows from earnest love for one another from a pure heart, it is right that "from a pure heart" should come first and "for brotherly love" follow. It should be noted, however, that he also uses the preposition "for" [eis] in place of "through" [dia], so that it means "through brotherly love."

"So put away all malice and all deceit, hypocrisy, envy and all slander. Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk, so that by it you may grow, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good. Come to him, a living stone, rejected by men but chosen by God and precious, and like living stones you yourselves are being built up as a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. Behold, I lay in Zion a cornerstone, chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." He has shown how far spiritual rebirth surpasses birth according to the flesh. He has set out how worthless mortal glory is: our birth is [?] and filthy, and our glory differs in no way from the shoots of spring. The word of the Lord, however, does not suffer the same fate. Every human opinion soon ceases, but the word of God does not; it always endures for ever, and its promises cannot fail. That is what the addition "which was preached to you" means. Having woven these things together in what came before, he now takes from each what is useful and serves our need, and gives his moral teaching. He says, "So put away all malice," and with these few words he points to so many and such great things. For it is [?] for those who have been reborn to incorruptible life to be caught in the snares of wickedness, and to prefer what is not to what is. Evil is not a substance; it is something that arises around the fault of a created substance. And there is a great difference between life that subsists in its own right and what merely exists alongside something else [?]. You yourselves, he says, deserve to be shown free of deceit, hypocrisy, envy and all slander. Deceit and hypocrisy are [?] from the truth and from the word that was preached to you. Deceit leads those it deceives to ruin, and hypocrisy proceeds by departing from what really is, while the saving word that instructed you is seen to move in the opposite direction. And what room will envy and slander have among you, who are held fast by the unbreakable bond of brotherly love and can be harmed by none of those who sow division? Envy and slander cause division and hatred of one's brother. Anyone who does not know this does not know Cain either, or the tragedy of his story. Through envy he tore himself away from brotherly union, and plotted deceit, hypocrisy and murder. Nor is the envious man free of slander, if Joseph's brothers are enough

to confirm these words, since they made countless accusations against him to their father. Therefore, he says, keep yourselves clean of all these things and come like newborn infants (for the Lord declared that the kingdom belongs to such as these). Be nourished by the pure word and grow, even to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. You have tasted, that is, you have advanced by practising the sacred commandments of the Gospel, and so you have come to know the goodness of the teaching by experience. Experience gives knowledge more effectively than any word, since what one has tried for oneself is more delightful than what comes through any word. So, having tasted the goodness of the Lord, do not [?] the good of that goodness toward others [?]. Bind yourselves closely to one another on the cornerstone, which was rejected by men but is precious to God, chosen, living, and proclaimed by the prophets. Be united and fitted together through love to complete the spiritual house, and pay no heed to the contempt of men, for Christ the cornerstone paid none when they rejected him. Once you have been fitted together, have made yourselves into a spiritual house and have shown yourselves a holy priesthood, offer spiritual sacrifices, which please God more than the sacrifice of irrational animals. Do not suppose that you can offer blameless sacrifices to God without keeping the bond with one another that love makes strong. For he says, "[lifting up] holy hands, without anger or quarrelling." How will someone who hastens to unite himself to God through prayer attain it, while he tears himself away from his brother through anger and evil thoughts? [?] "So the honour is for you who believe, but for those who do not believe [?], the stone that the builders rejected has become the head of the corner, and [?] a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence. They stumble at the word, because they disobey it, as they were destined to do. But you are a chosen race, a royal [?] priesthood, a holy nation, a people for [God's] own possession, so that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvellous light. [?]"

"... but now you have received mercy. Beloved, I urge you [?], as sojourners and exiles, to abstain [?] from the desires of the flesh, which wage war against the soul. Keep your conduct good among the Gentiles, so that where they slander you as evildoers, they may see your good works and glorify God on the day
"So the honour is for you who believe." The honour is plainly granted by God, who said, "I lay." For even now God says to the disobedient, "I lay for you in Zion a stone of stumbling,"

which is also a rock of offence and a stone of stumbling to the disobedient, "who stumble at the word" because they disobey the word, plainly, "as they were destined to do." So the whole passage will run like this: "Behold, I lay in Zion a cornerstone, precious and chosen, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." It is precious to you who believe, but to the disobedient it is a stone of stumbling. "The stone that the builders rejected has become the head of the corner," joining together those who believe in him. But it is a stone of stumbling to those who stumble at the word of the Gospel, clearly because they disobey it. "As they were destined to do": this is not said of people whom God marked out for this end. He who wills all people to be saved assigns no one any cause of destruction. Rather, disobedience followed in those who had prepared themselves as vessels of wrath, and they were placed in the rank for which they had prepared themselves. Man was made with free will, and free will cannot be forced. So no one could reasonably blame the one who judged him to deserve such a lot, since the man who did these things assigned it to himself by his own works. Christ is called the cornerstone because by his own touch he joins the two walls that make up the [?] house, that is, believers from the Gentiles and from the Jews, and binds them into a single fitted structure. Now he abolishes the useless sacrifices of the one, and turns the demonic superstition of the other into true religion. "But you are a chosen race." Having denounced the perversity of the disobedient, and shown how they became the cause of their own disobedience, he now passes on to praise those who have done what is right. He says, "You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood." It is as if he said: they stumbled at the cornerstone through hardness of heart and disobedience, and were not built upon it. Not so with you. Through your ready obedience you were built together into a royal priesthood, as a chosen race and a holy nation. But he does not want to make them slack with excessive praise. Above all he does not want them to think they hold the title "holy nation" and what follows by inheritance, as if they had been granted this honour because they were the race of Abraham and had never stumbled. So he adds a check to their pride and says: do not be proud of your race. You were not chosen for a royal priesthood because of Abraham. Those descended from him had the priesthood separated from the kingship. So it is not because of Abraham that you are a nation, a chosen race, and set apart for a royal priesthood, for Abraham was called none of these things. It is because of Christ. He was called a priest after the order of Melchizedek, and also a king, meek, righteous and bringing salvation, riding on the colt of a donkey. Since you have been reborn through holy baptism from him who holds both offices, you are rightly called a chosen race and a royal priesthood. This

you have through the mercy of him who called you out of darkness into his marvellous light. So by your works of light you proclaim his excellencies to other people. This, he says, you have from his love for mankind, since, as far as it depended on you, you are a people who once were not a people, and you have received mercy who had not received mercy. To make the reproach less hard to bear, he confirms it from Hosea. So proclaim his excellencies through good works. And how do they proclaim them? The Lord himself teaches this, through [?] saying: "Let your light so shine before men that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven." "A people for possession" stands for "for acquisition," that is, "for an inheritance." All are God's creation, but those who have been found worthy of it through their own [?] good works are his possession. "That you may proclaim the excellencies." This is why you were chosen, he says: so that through your obedience and your good works you may become heralds of the excellence of him who called you. "Beloved, I urge you." The sequence runs like this: Beloved, I urge you, since you are sojourners and exiles in this world, to abstain from the desires of the flesh, which wage war against your soul. It is the custom of teachers to bring in moral teaching after doctrinal teaching, and this is what the blessed apostle now does. He calls them "beloved," not "loved," because they are to be desired in every respect [?]. People loved for some particular reason are called "loved," not "beloved." He says that the desires of the flesh wage war against the soul, since, as the blessed Paul also says, the flesh desires against the spirit. The desires of the flesh are taken up with enjoying the things of the senses. They cloud our reasoning and reduce the soul to slavery. And I urge you to do this too, he says: keep your conduct good among the Gentiles. "To keep" has been changed into "keeping." He presents the pagans as slandering us. Anyone who wishes to learn about this could learn it in detail from what Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons in Gaul, wrote about the martyrs Sanctus and Blandina. Put briefly, it is this. The pagans seized the slaves of Christian catechumens and tried to force them to reveal some supposed secret about the Christians. These slaves had nothing to tell that would satisfy those compelling them. All they had heard from their masters was that the divine communion is the blood and body of Christ, and they thought it really was blood and flesh, so they told this to their questioners. The pagans took it that Christians literally did this and spread the story among the other pagans. Then they tried to force the martyrs Sanctus and Blandina to confess it under torture. Blandina answered them boldly and aptly: "How could people do such things when, for the sake of their ascetic discipline, they do not even eat the meat that is permitted?" By "the day of visitation" he means the scrutiny we undergo in the world. For when our life is examined by them,
and the facts turn out to be the opposite of what they supposed, they themselves are set right by what puts them to shame, and God is glorified.

On submission to rulers, and on brotherly love and piety. On the submission of slaves, and on patient endurance of wrongs for Christ's sake. On the obedience of wives and their harmony with their husbands, and on salvation in the Spirit as a type of [?]. On how husbands should treat their wives. On gentle forbearance toward everyone. Its type is God's love for mankind in the time of Noah, and for us it is the compassion of Christ through baptism. "So be subject to every human institution for the Lord's sake, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him to punish evildoers and to praise those who do good. For this is the will of God, that by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish people. Live as free people, yet not using your freedom as a cover for wickedness, but as slaves of God. Honour everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. [Honour] the king.

By "human institution" he means the offices appointed by the kings, or even the kings themselves, since they too were set in place, that is, established, by men. Hebrew usage also calls establishing "creating," as in "that he might create in himself one new man out of the two," where "create" stands for "establish" or "set in order." So he says: be subject to worldly rulers, but be subject for the Lord's sake. "For the Lord's sake" means "as the Lord commanded." And what did the Lord command? "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." So whatever they command that lies outside God's will and goes against God's ordinance is not to be obeyed. The Lord and his disciple give this command so that the pagans cannot say that Christianity overturns ordinary life and causes disorder and confusion. He also adds "for the Lord's sake" because of the faithful. It is likely that some of them would say: "You count us worthy of the kingdom of heaven and clothe us with great dignity through it. Why do you then cheapen us again by subjecting us to worldly rulers?" If anyone says this, he says, let him learn that this command is not my word but the Lord's. Peter himself also showed to whom, and to what sort of rulers, we must submit: to those who uphold justice. He also adds the reason. It is God's will. Our submission to rulers is a proof of our goodness. Above all, it shames the unbelievers. They slander us as arrogant, self-willed and insubordinate, but when they see us humble and obedient in

what is required, they will be silenced and put to shame all the more. "As free..." Be subject as free people, yet not using your freedom as a cover for wickedness, but as slaves of God. Honour not only rulers but everyone: love the brotherhood, fear God and honour the king. The golden-mouthed John explained "as free" like this. People might say: "We have been freed from the world and have become citizens of heaven, and you subject us to rulers again and urge us to obey them." That is why he says: obey in this way, as free people. That is, obey as those who have believed in the one who freed you and commanded you to do this. In this way you will not seem to use your freedom as a cover for deliberate wickedness, that is, for disobedience and insubordination, as an excuse for refusing to obey. The verse can also be explained in another way. A person is free in the Lord's eyes if he gives way to nothing improper. Now living in hypocrisy is not the mark of a free person. It belongs to someone subject to passions, whether the desire to please people or some other shameful pleasure. For their sake he disguises himself so as not to appear what he is, and he consents to be their slave. Such behaviour is foreign and alien to the servants of God. So he now commands us to show submission to rulers with a true and guileless disposition. We must not be hostile to them and obey only under compulsion, harbouring such wickedness within while we use a supposedly guileless and simple manner as a cover, so that our submission is only for show and does not come from the heart. "Fear God." Notice the precision here: he says to render fear to God, but honour to the king. So if fear must be rendered to God, who can destroy both soul and body, we will not give way to kings who urge us to do anything improper. Fear of God knows how to prevail even over the honour we owe to kings. Indeed, anyone who is pressed by them toward [wrongdoing] will deny them even that honour, as the saint said: "The evildoer is despised in his sight." "Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear, not only to those who are good and gentle,

he himself bore in his body on the tree, so that we might die to sins and live to righteousness. By his wound you were healed. For you were straying like sheep, but now you have returned to the shepherd and overseer of your souls." "Servants, being subject." We must supply the word "be," so that it reads: "Servants, be subject." The same applies to "Wives." "With all fear." Fear is spoken of in many senses. There is the fear that goes with knowledge. This is what he means here by fear "for conscience' sake," and it is also called reverence. There is the fear that comes from suffering, which arises in some people when they have experienced punishment. Even wild beasts feel this fear. There is also the preliminary fear, which comes upon those who approach the Lord because they know they are guilty of many things that call for punishment. With this fear the harlot in the Gospels approached Christ. And there is the perfecting fear, which is always present in all the saints. They are afraid of falling short in anything that ought to be found in those who have been taken up into perfect love. Since fear is spoken of in all these senses, if it is right for slaves to behave toward their own masters with every one of them, the apostle who now urges slaves to be subject to their masters with all fear would not forbid it. Both the preliminary fear and the perfecting fear, if present, would serve them well. The first would keep them from ever being suspected of some fault and suffering something irreparable. The second would keep them from even thinking of doing anything unpleasant to their master. Here, however, he means fear for conscience' sake, that is, the fear that arises with knowledge of right reason. This is the fear that crooked masters inflict on their servants when they have done nothing wrong. He judges this fear worthy of praise, and urges them to accept it with patience. Some slaves have fear because of sins they have already committed or are taking care not to commit, and endure whatever they may suffer for them. This too belongs to well-disposed slaves who are inclined to correct themselves. But it does not yet reach the philosophy of a man who knows he is guilty of no evil and endures with thanksgiving. This is the great thing. Few achieve it, and it finds acceptance with God, because it emulates the sufferings of Christ. For he himself also says that Christ did not suffer for his own sins. He committed no sin, but suffered for us and for our sins. "Because of the iniquities of my people," that is, on account of the people's lawless deeds, "he was led to death," says the prophet. So he presents this fear as praiseworthy. Yet he also wants slaves to be protected by the other kinds of fear, as is clear from his words "with all fear." And he did remarkably well in setting fear for conscience' sake against the other fears and declaring, with the truest reasoning, that this alone deserves praise, since those who bear the cause of their masters'

…of wrath against them, but of nothing at all. [?] “He handed himself over to the one who judges justly,” that is, to God, he says, who will repay each according to his works. For this is what is just. But perhaps someone will say: How can Peter now say that the Lord, when reviled, did not revile in return, and when suffering did not threaten? Yet we see him calling the Jews dogs and the Pharisees blind, and threatening Judas when he says, “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born”; and, “It will be more tolerable for Sodom than for that city”; and, “Where their worm does not die”; and countless other things. We will answer, then, that Peter does not say that the Lord never reviled or never threatened. He says that when reviled he did not revile in return, and while suffering he did not threaten. If he did revile at all, he was not retaliating against those who reviled him. He was rebuking and exposing those who would not repent. When he himself was reviled and heard, “You have a demon,” and, “By the ruler of the demons you cast out demons,” and, “Look, a glutton and a drunkard,” consider: did he revile them in return by saying anything slanderous against them? Not at all. To the first he said, “If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out?” To the man who called him [?] “a glutton and a drunkard,” he answered with the parable of the children in the marketplace complaining to their playmates that when they piped, the others did not dance, and when they mourned, the others did not beat their breasts. And when he was crucified and suffering [?], he prayed instead and did not threaten. He threatened Judas before the betrayal, before he had suffered any harm, in order to hold him back from his wicked undertaking. In the same way he declared that those who did not receive the disciples would suffer something worse than the people of Sodom. In part he was urging them to hospitality, and in part he was using fear to open up room for the preaching of the Gospel. So he did not make these threats while suffering harm, and what Peter says about patient endurance for the Lord's sake is entirely true, since he says that the Lord did not retaliate in any way against those who set out to abuse him. “So that, having died to sins” (that is, “having died”) “we might live to righteousness.” “By his wound.” For when he was scourged by Pilate he also bore wounds on his body. [?] “Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won over without a word through the conduct of their wives, when they observe the conduct in fear,

the pure conduct, that is yours. Let your adornment not be the outward kind, made of braided hair, gold jewelry or fine clothes. Let it be the hidden person of the heart, in the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is very precious in the sight of God. For this is how the holy women of old who hoped in God also adorned themselves,

by being subject to their own husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham and called him lord. You have become her children if you do good and are not frightened by any terror. Husbands, likewise, live with your wives with understanding. Pay honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since you are also joint heirs of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.”

Through all of these, kings, rulers, masters and slaves, he brings his moral teaching to completion. He has laid down for subjects that they are to be subject to kings and rulers, to the ones they should obey and in the matters in which they should obey. By this he has shown that the rulers themselves have the laws as a kind of spark of justice: whatever they do in accordance with the laws, they will not be condemned for [?]; but whatever they do against the laws, lawlessly, [?] without due judgment and tyrannically, they will perish for. For the law was given to them for the benefit of the nations, as Paul also declares [?], and the rulers, like the laws, were given for our benefit. It is not, as some wrongly claim, that authority over the things of earth belongs to the devil. Those who say this side with the devil, who said to the Lord, “All these things have been given to me, and I give them to whomever I wish.” Kings are not appointed at his command. Kings are needed to correct evils, while the devil [?] is eager to bring nothing of the kind into human life. Authorities and rulers were given by God: some to preserve justice and to correct and benefit those under them, others to punish and rebuke sinners through fear, and others again so that those who have committed outrages may pay the penalty they deserve. He has shown this, and that being subject to them is good and disobeying them is bad. He has likewise laid down that slaves are to obey their masters according to the flesh, and that those who suffer without cause at the hands of bad masters and endure it are the ones who win the most approval. In a way, he has also used these points to discipline the masters, by censuring bad masters. Now he moves on to the women's quarters. He says that wives should be eager for two things: to be subject to their own husbands, and to keep themselves strangers to all adornment and finery, imitating the holy women, since these too knew only obedience to their own husbands. And what is gained from this? The good emulation of those outside the faith, which also springs from our subjection to rulers, and the thanks they give to God because of us. This is the great boast of Christians: that because of us the name of God is not blasphemed but blessed. After speaking of the holy women in general, he names one in particular, Sarah, and adds something more inviting [?]: he calls them daughters of this Sarah, whether by faith or by descent. For daughters must imitate their own

[?] mothers. Along with the becoming adornment that suits Christians, he also urges them to be generous to the poor, and not to be wary at all of the reckoning their husbands might demand of them for it. This is what “not frightened by any terror” indicates, for husbands may well sometimes demand an account of their expenses. In this way he raises the level of his discourse and urges the stinginess and pettiness of women toward a more generous use of the household's goods. He then checks the severity of husbands toward their wives as well, and says, “Husbands, live with them with understanding.” That is: take into account how light-minded women are, how easily they are carried away in everything and how easily they slip into pettiness, and be patient with them. Do not bitterly demand an account of the household goods entrusted to their stewardship. As we said before, he advises this so that, since the women deal generously in giving to the poor, their husbands will not be exacting inspectors. But to me he also seems to bring in something deeper with these words, and to hint, more modestly than Paul, at married relations. Paul states it openly: “Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement,” and so on. Peter, as I said, speaks more modestly. By saying “understanding” he hints at the matter. He advises that, since the female sex is more inclined toward this, husbands should not withdraw from their wives with harsh reproaches. They should first treat them indulgently as the weaker party, and then persuade them gently to accept such abstinence. This is what he means to show (the gentleness, I mean) by saying “paying honor,” for unless honor is seen in someone, gentleness does not follow either. So husbands must treat their wives this way in such matters of intercourse, whether as the weaker party or as joint heirs of the grace of life. What follows shows that we have not taken this sense wrongly, for it says, “so that your prayers may not be hindered.” What hindrance to prayer does a husband's severity toward his wife bring? Rather, it is attention and eagerness toward her that bring a great hindrance at the time of prayer [?]. That is how it seems to me. But if a better interpretation is judged right, I do not begrudge it. “Without a word.” Either with all talk and all argument laid aside, or because a demonstration through deeds carries more authority than elaborate words, for a silent deed is better than an ineffective word. “But the hidden person of the heart.” For all the glory of the king's daughter is within. Like blessed David and Paul, Peter too knows of an inner person distinct from the outer one. “They adorned themselves.” You see that here he calls subjection adornment

…knowing that you were called to this, so that you might inherit a blessing. For whoever wishes to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit; let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer, but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil. And who will harm you if you become imitators of what is good? But even if you should suffer for the sake of righteousness, you are blessed. Do not fear what they fear, and do not be troubled, but sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to make a defense to anyone who asks you for an account of the hope that is in you, with gentleness

…so that, in the very thing for which they speak against you as evildoers, those who abuse your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame.” Having finished his separate instructions to husband and to wife, he now addresses his exhortation to everyone in common: men, women, the old, those past their prime, the young, kings, rulers, subjects, citizens, foreigners, natives, rich and poor. That is why he adds, “Finally.” This means: Why should I address each one separately? I say it simply to all. For this is the end. The goal of salvation looks to this for everyone, and this is the law of love for everyone. From it springs every virtue: humility, sympathy, compassion, and the other virtues he lists. Of these, like-mindedness is a zealous agreement about something, without discord. Sympathy is mercy toward those who suffer, as if one were suffering oneself. Brotherly love is the disposition we owe our neighbors as if they were our brothers. Compassion is the impulse of the soul to do good to those of our own kind. Courtesy is gentleness and affability toward everyone, which can be shown to strangers as well as to friends. Humility, or lowliness of mind, is bearing another's reproaches, acknowledging one's sin and putting up with accusations, which would also be good sense. Reviling is an eagerness for slander that comes from evil habit. Adorned, then, he says, with the virtues just mentioned, you will be shown to be beyond the reach of evil, and beyond this, he says, you will also be admired, since you are guided by the divine way of life. For whoever is spoken well of by all is surely admired too. For this he brings in David as a witness, who says, “Who is the one who wishes to see life?”: not the life that even irrational animals live, but the life that a godly person lives; “and days”: not evil days but good ones. For the days of this age, as the patriarch Jacob says, are few and evil. Having completed the prophetic citation, which contains “the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous” and “his face is against those who do evil,” he adds to it: If you live in this way, you will have God gracious toward you and attentive to you. And when that is so, with him on your side, who could be brought against you to do you harm? For all things are in his hand. Death and life are in the hand

of the Lord. But since for some the circumstances that [?] because of the [?] you boast, but having worked the sanctification of the Lord in your inner chamber [?], sanctify him in this way. This sanctification comes about through separation from the pollutions, that is, from the wicked customs of the Gentiles. You sanctify him through your good conduct, when other people glorify him, as the God-man himself commands: “Let your light so shine before men.” With “ready,” the earlier “You shall all be like-minded” is understood: the “you shall be” applies to this too, so that it reads, “You shall always be ready.” He wants to urge believers always to answer readily about the faith, since we may be asked for an account of it at any time. And when they answer, they should do so with gentleness, as though God himself were present, for no sensible slave behaves presumptuously in his master's presence. He adds the gain from this: the recognition and goodwill of unbelievers toward us. We should note that this does not contradict what the Lord said. The Lord says not to worry about what we will say in our defense when we are brought before rulers and authorities, while Peter now commands us to be prepared for this. But the Lord was speaking about martyrdom. He says that the martyrs will be given power and speech greater than human wisdom, and freedom from concern about the terrors around them. Peter, by contrast, is speaking about teaching. For to appear to know something without understanding and examination brings blame, since the knowledge of the unintelligent is unexamined words. Besides, since people accused us of many wicked things and also declared our hopes empty, he says we should give reasoned answers about these matters, and have a life that agrees with what we praise. This is what he calls conscience. “Knowing that you were called to this.” This does not follow on the construction immediately before it. Rather it goes with “Finally,” that is, the most comprehensive point: “You shall all be like-minded,” and so on, “knowing that you were called to this,” to blessing, that is, to speaking well of everyone. Paul too says, “Bless those who persecute you.” By doing this you will inherit the name that all will call you by: “those who bless.” For it is not right that one

who holds fast to eternal life should slander anyone with his tongue. That is why David also advises that whoever wishes to be lovingly devoted to the true life should keep his tongue clean of reviling, and so on. If you are prepared in this way, you will have the Almighty and All-seeing attentive to you and looking on you gently, not angrily, as he looks on evildoers. If that is so, who can harm you? And even if affliction should come upon you, who work at and imitate what is good, do not lose heart. Rejoice instead: first, because these things are not evils, and second, because through them you are blessed and not wretched. Therefore, sanctifying God in your hearts, do not fear human fear and do not be troubled. You will also be ready always to make your defense, to give an account to anyone who questions you about your hope. And give it while also displaying good conduct. For when you do this gently and with forbearance, you will be assured that your conscience is good, and you will put to shame those who hold evil opinions about you. “Having a good conscience.” That is, conscious of good in yourselves and not of evil, as those who slander you would have it. “Those who abuse.” That is, those who make mischief with words, who examine you bitterly. “For it is better, if the will of God should will it, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil. For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, in order to bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the

This reason is given not for what was said just before but for what was said a little earlier: that “even if you should suffer for the sake of righteousness, you are blessed,” because it is better to suffer harm for doing good than for doing evil. Or, if someone wishes to refer the reason to what immediately precedes, then “doing good” must not be taken as doing good to someone else, but absolutely, in the sense of “doing good works,” and “doing evil” likewise. He adds, “if the will of God should will it,” to show that nothing happens to us without God's leaning toward it. It happens either to lighten our sins, or for the public proclamation and glory of [?], or for the salvation of others. This last is twofold. Either a righteous person suffers [?] to correct other sinners, as it is said, “If the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the sinner appear?” And this too brings a twofold benefit: to the righteous person who suffers, an increase of righteousness through endurance; to the sinner who sees it, conversion, as we said. So the righteous person suffers either for these reasons or for the

salvation of others, as Christ did. For this reason Peter now adds the example of Christ: Christ too did not suffer what he suffered for his own sins but for ours. That is why he adds, “the righteous for the unrighteous.” For, as he showed later by citing the prophet, Christ committed no sin. And to show the effectiveness and power of the one who suffered, he adds “once.” So great, he says, was the power of the one who suffered on behalf of humankind that, many as their sins were found to be, the Lord's one suffering alone was enough to blunt the whole force of our sins. Since he suffered in order to bring us to God his Father, he showed that not everyone who suffers suffers for sins. And since Christ is twofold, God and man, by his suffering he also gave us a twofold grace. By dying as man he freed us from death and corruption, inaugurating the resurrection for us. Through his own resurrection he gave us an example, so that those who die no longer undergo a death without hope of resurrection. “Made alive”: that is, rising from the dead by the power of the Godhead (for he rose from the dead not as man but as God), he made alive together with himself those in the [?], raising them with himself. For, as the divine evangelist says, many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised and appeared to many. Having brought his argument this far, two questions remained: how by dying he benefited those who had fallen asleep before him, and, since there is much inquiry on this point, if the Lord became man for the salvation of all people, what salvation those who died before him obtained. He resolves both with a single answer, saying that the Lord's death accomplished both: hope of resurrection through his own rising, and also the salvation of those who had fallen asleep before. Some during their lifetime adorned their lives with good works, so that if Christ had come into the world in their day, they would not have missed out on his life-giving preaching. These obtained salvation even then, through the Lord's descent into Hades. The divine Gregory also thinks so, for he says: “Does Christ, when he appears, simply save everyone” (clearly meaning in Hades), “or there too only those who would believe?” By “those who would believe” he means those who had so prepared themselves that if he had come in their time, they would have believed. And there is nothing blameworthy in this. Salvation is not handed out by lot, since even though he came to all the living, he does not save everyone, but only those who would believe. It was also the work of each person's free choice, as a rational being, not to be insensible to the generosity of the Maker who gives good things, but to make oneself worthy of the giver's goodness. He put in “who were disobedient” to answer an objection. For someone might well ask: And who else preached before Christ, that they then disobeyed? Or did they become deserving of condemnation, or were they condemned?

…before Christ? He could have refuted them, as Paul does, from the rational powers sown within us: having been made judges of good and evil and then not doing the good, such people deserve condemnation. But he does not do this, since that belongs to a higher and more philosophical kind of reasoning than the Jews could follow. Instead he proves their disobedience from Scripture, and not from the times of the Prophets but almost from the creation of the world itself. Though there were countless people at that time too, only eight persons, persuaded by what was proclaimed through the building of the ark, were saved. And since salvation came through water, he at once applies this to holy baptism and says that that water foreshadowed your baptism. For baptism too drowns the disobedient demons and saves the faithful who come to the ark of the Church. At the same time he says: just as water washes away dirt, so does baptism. Yet it does not bring about the removal of the filth of the flesh. Rather, it symbolically represents the washing away of the soul's stain. It is also a kind of earnest and pledge of a good conscience toward God. For those who are conscious of good in themselves, that is, those who hold to a blameless life, seek this by every means and, as it were, ask for it (asking follows naturally on seeking something), and these are the ones who run to holy baptism. And what, he says, gives us this seeking and asking for divine baptism? The resurrection of Christ. Before his resurrection and passion he declares, "Unless one is born of water and the Spirit." But after the resurrection he says, "Baptize all the nations that come, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." Having gone through the account of the dispensation, I mean the Lord's journey into Hades and why he went there (that even while in Hades he was there for salvation), he again takes the Lord's death as a fresh starting point for an exhortation to virtue. He says: if Christ died for us in the flesh (not in his immortal and divine nature), then surely you too, repaying him by dying to sin for his sake, will no longer be captured by human desires, but will live the rest of your time in the flesh according to the will of God alone. "Put to death in the flesh": put to death in the nature of the flesh, that is, in the human nature, but raised by the power of the Godhead. For God is spirit, as the very wisdom of theology has taught us. "In which he also went and preached to the spirits in prison, who had once been disobedient, when God's patience waited once in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built, in which a few, that is,

eight souls, were saved through water. This water, as an antitype, now saves us too: baptism, not the removal of the filth of the flesh, but the pledge of a good conscience toward God, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels and authorities and powers made subject to him." "In which he also… to those in prison": this stands for "Therefore" and gives the cause. Having said that he died for us, the unjust, and having thereby indicated that he underwent death for the salvation of all people, he says that therefore he also preached to those held in Hades. "Which as antitype": the order of the words is as follows. Which, as an antitype, baptism now saves you too, being not the removal of the filth of the flesh but the pledge of a good conscience toward God, or according to God. "Pledge" means earnest, surety, proof. "With angels made subject to him": to the one who was united to the man.

On putting off evil deeds, and taking up the fruits of the Spirit according to the diversity of gifts. "Since therefore Christ suffered for you in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same thought: that whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin, so as to live the rest of his time in the flesh no longer for human desires but for the will of God. For the time that is past [?] of our life is enough for having done the will of the Gentiles, walking in licentiousness, lusts, drunkenness, revels, carousing and lawless idolatries. They are surprised at this, that you do not run with them into the same flood of dissipation, and they blaspheme. They will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and

The order of the words is as follows: since Christ then died in the flesh, you too prepare yourselves according to the same thought. For you too have died, clearly to the world. And whoever has died has ceased from sin, and so on. "For it is enough for us": that is, quite enough, in our past life, we did the will of the Gentiles; that is, we lived like Gentiles, having walked as the Gentiles do. That is why these Gentiles are now surprised. "The same thought": instead of "according to the same thought", meaning with the same aim. It is said elliptically, with the preposition "according to" left out. "Whoever has suffered in the flesh": instead of "Whoever has died". He says something similar to Paul: "If we have died with Christ, we shall also live with him," and, we shall be dead to sin but alive to God. "For it is enough for us": as if he were saying, What then? Have you not had enough of spending so much time among the pleasures of life? Or did you not live licentiously like the Gentiles? And he lists the kinds of licentiousness, to put them to shame. "Drunkenness": drunken-

-ness means the uncontrolled cravings for wine. "They are surprised at this": "they are surprised" stands for "they marvel". What he is saying is this: having once for all renounced the Gentile practices in which you once lived, hold fast to the dignified life you have chosen. For in this way even the Gentiles themselves will marvel at you, when you do not run with them into the same flood, or confusion, of impiety as theirs. And so, as they marvel and are at a loss over your change, they are not only put to shame but also blaspheme, that is, they mock you. For godliness is an abomination to a sinner. But they will not go unpunished for such blasphemy. They will give account to the judge of all, who will sit for this very purpose, immovable and firm. For this is what "ready" means here, as also in "who makes the mountains ready by his strength", and in "Your throne is made ready." So those who scoff at you will give account to him who judges the living and the dead, immovably and firmly. How he is judge of the living and the dead, what follows will show. "For this is why the gospel was preached even to the dead, that they might be judged according to men in the flesh, but live according to God

The order of the words is as follows: these who blaspheme you will give account to him who will judge all, living and dead. For the dead too are judged. This is clear from the Lord's coming into Hades. He went there too, clearly in his death on the cross, and preached just as he had preached on earth to the living. But he preached not by word but by deed. And just as, when he came into the world, he came for justification to those ready to recognize him, but for condemnation to those who did not know him, so too with those in Hades. To those who had lived according to the flesh, in a merely human way, he came for judgment [?]. To those who had lived according to the spirit, that is, a spiritual and virtuous life, he came for glory and salvation. So he may rightly be called judge of both the living and the dead. Another interpretation. The ancient Fathers [?] interpreted "And the gospel was preached to the dead" as a separate passage. They paid no attention to its connection with what comes before, nor to the fact that, since it is stated as a cause, it must be referred to what precedes it, as anything stated by way of cause must be. But, as has been said, they interpreted it as a separate passage, in this way. They said that the divine Scripture speaks of the dead in two ways: either those who have died in their sins, who will never see life, or those who have been conformed to the death of Christ, who have died to the world, that is, to worldly desires, and live to Christ alone. As Paul says: "The life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God." So they say that those who have died to Christ in this way condemn themselves in the flesh for their own former careless and slothful life, and this is what it means for them to live in the spirit, that is, in the life according to Christ. For condemning their former

ways makes them more cheerful about the [?] but will not be ranked in part [?]. [?] "that they might be judged in the flesh" is to be taken thus: when the Lord visited those in Hades, those who had lived carnally in the world were condemned, while those who had lived spiritually lived, either by coming back to life with the Lord (for many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised), or in good hope. "Be judged" and "live" are taken with one tense in place of another, the future in place of the past, which is customary in divine Scripture. "For the end of all things," he says, "is at hand," that is, of both those justified in this life and those in Hades. For at the second coming what is laid up for each will be fulfilled. But suppose someone rejects the Lord's preaching in Hades, saying that it can do the dead no good, because, according to the prophet David, in Hades no one confesses. That person understands the preaching in Hades crudely, and takes "confession" to mean not the praise of God but the declaring of sins. He has not heard "The dead will not praise you, Lord." The meaning of "In Hades who will confess to you?" is this: confession is thanksgiving to God for being delivered from hardships. In the present life all deeds are carried out and performed, but for the dead everything is idle. So it is fittingly said, "In Hades who will confess to you?", since nothing is done there from which someone might be delivered and then give thanks.
"The end of all things is at hand. Be sober-minded, therefore, and watchful in your prayers. Above all

[?] love will cover a multitude [?] to one another without grumbling. [?] has received a gift, [?] to one another as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. If anyone speaks, let it be as the oracles of God. If anyone serves, let it be as from the strength that God supplies, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever.

"The end" means the fulfillment, the consummation. Or else he means that the end of all the prophets has drawn near, and in true reckoning this is Christ. For he is the perfection of all things, not as the Greeks babble. Some of them say that pleasure is the end, like Epicurus, and others say knowledge, whether contemplation or virtue. Since, then, Christ, the perfection of all things, has come, conform yourselves to this perfection, he says, and show yourselves lacking in nothing in every respect: in sober-mindedness, in watchfulness in prayer (for prayer belongs to the sober, that is, the wakeful, not to those held in a stupor by the drunkenness of worldly things), and in love for one another. Paul calls love the fulfillment of the law, while Peter says it can cover sins. For mercy toward our neighbour makes God merciful to us, and mercy would not go forward as it should unless it came from much love. Having mentioned love, he adds the things that follow from love, such as hospitality, which he commands to be practised without grumbling, since this belongs to true love. He also commands that each share the gifts he has in plenty with a brother who lacks them. For example, he who has the gift of teaching (this is what "as the oracles of God" is meant to indicate) should share it with the one who needs it. He who possesses a supply of food should give to the one who has none, not grudgingly, but as far as the power of God's supply allows. I urge these things, he says, so that in all things, whether in [?] or in your works, God may be glorified. Having given these instructions, he saw that some were scandalized by the afflictions brought upon them [?], since the law lays down a promise of an untroubled life for those who serve the Lord. Earlier, when he was giving rules for slaves, he exhorted them about this briefly. Now he treats it at greater length, and says "Beloved", showing at once by this name that these things happen to them not because they are hated but because they are greatly loved. "Do not be surprised" means "Do not marvel": do not consider it something strange [?]. Then, by calling the afflictions a "fiery ordeal", he showed [?] that they are brought upon them for testing.

Testing makes what is tested highly prized, as with gold and silver. To these points he added what is more blessed than all of them: that those who suffer these things rival their teacher Christ, and are dishonoured with him now so that they may also be glorified with him in the age to come. With this he completed the whole [?]. "Fervent love" means lasting love, love that stretches far. "As each has received a gift": among the things that lie in our power and are under our control, failing to do them carries the full weight of injustice. This is not only true of possessing money. It is also true of other natural advantages, that one is obliged to provide for the person who lacks them, because he himself did not have them but received them from God, so that he might provide for those in need.

That through fellowship with Christ we must master the natural passions, and through hope in him bear the injuries done to us by others. "Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal among you, which comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. Rather, rejoice insofar as you share in the sufferings of Christ, so that you may also rejoice and exult at the revelation of his glory. If you are reproached for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you. On their part he is blasphemed, but on your part he is glorified. Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or an evildoer, or as [?]. But if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in this name. For it is time for judgment to begin with the household of God; and if it begins first with us, what will be the end of those who disobey the gospel of God? And if the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear? Therefore let those who suffer according to the will of God also entrust their souls to a faithful Creator in

"The fiery ordeal among you" means the testing. "For the name of Christ" means for being called Christians. "On their part he is blasphemed": we must supply "he seems", so that the sense is that the Spirit of God seems to be blasphemed on the part of the ungodly, but is glorified on your part. How so? Because when they falsely accuse you, shame is poured upon them, but glory upon you. "Or as a meddler": one who busies himself with other people's affairs so as to find an occasion for abuse. This is the mark of a foul, crafty, malicious and reckless soul, ready for every evil. "For it is time for judgment to begin with the household of God": this makes them anxious and fearful, rousing them from sloth and a slack way of life. That is why he adds: if the examination of how people have lived begins first with you, who are the household of God, what must we think the end will be of those who disobeyed? Here we take "judgment" not as condemnation, but as examination, inquiry, reckoning. And it begins first with

the household of God. For, as our great Basil says, we are naturally most vexed with those closest to us when they sin against us. And none are closer to God than the faithful who make up the household of God, that is, the Church. That is why the Saviour said: "He will say first to those on his right." Here, by "judgment" he means the trial, the afflictions brought upon the faithful by the ungodly. The Lord also foretold that these would come, saying, "They will hand you over to councils," and so on. Then, as if consoling them, he adds: if he does not spare you, who are so close to him, think what the end of the ungodly will be. And he confirms this from Scripture, which says: "If the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?" What he means the scriptural passage to signify is this: if the righteous attains salvation through toil and labour (for the kingdom of God is taken by force, and it is through many afflictions that one attains it), what will those attain who live an easy and pleasure-loving life? What is said about the ungodly is to be understood of the age to come. So, he says, if this is so, let us too, suffering according to the will of God, not grow slack, but entrust our souls as to a faithful Creator in well-doing. He said "according to the will of God" either to show that our sufferings are not outside God's providence, but [?] are awarded to us by him as a kind of test, or because, since we suffer for the sake of God's will, we should also leave the outcome to him. For he is faithful, that is, sure and truthful in his promises, and will not let us be tempted beyond what we can bear. And how must one entrust oneself to God? "In well-doing", he says. And what is this? It is to commit oneself in humility, not thinking highly of oneself for what one suffers. Rather, the more one seems to suffer, the more one should keep counting oneself unprofitable, and say: "You are righteous in all that you have done to us." The ungodly and the sinner differ in this: the ungodly is the one wholly outside God, while the sinner holds to God to some extent, but otherwise despises and transgresses his laws. Yet the same person can be both ungodly and a sinner. For whoever works lawlessness is altogether ungodly, since he does not reckon, while he sins, that there is a God.

An exhortation to the elders concerning the oversight of the flock, which also speaks of the humility all should share toward one another, for victory over the devil. "[?] a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and also a partaker in the glory that is to be revealed: shepherd the flock among you

of Christ, exercising oversight not under compulsion but willingly, not for shameful gain but eagerly, not as lording it over the clergy, but being examples to the flock. And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory. Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders, all of you being subject to one another. Clothe yourselves with humility, for God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of

Since he is about to discuss humility, which he had already touched on in saying "in well-doing", he calls himself a fellow elder. By this he means to indicate either his age or the honour of a bishop, for the book of Acts also knows bishops being called elders. Then, wishing to show his own pre-eminence, and that he calls himself a fellow elder out of humility, he adds his own rank: "a witness of the sufferings of Christ". By this he means: if I, who tell you of such sights, do not disdain to call myself a fellow elder, then neither are you right to exalt yourselves over those ranked under you. For this reason Christ too, his teacher, when teaching humility, puts forward the words: "If I, then, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet." He adds "a partaker in the glory that is to be revealed" to show how excellent humility is, as Paul [?] also says: "When Christ is revealed, then we too shall be revealed." The one who shepherds not under compulsion is the one who sets himself before those under him as a model of good works, and so has his disciples urging one another on in zeal for his school. And the one who shepherds not for shameful gain is the one who does not go about in arrogance, exalting himself over those under him, but lives in humility. He has humility as his companion, and she needs no expense for costly garments or a Sybaritic table, things that cheer on arrogance and seek to be supplied by shameful gain. He calls the sacred order "clergy", just as we do now. By adding "being examples to the flock", he explains what it means not to shepherd the flock under compulsion. In "And when the chief Shepherd appears", "and" stands as a causal conjunction, in place of "so that". That is: so that, when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown. It is the same in "Look upon your servants and upon your works" in Psalm 89, for there "and" stands in place of "therefore". "Clothe yourselves" means wrap yourselves, put on. "…so that he may exalt you in due time, casting all your anxiety on him, because he cares for you. Be sober, be watchful, for your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him

The words "In due time" are added because they point to the exaltation in the age to come. That alone is true exaltation, since it is unchanging and lasts forever. Exaltation here is neither secure nor stable: humiliation always lies in wait for it, and it is brought low faster than it was raised up.
