For the humility that wins true height, the Lord himself is the trustworthy guarantor, since he says, "Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted," and, "Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be last of all." As we said, by "In due time" he hinted that the exaltation that comes from humility is promised for the future. The time of unchanging things is in the future, incorruptible age, for what is incorruptible has nothing perishable about it. Then he removes the fear that humility might bring. Perhaps he saw that some were anxious that, if they humbled themselves in this present life, they would suffer some harm. So he says, in effect: Do not be afraid. If you cast all your care on the Lord, you will have entrusted yourself to a safe guardian. "For he cares," that is, the concern for all these things rests with him. "Be sober, be watchful." Some are in the habit of sleeping spiritually (that is, gaping after vain things) and so weighing down the sobriety of their souls. On them the wicked and most grievous beast of despair pounces. To guard against this, Christ's disciple urges us to stay awake always and to beware of the sower of tares. Otherwise, while we sleep, that is, while we live carelessly and lazily, he may secretly sow evil thoughts in us and lure us away from the true life. For he never stops, he says, prowling around like a roaring lion, looking for someone to devour, and you must resist him through the firm steadfastness of the soul. The holy martyr Justin also speaks of this relentless scheming and gives the reason for the devil's diligent villainy against us. He says that before the Lord's coming the devil did not know so clearly how strong his own punishment would be, because the divine prophets had proclaimed it in riddles. Isaiah, for example, veiled the whole drama of the devil by presenting it, like a tragedy, in the person of the Assyrian. But when the Lord came, the devil heard plainly that the eternal fire was laid up and prepared for him and his angels. Since then he never stops plotting against the faithful. He wants many partners in his own apostasy so that he will not be put to shame by being caught in it alone, and he comforts himself with this cold and spiteful consolation. "Knowing that the same sufferings..." It seems that the people Peter is writing to were beset by many afflictions for Christ's sake. That is why he comforts them about this again and again. Earlier he did so by saying that, in suffering, they become sharers in the Lord's sufferings [?]...

...and heirs of the glory that is to be revealed. Here he does so by pointing out that they are not suffering alone: all the faithful throughout the world suffer too. The burden is made lighter by the [?] of those who share in it.

A prayer for the perfecting of believers. "And the God of all grace, who called us to his eternal glory in Christ Jesus, will himself, after you have suffered a little while, restore, establish, strengthen and settle you. To him be the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen. I have written to you briefly through Silvanus, a faithful brother, as I regard him, exhorting you and testifying that this is the true grace of God, in which you stand. The church in Babylon, chosen together with you, greets you, and so does Mark my son. Greet one another with a kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ Jesus. Amen." At the beginning of the Epistle he said that the Father had shown us mercy through the Son. Now, as he concludes, he teaches that the same Father called us through the Son. Their aim is to proclaim the mystery, even when they do it alongside exhortation. "Through Silvanus." This Silvanus was exceedingly faithful and contended eagerly for the preaching. Paul too mentions him and names him as a fellow worker with Timothy in his epistles, saying, "Paul and Silvanus and Timothy." He calls Rome "Babylon" because of its renown, which Babylon also enjoyed for a long time. He calls Mark his son in the spirit, not in the flesh, and it was to Mark that he entrusted the writing of the Gospel. Some, however, have dared to declare that this Mark was the fleshly son of the divine Peter. As proof they use what Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles. Luke says that Peter was miraculously brought out by an angel of God from the prison where Herod had shut him up, and that, once the angel's instruction had released him, he hurried to the house of the mother of John called Mark. They take this to mean that he was returning to his own house and his lawful wife. Paul writes that they should greet one another with a holy kiss; Peter says "with a kiss of love," but he means the same thing. Paul too knows that love in Christ is greater than all the virtues, greater even than martyrdom for Christ. So Paul speaks of a "holy kiss," meaning one set apart in God, and Peter likewise speaks of a kiss of love, the true love that Paul also praised. That is why he adds, "Peace to all of you who are in Christ Jesus." He does not mean the ordinary peace among people, which they pursue out of passion, for vain glory and the enjoyment of pleasures, the things to which people give themselves up when they are free from war. Rather, he prays that they may obtain the peace that Christ their teacher also granted them as he went to his passion,

saying, "Peace I leave with you," and then adding the difference: "Not as the world gives." We are not to keep peace out of passion. We keep it because we are bound together by love, and so we can withstand the darts of our adversaries. Everywhere the Lord's disciples place the prayer at the end like a seal, and in this way they show the genuineness of their holiness. Written from Rome.

THE SECOND CATHOLIC EPISTLE OF PETER. The same Peter sends this letter, too, to those who already believe. The Epistle is a reminder of the first teachings. He knew that his departure from the body would come soon, so he was eager to remind everyone of the teaching in which they had been instructed. First he explains the faith, showing that it was announced as good news by the prophets, and that the prophecies about the Savior are not human but were spoken by God. Then he commands them not to pay attention to deceivers, saying that they will be destroyed, as happened to the angels who transgressed. In the epistle he also foretells that days will follow in which scoffers will go about and try to deceive some people. They will say that we speak of the Savior's coming in vain, because it is always being talked about and has not yet happened. He commands them above all to keep away from such people, teaching them not to grow negligent because of the length of time. All time is nothing before the Lord, he says, since one day is a thousand years and a thousand years are as one day. He affirms that the day of the Lord will come quickly and proves it. He commands everyone to be ready for it with good works, to love what the apostle Paul wrote, and to pay no attention to those who slander his writings, since they slander all the divine Scriptures as well. So, having reminded them and taught them all to know beforehand [?] what is to come, he urges them not to fall away from the goal of the faith. And in this way he concludes the Epistle.

[?] CHAPTERS OF THE SECOND CATHOLIC EPISTLE OF PETER. 1. On the calling in faith, which is confirmed by works of virtue and by the hope of the good things to come. 2. A charge to remember the teaching after his departure, and how on Mount Tabor they heard the voice of God concerning Christ. 3. A prediction of the deceitful uprising of heretics, of their impiety and their coming punishment. 4. A recapitulation on the wickedness of heretical men. In it he speaks of how Christ will come suddenly at the consummation of this age, so that we must prepare ourselves with how much [?]...
THE SECOND CATHOLIC EPISTLE OF THE APOSTLE PAUL [?]. On the calling in faith, which is confirmed by works of virtue and by the hope of the good things to come.

"Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who have obtained a faith equal in honor to ours through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ: may grace and peace be multiplied to us in the knowledge of God..."

"Simon." It is also written "Symeon," for Simon is a shortened form of Symeon, just as Metras is of Metrodorus, Menas of Menodorus, and Theudas of Theodosius. Right from the opening he lifts up the minds and souls of the believers, rousing them to the same zeal for the preaching as the apostles. Those who have received a gift equal in honor would not be right to fall short in anything of those they have been shown to equal. Everywhere he greets them warmly with peace. He does not mean the world's peace, but the peace that lies in the knowledge of God. This alone is peace, because it frees us from offense, including offense toward God. That is why Christ gave it to us when he was departing to the Father, and when he rose from the dead, crying out, "Peace be with you." In the churches, too, we pray that the angel of peace may be given to us, and the priest

often offers peace to the people from the holy altar. We also use it when we greet one another, because it is the mother of all good things and the foundation of our joy. That is why the Lord commanded his disciples to offer it first when they visited houses. "Grace to you and peace." The sense runs as follows: Grace to you and peace, since his divine power has granted you all things that pertain to life and godliness in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord. This grace has given you the knowledge of him, the glory, the virtue, and through these the greatest promises have been granted, so that you may escape the worldly corruption that comes through desire and become partakers of the divine nature. "In the knowledge of God." The sense runs: To you who, in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord, have obtained a faith equal in honor to ours through the righteousness of our God, may grace and peace be multiplied. Or else it runs like this: In the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord. This knowledge, through his divine power, has granted all things that pertain to life and godliness. It is the very knowledge of him who called us through glory and virtue, and through that glory and virtue the precious and greatest promises were given, so that you might become partakers of the divine nature by escaping the corruption of worldly desire. And for this very reason, that is, for this very purpose, bring all diligence to it and supply virtue in your faith, knowledge in virtue, self-control in knowledge, endurance in self-control, godliness in endurance, brotherly affection in godliness, and in brotherly affection

"Since his divine power has granted us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us by glory and virtue, through which he has granted us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through desire, for this very reason make every effort to supply virtue in your faith, knowledge in virtue, self-control in knowledge, endurance in self-control, godliness in endurance, brotherly affection in godliness, and love in brotherly affection. For if these things are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being idle or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. Whoever lacks these things is blind and short-sighted, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his old sins."

This is stated at some length, but the meaning is this. We have received countless good things through the appearing of Christ, and through them we can become partakers of the divine nature and be led up to life and godliness. So we ought to live in such a way that we add virtue to faith and walk along the road toward progress in godliness, until we reach the perfection of all good things, which is love. We have become partakers

of the divine nature through the coming of our Lord and God. He established in himself the firstfruits of our nature and sanctified it by assuming it. "If the firstfruits are holy, so is the lump." And the lump of the firstfruits is nothing other than those from whom the firstfruits came. He speaks of the corruption that comes from worldly desire, because that desire is made up of corruptible things and is directed toward corruptible things. He knows the steps of progress. The first is faith, which is the foundation and groundwork of all good things. The second step is virtue, that is, works, for without them faith is dead, as James says. After these comes knowledge. And what is this knowledge? It is the understanding of God's hidden mysteries. It does not come to just anyone, but to the one whose disposition has been trained by better works. After these comes self-control. Whoever has reached this stage needs it, so that he may not grow insolent at the greatness of the gift. But one who practices self-control only for a short while cannot hold the gift securely, for the passions, once freed from what restrains them, always tend to move toward what is worse. So endurance comes in, completes the whole, and secures godliness by producing a more perfect trust in God. That is why brotherly affection was added to godliness. It would not have arisen if godliness, with its kindly disposition toward everything, had not opened the way. And above all comes love, the fullness of all good things, as Paul and the Truth itself hold. Love compelled both the Son of God and his Father: the Father to give his beloved, and the Son to shed his blood for us. "For if these things are yours." What things? Faith, virtue, knowledge, endurance, godliness, brotherly affection and love. These must not only be present but also abound. If their presence is of benefit, their abundance is much more so. And what is their benefit? Boldness at the Lord's second coming. When the Judge comes in glory and flashes like the sun, blindness follows for whoever lacks these things. Even someone with strong sight could not look at such surpassing brightness without harm, for what shines with an overwhelming light naturally dims the eyes of those who fix their weak gaze on it. "Short-sighted" means being blind. The word comes from the moles that live under the ground and remain blind all their lives. "Having forgotten that he was cleansed from his old sins." This is like what blessed James says: "If anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks at his natural face in a mirror. He looks at himself and goes away, and at once forgets what he was like." This man, too, came to know himself through being cleansed in holy baptism and learned that a multitude of sins had been washed away. Knowing that by his cleansing he had also received holiness, he should have stayed sober so as to keep his sanctification always, for without it no one will see the Lord. But he forgot.

A charge to remember the teaching after his departure, and how on Mount Tabor he heard the voice of God concerning Christ. "Therefore, brothers, be all the more eager to make your calling and election sure, for if you do these things you will never stumble. In this way entry into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ will be richly provided for you. So I will not neglect to remind you of these things always, even though you know them and are established in the truth you now have. I think it right, as long as I am in this tent, to stir you up by way of reminder, since I know that putting off my tent will come soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me. And I will make every effort that after my departure you may be able at any time to call these things to mind." "Therefore," he says, "my brothers, be all the more eager" to show that your calling and election are lasting and immovable. That is, be eager that the instruction you heard at your election and calling should remain unshaken, so that you may not be judged as people who have forgotten God's gift, but may continue to hold your calling firm. "For if you do these things." What things? The ones mentioned earlier, such as virtue, knowledge, self-control and those that follow. Notice how he first urged them on by the terrors of the Judge's tribunal, and now urges them on by the good things of entering the eternal kingdom of the Lord. "Even though you know them." He did not want them to think that, because they were constantly being reminded of the same things, they were being condemned for idleness, and so to be hurt. For that reason he added, "even though you know them and are established in the truth you now have." And to give the reason for his constant reminders, he added that he knew his release from this body would come soon. As for what follows, I mean, "And I will make every effort that after my departure you may be able at any time," that is, every day and continually, "to call these things to mind," some want to show from it that the saints remember the things of this world even after death and intercede for the living. Others take the saying in its simple sense: "I will make every effort that after my departure you may be able at any time to call these things to mind." That is: Do not be surprised, and do not find it burdensome that I keep proclaiming the same things to you. I do not do this because I condemn you for ignorance. Rather, by teaching these things to you continually, I am making your grasp of them lasting and immovable, so that, once you are confirmed in them, the teachings about these things will keep echoing in you and remain indelible even after my death. "For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eye-

witnesses of his majesty. For he received honor and glory from God the Father when this voice was borne to him by the Majestic Glory: 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.' And we ourselves heard this voice borne from heaven [?] while we were with him on the holy mountain. And we have [?]... [?] while we were with him on the holy mountain. And we have the prophetic word made more sure [?]... You do well to pay attention to it as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts. Know this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture [?]... [?] was ever prophecy [brought], but holy men of God spoke as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit."

He has said that they ought to be very earnest [?], namely about what he had preached to them as the gospel. He has spoken about these things at length and often, even though they already knew them and had heard them in various ways. Now he adds what makes them trustworthy, and says, in effect: I do not show this concern for them in vain. Rather, because I know how timely and how utterly true they are, I hold on to them all the more. And what is that? That we did not use human wisdom [?] or bewitch your ears with elegant words when we made known to you the power and coming of the Lord. That is what the Greeks and the heretics do: the Greeks use fine diction and deceive, while the heretics use fabrications, like the followers of Valentinus with their marvelous tales of the Depth and Silence. It is likely that such people were already beginning to spring up. Nothing of that kind, then, can be found among us. For we have [?] the word [?] for teaching, as Paul too says to the Corinthians, and we have what we saw with our own eyes, we who went up with him on the holy mountain. He means the glory of the Only-begotten that was shown to them at the transfiguration, and the voice that they heard borne from heaven by the Father on account of the Lord. And since we have come to know through the events and through experience the things the prophets foretold, we judge, he says, that their prophecy is made more sure by these things. The events followed the words. So you too do well to attend to the prophecy, that is, to what the prophets spoke beforehand, even if they spoke dimly at the time, like a lamp burning in a gloomy place. For that is what a squalid place is like: it is parched [?] by the heat of the sun and deprived of the moisture that gives the air its form. [?] ... the air that serves the sun's [?], being in danger of losing its own property, must offer itself as a counterfeit servant to the sun, and the ray, carried through a counterfeit medium, shows only a dim brightness. If you attend to what the prophets said so obscurely, you will not miss the hope. For the events, he says, coming about at their own proper time [?]...

…[of the things] to come, which he also called "day." Here he keeps up the figure very wisely: he had spoken of a lamp and of a squalid place, that is, a gloomy and dark one, which is exactly what night is. And every night is followed by day. "So when the day comes," he says (I mean the actual presence of the events), "you will have the morning star rising in your hearts." That is, the knowledge of Christ, or his coming that was foretold by the prophets, will shine on your hearts like true light. Then he goes on to explain why the prophets did not interpret what they had said. At the same time he distinguishes true prophecy from the demonic and counterfeit kind, which is found at work among the heretics too. He says: "No prophecy of Scripture is a matter of one's own interpretation." That is, the prophets do receive prophecy from God, but not as they themselves wish; they receive it as the divine Spirit that moves them works. They knew and understood the prophetic word sent down to them, but they did not give its interpretation. That the prophets moved by the divine Spirit knew the word was being sent down to them from God is clear from the fact that they served willingly, speaking what they wished and keeping silent about what they did not wish. Jonah the prophet, for instance, declined to preach to Nineveh, and Balaam was commanded to speak what was put into his mouth. It is not so with the false prophets or the oracles of the Greeks. They did not know while they were being moved. Carried away in frenzy, they did not know what was happening to them, like people who are drunk. The holy prophets, however (I mean the ancient ones), though they knew, had no need to interpret what they said, but ministered these things to others. [?] At the same time this was so that the Lord's coming might stay hidden and not be plotted against by the ungodly. Even if it were plotted against, it could indeed have escaped through the surpassing power of God. But if the escape had sometimes been accomplished by miracles, what was accomplished in the incarnation would probably have seemed a mere portent. That this is so [?] is clear from the prophets of the New Testament, who did interpret when they prophesied, if indeed they did so at all [?], as the divine Paul says in First Corinthians. In the New Testament there was no suspicion of any such thing. And that the prophets did not deliver their oracles in a state of ecstasy is also clear from

this: since those in the Old and the New Testaments prophesy from one Spirit, Paul says, "If a revelation comes to another who is sitting by, let the first be silent." This makes it clear that the prophets prophesied willingly, remaining in their natural state and understanding. That is why, when another man who has been inspired stands up, the first speaker is told to be silent. You would not find this among madmen. How can a man keep silent when he does not even know what he is doing? And the same Paul says that it is the Holy Spirit who works in the prophets, in these words: "To one is given the word of wisdom, and

…of prophecy." But this one too through what precedes [?]: "For having received from God the Father." He used "having received" in place of a finite verb, that is, for "he received," since the main clause does not follow on in the sequence the participle requires. If not, and someone wants to take "having received" here strictly as a participle, the sentence will necessarily slide into broken syntax. But if the participle is taken for a finite verb, what follows will be consistent, like this: "For he received glory from God the Father." From this we have all the prophets' foretelling about him made more certain. It is not that there is any prophecy about the voice that was borne from the Father above. Rather, the Father's voice from above bore witness to his sonship, and so we have been made firm in the conviction that all the oracles given through the prophets come to us attested beyond dispute by the Father. "This is my Son." The Father bore witness to the Son three times: at the baptism; in the passion, with "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again"; and on the mountain. "Knowing this first," and what follows. The prophets knew both what they were inspired with by the prophetic spirit and whom it concerned, but not precisely [?] how and when each thing would be fulfilled. That is why, though they understood, they longed to see how these things would turn out, as the Lord also says.

A prediction of the deceitful rising-up of the heretics, of their ungodliness, and of their coming punishment.

"But there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you. They will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, and bring swift destruction on themselves. Many will follow their destructive ways, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. In their greed they will exploit you with fabricated words. Their condemnation, pronounced long ago, is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep."

The name of prophecy is used in common for both the prophets and the false prophets, so he now puts them on their guard not to pay heed to the false prophets. What distinguishes the two Paul taught: no one says "Jesus is Lord" except by the Holy Spirit. From here he begins his attack on the heresy of the Nicolaitans, describing their wickedness as twofold. In doctrine they are utterly impious, as they showed by their blasphemy against Christ the Master, and in life they are utterly licentious. This second point he presents for now through their shameful greed, and a little further on he will set it out more clearly. By saying "greed" he here meant shameful gain, for the word sometimes means injustice and sometimes simply gain. Hence he fittingly added "they will exploit," that is, make merchandise of you. And to set them wholly apart from the divine teaching, he said that they used fabricated words.
1 Cor. 3:3.

But they will receive, he says, the wages of ungodliness, which is death. "Long ago" points to God's foreknowledge: [?] just as in his foreknowledge he prepared good things for the good, so also he prepared for the wicked the place that suits them. "Who," and what follows. The order is: "Who, bringing swift destruction on themselves, will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who will buy them, and exploiting you in greed with fabricated words."

"For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into Tartarus in chains of gloom and handed them over to be kept for judgment; if he did not spare the [?] world, but preserved [?] a herald [of righteousness] when he brought a flood on the world of the ungodly; if he condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to destruction, reducing them to ashes and making them an example for those who would be ungodly; and if he rescued righteous Lot, who was distressed by the licentious conduct of the lawless (for that righteous man, living among them, tormented his righteous soul day after day by the lawless deeds he saw and heard)…"

God did not spare even angels when they sinned, nor the ancient world. He also condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, reducing them to ashes, and made them an example for all who would be ungodly after them. But he preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, when he brought a flood on the world of the ungodly. He also rescued Lot when he was oppressed by the ungodly: that is, when the men of Sodom were seeking the angels who had been his guests, and when he was being urged day after day to imitate their ungodly deeds and tormented his own soul by keeping away from them and practising self-control. So in the present time too he will all the more hand these men over to destruction, like the angels who transgressed, the people at the flood and the Sodomites. And will he not save us who live among them in the world as sojourners, as he saved Noah and Lot, who then lived alongside the lawless? He will certainly do so, and no one will contradict it. For he knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to keep the wicked to be punished on the day of judgment.

Notice that above he first set out the example of the evildoers, but now he puts the example of the righteous first. By this he encourages those who imitate the righteous, as being more honoured than the ungodly. That is also why Christ first gives the rewards to the righteous, the lambs on his right, and then gives the punishments to the goats on his left. In the same way pleasant things are put before grim ones. "He did not spare angels when they sinned." The argument is from the more honoured. He is saying: these were angels held in honour by God because of the purity of their essence, and yet when they sinned they obtained no pardon; neither did the human beings who lived closest to their own creation.

So much more will he not spare these men when they sin. By the "chains of gloom" he signifies that the condemnation cannot be escaped or evaded, for these are the kind of bonds with which we punish those who have been strictly condemned by us. But someone will ask how such a condemnation of the demons is known. Clearly from the demons themselves. In the Gospel they beg not to be sent into the abyss, as though all the others had suffered this. It should be recognized, however, that the argument is put forward as a hypothesis in form only. In reality it is not one, because it lacks the corresponding conclusion. It is framed this way only in form; in truth it is a simple proof by example. Why this is so will now be explained. If it followed the form, it would have run like this: "For if he did not spare angels when they sinned, nor the ancient world, nor Sodom and Gomorrah, will he then spare these? By no means." Or like this: "He will certainly not spare these." He is not simply arguing from the more honoured. He wants to show that these men are all the more liable when they sin. They too hold a place of greater honour, since they were called to the apostolic faith [?], and since they turned aside from the divine way, their condemnation is also greater. Having begun the proof by example in the form of a hypothesis, he did not supply what the form requires next. He mixed up the example by adding the righteous. He ought to have given the conclusion about what he set out at the start, that is, about those who sinned, for whose sake the example was given, and to have said: "If he did not spare these, will he then spare the licentious men of the present?" Or, as a negative statement: "Much more will he not spare these." He does not do this. Why? Because with two examples set out, one of good and one of bad, this conclusion would have applied to the bad alone and no longer to the good, since evil is not repaid to the good. So because one conclusion could not complete what he had set out, he expressed it differently in his wording [?] and accomplished what was required through a closing exclamation. Why he adds the examples of the good to those of the bad will be explained in the proper place. "But [he preserved] Noah, the eighth," and what follows. As we said before, the sense of what is set out does not follow the apparent form of the wording. The conclusion that usually follows such constructions is missing. Rather, it is a simple proof by example, both of those punished for sin and of those honoured for righteousness. It is as if he said: God knows how to punish sinners inexorably and without sparing, like the angels who sinned, like the people at the flood, like the cities of Sodom; and again how to honour those who work righteousness, like Noah, like Lot. The construction is as follows. Having said that the false teachers will be punished for their blasphemies, he brings forward the examples on account of their licentious life. For God did not spare angels when they sinned, nor the ancient world,

nor did the cities of Sodom escape destruction. They were reduced to ashes as an example for those who would be ungodly. And again, God knows how to honour those who have practised righteousness, like Noah, like Lot. He also explains for what righteousness each was honoured: he preserved both Noah and Lot from the destruction of the people of their time because of their self-control. Noah did not follow [?] the ungodliness of those before the flood, and Lot imitated nothing of the licentiousness of the people of Sodom. Day after day he was stung, as it were, by the sight of the licentious and urged to their very licentious acts, yet he did not give in. That is the meaning of "by what he saw and heard." He had many things calling him to licentiousness: what he saw, what he heard, and his life among the wicked. Yet he did not even hand over the angels who were his guests in human form to those who demanded them for licentious purposes, though he was abused in countless ways by those who demanded them. This is what he indicated with the word "distressed." To all this he adds a kind of closing exclamation: "The Lord knows how to rescue the godly," and what follows. He had said nothing before about the righteous, only about the ungodly and their punishment, but he inserted the examples of the righteous as well. First, because the history itself records the destruction of the ungodly and the salvation of the righteous together. Next, because by setting them side by side he magnifies the fault [?] of those who sinned and makes the achievement of those who did right shine out. Further, he persuades his hearers to hate the licentiousness of the one group because of their punishments, and to take up the achievement of the other because of their salvation. That is why in the closing exclamation too he mentions both, the ungodly and the godly, and both punishment and salvation. Why he does this [?] has already been said: he wants them to loathe the vice of the one group and imitate the virtue of the other. "For by what he saw and heard the righteous man." Though he had many things, he says, that inflamed, maddened and urged him to licentiousness, namely what he saw, what he heard, and his association with the wicked, none of them drew him to imitate those men.

"The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trial and to keep the unrighteous under punishment for the day of judgment, especially those who follow the flesh in polluting lust and despise authority. Bold and self-willed, they do not tremble to blaspheme the glorious ones, whereas angels, though greater in strength and power, do not bring a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord. But these men, like irrational animals, born by nature to be caught and destroyed, blaspheme in matters they do not understand, and they will be destroyed in their own corruption, receiving the wages of unrighteousness. They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime."

"Especially those who follow the flesh." Here he skilfully passes from the examples already given to the subject at hand. He is speaking of the accursed Nicolaitans, also called Gnostics, or

Naassenes [?], or Cerdonians. Their wickedness has many names, and it is as confused in its names as in its foul deeds. As we said earlier, these men posited Depth and Silence as the first principles of the world's existence, and told marvellous tales of certain Mothers and Aeons that came from them; Marcion too took evil seeds from them. Then, having through these notions rejected the Lord's sovereignty over the making of the world and his oversight [?], they went on fearlessly into every kind of fleshly impurity. Anyone who wants to learn about them should take up the book that Irenaeus the Celt, a blessed man, laboured over concerning them, which he entitled Against Knowledge Falsely So Called. There he will find their impurities, especially through Mark, the most licentious of them, and the wretched women whom he deceived and corrupted. "Bold, self-willed." We must supply "who are." Since they rejected the overseer and maker of the world, it is not surprising that such men also became bold and self-willed, that is, men who pursue whatever pleases themselves. He also calls them blasphemers. Those who out of contempt do not fear the Lord's sovereignty, what wonder is it if they also behave fearlessly toward every glory? The blessed apostle Jude will speak about these men more clearly, where he will also mention the body of Moses. Peter has only touched on the matter here, raising it and closing the discussion of it at the same time. So we take our starting point for the present passage from Jude as well, and we say that "they do not tremble at the glorious ones" means that they are contemptuously ready to blaspheme every glory. Wishing to check their boldness in such matters, he says: "whereas angels, though greater in strength and power, do not bring a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord." As we said, he is saying the same as the blessed Jude. Jude too, in rebuking certain people's itching tongues, gives his admonition from the same example, though more fully, when he says: "But Michael the archangel," and what follows, "did not dare to bring a judgment of blasphemy." Peter too wants to say something of this kind here: these wretches have no restraint in blaspheming the glories, and yet not even those greater in power and strength (greater, that is, than these foul men) bring, or put forward, a blasphemous judgment against them, the glories, as it were, before the Lord. Michael the archangel is the witness to this. Since even the devil has a share in a certain glory, because he was the first of the Lord's creatures, Michael did not bring a blasphemous word against him. So the argument from these points runs rather like this: if the devil, who more deserved to be blasphemed, nevertheless did not suffer this from Michael before the Lord because he shares in glory, then those who readily blaspheme every glory cannot be in their right minds, falling so far short of the honour of the angels. By "glories" he means either the divine powers or the authorities of the Church, against which these utterly swinish men set themselves

and kept on blaspheming them. So much for the angels. "But these, like irrational animals by nature," that is, living by sense alone and not by mind and the life of the intellect. That is why they are easily caught by corruptible things, that is, by the ways of this perishing life, as they are led and carried along by anger and desire. "In what they do not know," that is, blaspheming out of their wilful ignorance, they will be destroyed by the corruption they deserve, receiving the wages of unrighteousness, which they willingly brought on themselves. "Counting it pleasure to revel in the daytime." What is truly desirable, he says, the true and lovely joy and pleasure, they place in the daily indulgence of the gullet. It should be noted, however, that when divine Scripture censures what is naturally present in human beings, that is, what is found in the animals themselves, it likens them to the irrational animals. It says, "Man, though he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts"; and "Do not be like the horse and the mule"; and "They became stallions mad for mares"; and "Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves." In saying this it does not change their natures, for that is impossible. Rather, it urges us to shun some of those natural impulses and to hold fast commendably to others. But when it commands something that leads to salvation, it points the likeness toward higher things, as when it says, "Be merciful, as your heavenly Father also is." Even here it does not change nature; it bids us do this as far as our strength allows.

"They are blots and blemishes, revelling in their deceptions while they feast with you, having [eyes] full of [adultery and unceasing] sin [?]. They entice unstable souls, and have hearts trained in greed. Children of a curse! They have left the straight way and gone astray, following the way of Balaam son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness but was rebuked for his own transgression: a speechless donkey spoke with a human voice and restrained the prophet's madness."

"Blots and blemishes." The order is: blots, blemishes, having hearts trained in greed, that is, trained by means of greed; children of a curse; feasting with you; full of adultery and unceasing sin; they entice unstable souls, the ones Paul called silly women laden with sins. These same men left the straight way and went astray in the way of Balaam son of Bosor, and so on. These same men are waterless springs, clouds driven by a storm, and so on. And why is the gloom of darkness reserved for them in the age to come? Because of their swollen vanity, with which they entice those who once lived in error and had truly escaped it, drawing them into licentiousness and the desires of the flesh, like a dog to [?]…

…to return to its own vomit." The words in between declare and confirm the emptiness of these people. "Blots and blemishes": having nothing, he says, that belongs to purity, but like blots on a clean garment, they fasten on a spotless way of life and find fault with everything. Whenever they draw some people away and manage to make the men and women in their company licentious, they count it a delight, satisfying their own licentiousness. But also, he says, "feasting with you," they do this not out of love or to share salt with you, but because they find it a convenient occasion for deceiving women. For these men have eyes that see nothing but adulteresses. Sinning ceaselessly in this, like children of a curse, they entice unstable souls. For their heart [?] has been trained for nothing but greed, whether for licentiousness or for possessions. Because of both of these they abandoned the way that directs them to salvation and strayed from it, suffering the same as Balaam son of Bosor. For he too, through taking bribes, loved the wages of unrighteousness, but was rebuked for his own lawlessness: a mute beast of burden, speaking with a human voice, restrained the prophet's madness. From this, then, we learn that because of his passion for money, which Balaam fed through his frenzied divination, though he had once been prevented by God, he contentiously pressed to go to Balak a second time. Yet, fettered by the fear of God and by the terrors along the way, he did not alter the word of blessing. That word did not belong to divination (for we have said that divination is uttered by a soul in frenzy that does not know what it is saying), but to prophecy. For the prophets know what they utter. That is why he also called him a prophet, as one who knew what he was saying; for he would not have been chosen among the better sort if he did not know what he uttered. The blessing, then, came not from divination but from the power of God. "These are waterless springs, clouds driven by a storm, for whom the gloom of darkness has been reserved forever. For, uttering swollen words of emptiness, they entice by the desires of the flesh, by licentiousness, those who have truly escaped from those who live in error, promising them freedom, while they themselves are slaves of corruption. For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is also enslaved. For if, having escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first. For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, having known it, to turn back [?] from the holy commandment delivered to them. What has happened to them is what the true proverb says: A dog returns to its own vomit, and a sow that has washed, to wallowing in the mire." Having interposed many things, among which he brought forward the example of Balaam, he takes up again his discussion of the impure Gnostics. And he likens them

to waterless springs, as having lost the water of life, that is, the pure and drinkable water of the preaching, which the Lord had and with which he promised to satisfy many of those who came to him. But he also compares them to clouds driven by a wind—the opposing one, clearly. That is why he called it a storm, as something that whirls about and throws into confusion whatever it drives; for that is what a storm usually does. They are not, then, he says, bright clouds, like the saints, but mists full of gloom, for whom the gloom has been reserved forever (he means the coming judgment). And why? He adds the cause: because, uttering swollen words out of emptiness, they entice through fleshly desire, in licentiousness, those who have truly and once for all escaped from those who formerly lived in error. So those who commit these things are guilty of licentiousness, arrogance and impiety. But also, he says, being themselves slaves of the impurity just mentioned, which he rightly also calls corruption, they promise freedom to those they deceive—not true freedom, but the freedom of an unrestrained way of life. Therefore he also adds an argument to show that they are slaves of sin, saying something remarkable: that by whatever passion a person has been conquered, to that he is also enslaved. Then he establishes this again by another proof, showing how one who is overcome by something is also its slave. And he makes the argument a fortiori. "For if, having escaped." By the present passage he establishes two things: that the one overcome must serve the one who overcomes, and that those who, after the knowledge of the truth, are again held fast by their former ways have fallen into evils worse than the former. To these he also adds the proverb as a supporting witness. The whole argument, then, is this: If, having escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome by them, surely they also serve them, and have become worse in their slavery to them than they were before that knowledge, since Satan, who plots against us, strives to bring them round to worse things, as if to make up for the time [?] they were idle from evil works. That is why the Apostle says that, since this is what is laid up for those who go back to singing the song of evil, it would have been better for them not to have known at all than, having known, to be caught by worse things. For a dog too, returning to its own vomit, is more loathsome: what nature hated and forced it to throw up, it makes its food once more, eating things that are corrupted and that nature has cast out, and so it is more loathsome. And a sow that seeks to roll about again, if it does so in mud, would appear filthier than its former filth.
A recapitulation concerning the wickedness of heretical men; in which [it is shown] how Christ will come suddenly at the consummation [?] of the age, and that one must be prepared in every way.

[…] letter, in both of which I stir up your sincere mind by way of reminder, so that you remember the words spoken beforehand by the holy prophets, and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through our apostles; knowing this first, that in the last of the days scoffers will come, walking according to their own desires and saying, 'Where is the promise of his coming? For since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they have from the beginning of creation.'" From this we learn that there are two letters of Peter in all. The words "in which I stir up your sincere mind by way of reminder" must be understood as a transposition, thus: in which letters, that is, through which letters, I awaken the sincere mind in you. For it belongs to a sincere and pure mind to remember the saving things already heard or laid down, and to be roused by them to take up their practice again with all strength and eagerness. And they were laid down through the words of the prophets and through the preaching of the apostles. That is why Paul also says, "Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets." For these [?] proclaimed the coming of the Lord, both the first and the second, and one cannot disbelieve so many and such great witnesses. And why, he says, do I speak of prophets and apostles, as having proclaimed both the first and the second coming of our Lord and Savior? And the construction is [?]: "to remember the words spoken beforehand by the holy prophets, by the commandment of our apostles, by the commandment of the Lord and Savior." For "by" applies to all in common. And he adds why he urges them to rekindle this memory: because those who live by passion according to their own desires see some who fear the coming of the Lord—which the Lord himself also foretold, along with other God-bearing men—and who on its account reject their own indecent way of life; and then, seeing that the fulfilment did not follow hard on the words but has been delayed for the salvation of many, they attack the faithful, jeering like the scoffers they are and saying, "Where is the promise of his coming?" By means of this one promise, which has not yet come to pass because of some divine dispensation, they maliciously lead people to disobey the Lord's other saving commandments as well. Such were the ravings of the Gnostics of those times, or Naassenes, who are also the same as the Lampetians and Euchites. All of these, he says, it escapes willingly: they voluntarily shut their eyes to the truth, as we have said before. "For this escapes them willingly, that the heavens existed long ago, and an earth formed out of water and through water by the word of God, through which the world of that time was flooded with water and perished. But the present heavens and earth, by the same word, have been stored up

for fire, and for the [?] destruction of ungodly men. But do not let this one thing escape you, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slow about his promise, as some count slowness, but is patient toward us, not wishing any to perish, but all to come to repentance." And what is it that escapes them? That just as at the flood there were heavens formed out of water, according to Moses' account of the world's origin (for he says that God commanded a firmament to come into being in the midst of the water, that is, a substance more solid than the waters), and the earth likewise appeared out of the waters at the Creator's command, having previously been submerged by them; and that, though heaven and earth had been formed out of waters, the flood came upon them unexpectedly—so too now the destruction of the universe is reserved to come about through fire, and with it the ungodly will also perish. For there are two elements that most hold the universe together, water and fire, from which the other two elements also receive their being: air when the waters evaporate, and earth when the same waters condense—evaporation coming as it were from fire, and condensation [?]; and no one with sense would disbelieve this (for the nature of fire has received this power from God who made it [?]). Since, then, there are two, and the earlier destruction of the ungodly came about through water, it is necessary, he says, that the destruction of the ungodly should in turn come about through fire. That the destruction of this universe will take place is held not only by Christians but also by the wise men of the Greeks, such as Heraclitus of Ephesus and Empedocles of Etna. But someone will say, "And what is the point of its coming into existence, if the world must go back to destruction?" And we will say that the world will not go to destruction entirely, but to renewal. That is why the Prophet also says, "And you will renew the face of the earth." For the sensible creation was at the beginning [made] good by God—and it could not have been otherwise than good [?]. But because of man's transgression the creation itself was also subjected to futility, that is, to not having a secure existence but being in constant flux and outflow. Then, through the flood, men paid a little more heed to godliness, and the world received as it were the beginning of a second composition through Noah and through the seeds preserved in the ark with the animals so that it might be established again. Yet not even then did human nature make progress; it slipped away into things worse than before. From these worse things neither the law given through Moses turned it back, nor even the coming of the Lord, except that salvation advanced among a few (for how large is the swarm of the saved compared with the multitude of the lost in each generation? That is why, it seems to me, the time of the consummation is being extended, so that the full number of those to be saved may be completed). Since, then, the call to salvation is manifold, and

the destruction that comes from disobedience takes many forms, for this reason the flood of fire is necessary. It is a destruction, though not a total one: not of souls, nor even of bodies. For we must all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, not as souls stripped of their bodies, but with bodies that have themselves become incorruptible. For how could a naked soul receive what was done through the body? It is not the part of a just judge, when two have sinned in the same thing, to let one go and bring the whole charge against the other. Besides, if we are accustomed to recast metals in fire, not to reduce them to utter nonexistence but to make them pure and unalloyed, no one could disbelieve that God, who promises the consummation through fire, will either not carry it out, or, in carrying it out, do so for destruction. But even if he does destroy, what would he destroy? The things that are superfluous and belong to the present life. And what are these? Cattle, grass, plants. Grass exists for the sake of cattle, and cattle serve this corruptible life: "He makes grass spring up for the cattle, and green plants for the service of men." As for plants, some serve for shelter and houses, others to supply food. And food for living creatures is a mark of corruption: for what else would need and replenishment imply but corruption? These things, then, which are superfluous for the incorruptible life, would be destroyed. But he will establish new heavens and a new earth, not different in their matter. For he who puts together a new [?] world would not now make it out of matter that did not previously exist. Since, then, God once established matter in the beginning and gave it form, whatever was necessary for the condition of that time but is useless and superfluous for the incorruptible condition that follows, he will destroy; and whatever contributes to it, he will transform with an incorruptible and inconceivable beauty, so as [?] to complete the second and incorruptible world. "From water": the earth is from water as from its material cause, and through water as from its sustaining [?] cause. For water is what holds the earth together, being a kind of glue for it; if it were not present, the earth would necessarily dissolve into dust and turn into air. But perhaps someone will assail us with idle talk [?]: why ever did God, when he established the visible world, not make it stable and unchangeable from the beginning, but compounded it with changes, so that it even needs to be set right again—in Noah's time through the flood, and at the consummation through fire, as Peter says? To him we shall reply that it could not possibly have unchangeableness. For how could it, when it obtained its very being from change? It was brought from not being into being, and no sensible person would call that anything but alteration. And since alteration advanced toward the worse, mixed up with worse things, its Creator, bringing it back to the better, necessarily made the cleansing through water in Noah's time, and at the consummation will make it through fire—just as we too are accustomed to recast metals in fire, not to annihilate them but to purify them. "Through which": that is, through heaven and earth, the earth sending forth the flood of water and the heavens letting loose their floodgates, that is,

driving the water down as through floodgates. "The world of that time, flooded with water, perished." "Perished" must not be understood of the whole world, but only of the living creatures, which as it were give the whole world its form; for a place empty of living creatures would not even be considered a world. And the words "kept for fire until the day of judgment and destruction" [should be read] thus: kept for the day of judgment and for the day of destruction. For "for the day" applies to both in common. And "judgment" stands for "condemnation." "The Lord is not slow." Having concluded his discussion of the consummation—that it will come, and that of necessity, and through fire, which we too have set out in greater detail—he passes on to the extension of the time before the world's consummation, and says that the Lord is not slow about his promise, as some count slowness, but is patient, awaiting our salvation, and not wishing us to perish, but all to come to repentance. For since he is infinite, a boundless ocean of being, nothing is drawn out for him; rather, a thousand years are with him as one day. Or rather, according to David, not even a small fraction of a day. For he says this: "For a thousand years in your eyes, Lord, are like yesterday when it has passed, and like a watch in the night," indicating by "watch" the briefest portion of the night. For the night is divided into four watches, since the Lord too comes to the holy apostles in the fourth watch. "But the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night, in which the heavens will pass away with a rushing roar, and the elements will be burned and dissolved, and the earth and the works in it will be burned up. Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in holy conduct and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set ablaze and dissolved, and the elements will melt as they burn? But according to his promise we wait for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells. Therefore, beloved, since you wait for these things, be eager to be found by him spotless and blameless, in peace, and regard the patience of our Lord as salvation." The uncertainty and unexpectedness of the arrival of the Lord's coming he has shown through the thief and the night: through the night, its uncertainty, for everything in the night is hidden; through the thief, its unexpectedness.

but those who do not expect it will be the ones robbed. That is why the Lord also says that just as in the days of Noah people were making merry with weddings and drinking, with no thought of the disaster about to overtake them, until the flood came upon them,

so too the coming of the Lord will come upon the ungodly unexpectedly. "With a rushing roar" means "with a din." Such a din is characteristic of fire among things [?] being devoured by fire. Notice that he said the earth and the things in it will be burned up, but not people, since he spoke of destruction only in the case of the ungodly, or rather of their impious deeds. For "[the way] of the ungodly will perish" [?]. He promised the faithful, saying, "I will come and take you to myself," and, "In my Father's house there are many dwelling places." That is why Paul also says that when the angel sounds the trumpet from heaven and the dead rise incorruptible, they too will meet the Lord in glory—"in glory" clearly signifying incorruptibility. And if they are incorruptible, they are surely new. And if these are new, it is clear that the creation too, whose nature is to change along with the condition of humankind, becomes new: corruptible because humanity turned aside to corruption, and incorruptible because of humanity's renewal. Notice also that he says the delay in the time of the Lord's coming, and his patience, are brought about for our salvation. "Just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him, as he does in all his letters too, speaking in them of these things. In them there are some things hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist, as they do the rest of the Scriptures, to their own destruction. You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, be on your guard, so that you are not carried away by the error of the lawless and fall from your own firm footing. But grow in grace and in the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen." "Just as our beloved brother Paul also." And where has Paul said such a thing? Where he said, "God's kindness leads you to repentance." And if God's patience leads to repentance, and repentance brings us salvation, then surely God's patience is for our benefit and for our salvation. By "hard to understand" he means the things which, he says, are also proclaimed by the ungodly in a distorted way; for that is what "being twisted" is meant to signify for him. And to show the whole from this one example: when Paul said, "Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more," these men distorted it and claimed that Paul is saying, "Let us sin more, so that we may be forgiven more." And this, he says, they do to their own destruction. For just as those who killed the prophets and the apostles, so also those who destroy their words through distortion are liable to the same judgment. For those men killed them in order to prevent those taught by them from benefiting from the saving things they taught, and [these men treat] their words likewise

…they twist them, so that some may not lay hold of salvation through them. And he says that their own steadfastness is faith in the Lord. And as in his other letters he ends with prayers, so also in this one, praying that they may grow in the faith of the Lord. End, with God's help, of the Second Catholic Epistle of Peter.

[ARGUMENT] OF THE FIRST CATHOLIC EPISTLE OF JOHN. The same John who wrote the Gospel sends this letter, to remind those who have already believed in the Lord. First, as in the Gospel, so also in this Epistle he speaks of God as he speaks of the Word. He shows that the Word is always in God, and he teaches that the Father is light, so that in this way too we may know the Word as the radiance that comes from his being [?]. In speaking of God he explains that our mystery is not something newer. It existed from the beginning and always, and has now been made manifest in the Lord, who is eternal life and true God. He also sets out the reason for his coming and appearing: it was to destroy the works of the devil, to free us from death, and to let us know the Father and the Son himself, the Lord. He addresses every age, little children, young men and old men, because God has been known and the work of the devil has from now on been defeated, now that death has been abolished. Then, through the whole Epistle, he teaches about love. He wants us to love one another, and shows that we must love one another, since Christ also loved us. So he explains the difference between fear and love, between children of God and children of the devil, between sin that leads to death and sin that does not, and the difference between spirits. He distinguishes which spirit is from God and which is the spirit of error, and when we are known to be children of God and when children of the devil. He says for what kind of sin we ought to pray for those who sin, and for what kind we should not pray, and that one who does not love his neighbor is not worthy of the calling and cannot be called Christ's. He also shows the unity of the Son with the Father, and that one who denies the Son does not have the Father either. He distinguishes

…also in this Epistle, saying that this too is a mark of the Antichrist: to say that Jesus is not the Christ, evidently so that, as if [?] … of that one, he may call himself [the Christ]. [?] the liar. Throughout the whole Epistle he urges those who believe in the Lord not to lose heart if they are hated in the world, but rather to rejoice. The world's hatred shows that, as believers, they have passed over out of this world and belong from now on to the heavenly commonwealth. And at the end of the Epistle he reminds them again, saying that the Son of God is eternal life and true God, and that we should serve him and keep ourselves from idols.

CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST CATHOLIC EPISTLE OF JOHN.
1. The Gospel's teaching about Christ. In which: on confession and on taking care not to sin; that keeping God's commandments confirms knowledge.
2. On the grace given to each according to age, and on turning away from love of the world.
3. On false brethren who deny God, and that confessing the Father is reverence toward Christ. For the [?] … In which: the glorification of the Father is teaching about the Son. In which: on the divine and spiritual gift in sanctification and in hope, unto God [?]. That everyone who is in Christ is without sin, for whoever sins is of the devil.
4. On love for one's neighbor and a disposition to share. In which: on a good conscience in the faith of Jesus Christ. On discerning spirits by their confession of the Lord's becoming man.
5. On brotherly love, which leads to godliness.
6. [?] … victory over the Evil One, through faith in Jesus Christ, unto life.
7. On helping a brother who sins by means of prayer, and on not sinning. In which: on keeping away from the worship of demons.

COMMENTARY ON THE FIRST EPISTLE OF JOHN. THE FIRST CATHOLIC EPISTLE OF JOHN THE APOSTLE. CHAPTER ONE. The Gospel's teaching about Christ. In which: on confession and on taking care not to sin. That keeping God's commandments [confirms] knowledge.

"That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon and our hands have touched, concerning the word of life: and the life was made manifest, and we have seen and bear witness…" [?] This is aimed at Jews and Greeks, who slander our mystery as something newer. So he shows that it is in fact ancient. "From the beginning" means: at the same moment as any beginning one can conceive. [It is higher] not only than the

Law, but higher even than visible [?] creation itself. Creation had a beginning, but this existed even before that beginning. As for the Greek things of yesterday and the day before, what could one even say? They are things applauded for their licentiousness. They came late into their unreal existence, when impurity was already at home among human beings, as a lesson and a reminder of our flowing away from what is better into the night that has spread over us [?]. So, to set forth the greatness of our mystery through its antiquity in this respect, he adds that it is also life. And it is life not measured by any stretch of time, but life that truly subsists and is always with the Father. Here he says the same things he says in his own Gospel, for there too he says: "And the Word was with God, and [God was the?] Word."

The word "was" does not indicate an existence in time. It indicates the being of a reality that subsists in itself, the foundation of all things, without which they could not subsist. Each thing that has come into being is said to be something: to be an angel, to be a sun, a heaven, and all the rest. But the Son alone simply is, and by sharing in him all things come into existence. That is why Paul says: "In him we live and move and have our being." A person first receives the hearing of this through introductory teaching. Then, after long training and inquiry, he comes to see him, not with the body but with knowledge. This is what is called "touching concerning the Word of life," the Life that

said, "I am the life." It can also be said of the Word who was in the beginning that we heard of him through the Law and the Prophets, who said he would come. Then, when he came with a body, we saw him plainly and touched him. "For no one has ever seen God unveiled." We did not simply assent to what we saw. Only after much "touching", that is, after examining together the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets about him, did we believe the Word who appeared in the flesh. "Which we looked upon" stands for "which, having seen with our eyes, we marveled at." For "to look upon" means to see with wonder and astonishment. So what we looked upon or touched was not what he was, for "who will declare his generation?", but what he became. We touched him either by the touches of knowledge, as already said, or by the touches of the senses, as Thomas did after the resurrection. For he was one and undivided. The same one was both visible and invisible, both held and not held [?], both intangible and touchable. He spoke as a man, and as God he worked the miracles. We say this because of the utter unity of the Word with the flesh. The sense runs as follows: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard and seen and looked upon with our eyes, and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life (which life was made manifest, which we have seen and bear witness to and proclaim to you; I mean the eternal life which is with the Father and was made manifest to us), that, then, which we have seen, this we also proclaim to you." The main clause, then, comes here, at "That, then, which we have seen." He did not lay out the statement as we would. First, he uses a condensed style. Second, he scorns Greek [?affectation] and shows that our salvation lies not in words but in deeds. Besides this, he makes us more attentive, so that we do not grow careless by finding the meaning ready to hand. And because he is speaking of God, he wanted to hide in obscurity things too high for profane ears, things that could not safely be divulged to them. To throw holy things to the dogs and cast pearls before swine is not the act of sober reasoning, not

which was with the Father and was made manifest to us. That which we have seen and heard we proclaim to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us. And our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. And we write these things to you so that your joy may be complete. And this is the message which we have heard from him and announce to you: that God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all. If we say that we have fellowship with him and walk in the darkness,

we lie and do not do the truth. But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin. "And we proclaim to you the life." "That, then, which we have seen and heard we proclaim to you," he says. What does this mean? That he, being eternal life, was made manifest to us, and we became eyewitnesses of him both before the cross and after the resurrection. For the same one was nailed to the cross in the flesh and rose again in that same flesh. "And what do you gain from this message you bring us?" he says. This: just as through the word we make you sharers in what we saw and heard, so we also make you sharers in the Father and his Son Jesus Christ. Once we have obtained this, we will be filled with joy, as people joined to God. Or else: because you share with us, our joy over you is most complete. It is the joy the sower will be laden with when he receives his wages, rejoicing with the reapers, who also rejoice because they enjoy the fruit of their labors. Having said this, he takes up his theme again and makes clear what the message is that he heard. He says it is this: "God is light, and in him there is no darkness." And where did he hear this? From Christ himself, who said, "I am the light of the world," and, "I have come as light into the world." So he is light, and in him there is no darkness. He is light for the mind. He rouses the eyes of our soul to grasp him and turns them away from all these [visible?] things, and he makes our desire hasten toward him alone with the passion of love. By "darkness" he means either ignorance or sin. In God neither ignorance nor sin is found, for these belong to matter and to our composite nature. Somewhere it is said, "He made darkness his hiding place." But it said "He made," not "He is darkness," as it says "He is" [light]. For what is placed is different from the one who places it. So darkness here signifies that God cannot be known, because he cannot be comprehended, and this belongs to us, not to God. For one places in something what was not already there, and not for one's own sake but for the sake of those around one. That he also calls sin darkness is clear from what is said in the Gospel. For what does he say there? "And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it." There he calls our sinful [condition?] darkness. For he came in [?the likeness of sinful flesh], that is, he took it on, yet he had no share in the defilements that come from it, for "he committed no sin," and so on. "Since, then," he says, "we are made sharers in God, and he is light, and in such light darkness cannot subsist, as was shown, let us who share in the light no longer admit darkness into ourselves either. Otherwise we would pay the penalty for falsehood, and along with falsehood be torn away from fellowship with the light." So by remaining in fellowship with one another (that is, clearly, our fellowship with the light), we make ourselves invulnerable to
sin. "But how will this be for us?" he says. [?] … The whole sense of the passage is an overturning of the Jews' [?] … will forgive us. [?] By the great severity of his reproof, saying, "If we say…"

"If we say, 'We have no sin,' we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, so as to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness. If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us." [?] … so that, by pressing the reproof so hard, he may make them consider how great the charge is, and urge them to confession. How great a good comes from confession he showed when he said, "Be the first to tell your sins, so that you may be justified." It is also the custom of this beloved disciple and teacher to go over the same things many times, first more briefly and then more fully. He wants to make his hearers' knowledge of what is said clearer, and he hastens to make it a settled habit in them. He called God "faithful" in place of "true." For "faithful" is said not only of one who is trusted, but also of one who gives assurance, who by his own true character is able to impart this to others as well.

So God is faithful in this sense, and just in that he does not thrust away those who come to him, however they may have sinned. So he forgives sins without question to those who run through repentance to holy baptism, whether they have offended against him or against someone else. "If, then, we confess," he says, "we shall also obtain pardon for our offenses against one another. But if we shamelessly say we have not sinned, we shall do a double evil: we shall show ourselves liars, and we shall slander God, who is above all truth, as false." For he himself says through the Prophet, "They repaid me evil for good." And again in his own person: "If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness to the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?" Since this is so, if we say we have not sinned, we deny his word, which is spirit and life. "For the words that I speak," he says, "are spirit and life." And we no longer have his word dwelling gladly in us. What then will there be [?] …

"My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. And if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. And he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the whole world. And by this we know that we have come to know him: if we keep his commandments. Whoever says, 'I have come to know him,' and does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him. But whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God has been perfected. By this we know that we are in him. Whoever says he abides in him ought to walk [as he walked]." He knows how unstable and faulty our nature is. We always have living with us the inclination toward what is worse, and the envious demon lies in wait for our salvation. So those who have already been made God's own through confession are bound to sin if they do not live attentively. He knows this, and so he adds these words, so that even if we stumble after receiving forgiveness, we should not despair of ourselves. For if we turn back, we may obtain salvation again through the mediation of the Lord Jesus Christ. He intercedes with the Father for us and will make atonement for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the whole world. He said this either because he was writing to Jews and did not want to confine repentance to them alone, but to extend it to the Gentiles as well; or because the promise is not only for those living at that time but also for all who come afterward. He calls "Advocate" the one who entreats the Father for us, that is, who appeals to him. These things are said in a more human way, suited to the economy of salvation, like "The Son can do nothing of himself." He speaks this way so as not to seem opposed to God. For he showed in the case of the paralytic that the Son too has authority to forgive sins. Moreover, to the

disciples too he gave this power of forgiving sins when he breathed on them. [?] … [Keeping the commandments] reveals the intimate union, while not keeping them reveals that one has in no way been made his own. So whoever has known God has also been known by God, that is, has been made God's own and taken up by God. And in this the love of God is seen. Through this love he will possess perfection in God, and he will make it the mark of his closeness to God. For it is through works that perfect love is shown. However, it is possible to carry out the commandments correctly and precisely while oneself being rather sluggish in disposition, and this is far from God. That is why he says that whoever is in God, having been made his own, ought himself to direct the paths of his life according to him.

[CHAPTER TWO.] On love, without which people are ungodly. In which: an exhortation on the grace given to each according to age, and on turning away from love of the world. "Brothers, I am not writing a new commandment to you, but an old commandment, which you have had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you heard from the beginning.
