Yet again, I am writing a new commandment to you, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining. Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in the darkness. Whoever loves his brother abides in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling. But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes." He now turns to love for one's neighbors. He says that intimate union with God, that is, love for God, is known first of all from love for one's neighbor. It is not possible for someone enlightened by the knowledge of God and filled with his love to have the darkness that comes from hating his brother, for light and darkness cannot exist together in the same thing at the same time. So whoever is enlightened by love for God is set alight by love for his brother. Whoever has God also has the light that shines toward his brother. But whoever says he loves God yet hates his brother remains in perpetual darkness as to his eyes. He has lost the light that comes from union both with God and with his brother, and no longer knows what to do with himself [?]. The Epistle is catholic and addressed to all in common, both Jews and Greeks. For Jews it makes sense to say that he is writing them not a new commandment about love but an old one. For on the tablets of Moses it is written, "You shall love, after God, also your neighbor as yourself." But to Greeks, what could anyone say about an old commandment, when it is found nowhere among them? We say, then, that for them too the law of love toward one's neighbors has been written. Where and how? It is inscribed on the [?tablet] of the heart, in its natural notions. That the natural notions sown in us are called a law, Paul is enough to confirm, when he says, "But I see another law waging war against the law of my mind," the law that is truly in me. So the Greeks too had a law, that is, an old commandment, without realizing it. Nature itself lays down the law that people should be gentle toward all their kin and love one another, since man is a social animal, and this could not be without love. Indeed, ancient histories record many people dying for one another, which is the mark of the greater love, which

[?] our Savior declares: "No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends." So, since the commandment of love toward one's neighbours had been laid down of old for [?] and for the Jews, he says: "Besides the old commandment you heard about love of neighbour, I also write you a new commandment, which has its truth both in God, who has made you his own through communion with him, and in you who have entered into communion with him." For since he says, "I have come as light into the world," and the true light, as he puts it, is already shining, and darkness by its nature cannot subsist in light, let the true light of love shine from now on in an unfeigned disposition toward one's brother, and let the darkness of hatred pass away, that is, depart and vanish. For this is what "pass away" means in blessed Paul too, when he says, "For the form of this world is passing away." — Another reading of "I write you a new commandment": this commandment is new because the commandment of Moses was not universal but restricted to people of the same race and tribe. It taught them to love only their friends and to hate their enemies, as when it says, "You shall love your friend and hate your enemy." But the commandment of the Lord and of his apostles has a great deal of newness stamped into it. It commands, "Love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you," looking to their natural being and not to the disposition [?] that grows upon it from the wickedness of malicious people. "But whoever hates his brother." By these words he says something like this: whoever says he belongs to Christ and hates his brother is lying and does not belong to Christ. For if Christ loved him so much that he laid down his life for him, how can one who says he is Christ's hate his brother, for whom Christ died? Or it can be taken this way: whoever says he belongs to God and hates his brother, who is Christ (for Christ himself says, "I will proclaim your name to my brothers"), does not belong to God but to the devil. For if he were God's, he would love his brother, and through him Christ. "I write to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven you for his name's sake. I write to you, fathers [?], because you have known him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, children, because you have known the Father. I have written to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. I have written to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the [evil one]." Since he had said, "I write you a new commandment," he also takes note of the disposition of those receiving the letter, and he does so by means of the progress and advance that follow bodily growth. For he knew that they would not all receive the word with equal regard or with equal zeal. Some would receive it as children, at a more elementary level, and to them he also promises forgiveness

of sins through faith in Christ. Others would receive it as those who have advanced to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, and so far that they can beget others as well; to them he bears witness that they have knowledge of him who is from the beginning. And who is the one from the beginning, if not God the Word, who was in the beginning with God? Still others would receive it as young men, and since they are youthful and vigorous, he bears witness to their victory over the passions of dishonour. Then he takes up the same points again from another angle, fitting his teaching to the measure of their spiritual age. Since, he says, I know that you will receive what I write according to the differences of your ages, I too must measure out my teaching to suit the condition of your age. I must speak to some as children who have come to know the Father (he means God). I must speak to others as fathers, who have more knowledge than the children, since they have come to know him not only as Father but also as without beginning and beyond all searching out. For he was in the beginning, and to these it is fitting to set out more advanced words. Others, as young men who are strong and fit for wrestling and contests, I must anoint for the fight. By saying that the glory of victory belongs to them, he shows that they need noble words, words more suited to a general. Having thus apportioned his word to the ages of the spirit, some being people who will be so disposed toward his words, others being of the sort who come to the faith and ought to be instructed in a way that matches their own character, he then brings in his word of exhortation and says: "Do not love the world." This he says as to children, for children are always excited by whatever looks pleasant. Then, after stating why one ought not to love the world and the things in the world, he directs the rest of his teaching to the fathers and the young men, for grasping these things belongs to a more mature state. And so that you do not think that by "world" he means the system of heaven and earth, he adds what the world is and what the things in the world are. By "world" he means the common rabble, which does not have the love of the Father in itself. And what are the things in the world? Those that are carried out according to the desire of the flesh, which stir up desire through the senses. By naming the eyes, the chief of the senses, he included the rest as well. Every evil is found in desire: adulteries, drinking bouts, unseemly loves, and arrogance, the urge to be above everyone, which desire suggests so that the arrogant man may fearlessly carry out whatever comes into his head; murders, some committed out of greed, others to get rid of opponents; deceits, and these so that we may bring everything in our way under the power of deceit. In short, everything hostile to God is by nature brought about through desire for carnal things. "Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the

world, the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not from the Father but is from the world. And the world is passing away, and its desire with it; but whoever does [?] the will of God abides for ever." We have already said that he calls the common rabble "the world." That is why the Lord says to his disciples, "You are not of the world, just as I am not of the world." And the father of this world, I mean of worldly self-indulgence and confusion, is the devil. That is why the Lord also says to the Father about his disciples, "I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one," that is, from the world, which elsewhere he says lies in the evil one. — Another reading: if the evil one is opposed to the good Father, and whoever serves the desires of the world is not from the Father but from the world, it is plain that whoever is not from the Father but from the world is from the devil. So too in the Gospels he says to the Jews: "You are from the Father? No, you are from the devil", that is, from worldly pursuits, of which the devil is the sower and the gardener. And these worldly objects of desire, he says, have nothing lasting or stable about them but pass away, while the things that accord with the will of God endure and last for ever. It is not the mark of sensible people to look down on what stands firm and cling to what vanishes; that is like someone who tries to build on a mirage. "But whoever does the will of God." And what is the will of the Father? That they believe in the one whom he sent.

On false brethren who deny God. And that piety toward Christ is confession of the Father, for [?] the glorification of the Father is the confession of the Son's divinity. In this section also: on the divine and spiritual gift in sanctification, in hope, leading to the knowledge of God. That everyone who is in Christ is free of sin, for whoever sins is of the devil. "Children, it is the last hour; and as you heard that Antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have arisen. From this we know that it is the last hour."

[?] "it is the last hour" [?] more [?] as follows. Since the Epistle is catholic and suits every individual person, and since there is not one fixed limit of life for everyone but each person's own end is hidden from him, he rightly set each person before his own end. In this way, as if the last hour of life were at hand for each, watchfulness would follow, and so a blameless life and purity of conduct would always be practised among Christians. There is no room for the gloomy person who mocks this, saying that although "It is the last hour" was said so many years ago, the end has still not been reached. For compared with the span from the beginning of time, how long is the time from then until now, I mean from Christ? Besides, if every thing is divided into three parts, first, middle and last, then surely

there is nothing strange in calling everything from the middle on "last." So if the Lord came around the middle of the ten millennia (for his coming on earth was about the five-thousandth year), no one could object to calling everything from that point on "last," since it comes after the middle. Take a hundred years, for example: even the first years after the middle, the tenth or the twentieth and so on, could be called "last." So here too, since the mass of a thousand years has gone past the midpoint from the Lord's coming, everything from then on could rightly be called "last." This is the truest explanation, and it agrees with the golden John. But "last" can also be taken to mean "worst," as when we say, "I have come to the last extremity of evil." At that time the world was tossed about in great evils, the devil stirring them up after the coming of the Good One, either to test the good or to throw the better sort into confusion, so that no one could tell what was good and what was not. For this reason he called that time the last hour, since "last" suggests "worst," having the character of dregs or sediment. And he confirms the "last hour", whether in the sense of the worst or in the sense of the actual time, by the Antichrist. For if, he says, we expect the Antichrist in the last times, and now many antichrists have spread through the world (he means Cerinthus and those like him), it is clear that the time of the consummation has also arrived, since the many antichrists are preparing the way for the one. Having said this, he then adds where the antichrists came from, that [?]: "They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would have remained with us. But they went out so that it might be made plain that they are not all of us. And you have an anointing from the Holy One, and you know all things. I have not written to you because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is of the truth."

"They went out from us." He adds this too without arranging his words at all for clarity. I mean that he ought to have asked himself, as it were, "And where do these antichrists come from?" and then added, "They went out from us." That is what he should have done, but he does not; he puts it in this confused way, perhaps showing by the confusion of his words how distasteful these people were to him. [?] But because the antichrists came from among the Lord's disciples, they could win the trust of those they led astray, presenting themselves as disciples who framed the message of the preaching according to the teacher's mind, while in fact they were moving in a direction wholly contrary to the preaching. That is why he says they came from these: "They went out from us," he says. For after becoming disciples they abandoned the truth and invented their own blasphemies. To make the passage clearer, one must supply, "And where do these antichrists come from?" "For they were not of

us", that is, of the company of those being saved. For if they had been, they would have remained with their own. But as it is, this has happened to them "so that they might be made plain," that is, become evident, as people wholly estranged from us who have attached themselves to those who are not ours. For among these there are some who are not of us, and it is to them, evidently, that those who went out from us joined themselves. Because of them, he says, I also said, "They are not all of us." For having broken away from their own, they joined others who are strangers to us, preferring to live like pagans in licentiousness rather than chastely with us. Having said this, so that he would not seem to claim knowledge of these things for himself alone, and to boast over the faithful by them as if he alone knew them, he adds: "And you have an anointing." It is as though he said: but why do I go through these things with you as if you did not know them? You are not ignorant of them. For through holy baptism you received the sacred anointing, and through it the divine Spirit, who guides you into all the truth. Since this is so, you know that I write these things to you not as to people who do not know them, but as to people who do. What are these things? The last time, the onrush of the antichrists, and that no lie [?] is of the truth. Because falsehood has multiplied, he says, I also say that the antichrists have become many. For if Christ is the truth, and you have come to know him and have the truth in yourselves, then surely the liar, being opposed to the truth, that is, to Christ, is an antichrist.

Here too the conjunction "and" must be supplied for clarity, so that it reads: "And who is the liar but the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ?" This is the nonsense the impious Simon talked: that Jesus is one and the Christ another. Jesus, he said, was the one born of holy Mary, while the Christ was the one who came down from heaven at the Jordan. Whoever, then, he says, makes a noise with this lie is Antichrist. And "This is the Antichrist" must be taken in two ways: of the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ, and of the one who denies the Father and the Son. And whoever denies the Father and the Son, he says, he too

is a liar and an antichrist. For other heretics in their turn, from whom the accursed Valentinus sprang, said that there is another, unnameable Father besides the one called the Father of Christ. These same people also deny the Son by calling him a mere man and not God by nature as being from God. That is why he adds: "Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father either." This is like the Jews, who deny the Son while pretending to know the Father. But let them know that they do not even know the Father. For if they knew him, they would know that he is the Father of an only-begotten Son. The followers of Simon babbled the same nonsense. Such is their teaching, he says; but you must keep among yourselves what you heard from the beginning, that is, the proclamation of Christ as God. This is what he means to convey by "Let it abide in you." [?] "For if what you heard from the beginning abides in you, you too will abide in the Son and in the Father", that is, you will be partakers of him. "And this is the promise." The conjunction "and" must be taken as giving a reason. What is the promise? The one that says, "that, as I am in you, Father, and you in me, they too may be one in us." And again: "that they may have eternal life. And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you sent." Having finished his discussion of these things, he adds, "I have written these things to you about those who are leading you astray," that is, because of the heresies that have gone out. Then he again adds what we mentioned earlier, taking care not to burden them [?] ... this, it has already been said that he means the Holy Spirit.) So the Holy Spirit whom you received, since you hold him securely within yourselves, means that you have no need for anyone to teach you. But as the same anointing, that is, the Spirit, teaches you about all things, and just as it has taught you, you will abide in him. For it is true and is no lie, namely, what it has taught you. "And you, the anointing that you received." The order of the words is this: and you, since the anointing that you received from him abides in you, have no need for anyone to teach you. "And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have boldness and not shrink from him in shame at his coming. If you know that he is righteous, you know that everyone who does righteousness has been born of him. See what kind of love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God. This is why the world does not know us: because it did not know him. Beloved, we are God's children now, and what we shall be has not yet been revealed. But we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. And everyone who has this hope in him purifies himself, just as he is pure." Having spoken of the onrush of the antichrists and all their perverted teaching, by which, as if by

some identifying mark, he made them easy to recognize, and having firmly strengthened his readers to hold unwaveringly to what they had been taught, he then adds the reward laid up for these things, as though fortifying them with the splendour of the prizes. He says: "Abide in him." Why? "So that we may have boldness in him when he appears." For what is more glorious or more to be desired than boldness, when we come to display the labours of our life to him, and do so with boldness and with no shame at all at his coming? Since some would probably ask what they must accomplish to become pleasing to him, he teaches this too, saying: if you have known that he is righteous, then surely you also know that whoever does righteousness has been born of him, for the righteous one begets righteous ones. No one is unaware of how much this adds to your pride and boldness, nor of how great and of what kind is the love and kindness of the one who granted it to you. For you have seen that he granted us both to become and to be called his children. But if this, he says, is hidden from those in the world, I mean that we are sons of God, do not be surprised. For this is why it does not know you: because it did not know the one who adopted you either. We have shown in many places that by "world" he means the common rabble. Then, since he has established the fact of adoption, he goes on to speak more plainly of the glory and boldness laid up for those who have been adopted, and says: "Beloved, we are God's children now." It is as though he said: surely, beloved, you have learned from what came before that we have been taken up as sons of God. But if this has not yet been revealed, do not be troubled. What is now hidden will become plain when he is revealed. For when we appear like him, we shall display the splendour of our adoption, since sons are certainly like their father. And having boldness toward him as sons, we shall see him as he is, though clearly not as he is in his nature (for that is impossible for a created nature). How, then? The righteous will see the righteous one, the pure the pure one. For they will cleave to one who is like them and will be like him. That is why, a little earlier, I said that we shall be like him, but not by nature. Otherwise he would have said not "like" but "the same." As it is, since he did not say that, he says "like", clearly with respect to the quality of glory. Note also that above he did not say "everyone who did righteousness" or "who will do it," but "who does it." For the virtues are matters of practice and have their being in being done. Once they have stopped, or while they are still to come, they do not even exist. "Everyone who commits sin also commits lawlessness, and sin is lawlessness. And you know that he was revealed to take away our sins, and in him there is no sin. Everyone who [?] sins has not seen him or known him. Little children, let no one lead you astray: whoever does righteousness is righteous, just as he is righteous. Whoever commits sin is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The Son of God was revealed for this purpose, to destroy the works of the devil."

In what precedes he built up his argument about righteousness from the good things that belong to righteousness. Now he presses on with the proof from its opposite as well, and from what belongs to that, and says: "Everyone who commits sin." What he means is something like this: "You who have been adopted as sons, practise righteousness, and do not show yourselves idle in it. With sin, the lawless one or the sinner is not the one who has sinned once or will sin, but the one who clings to evil and is active in it. In the same way the righteous one is not the one who does nothing, but the one who is active." We should know that sin is a falling away from the good, while lawlessness is an offence against the enacted law. Each of these has its own starting point: the one, falling away from the good; the other, offending against the enacted law. Yet they also come together in the same thing. The one who sins has missed the goal that is according to nature and set in nature, for the goal of human nature is to live according to reason, far removed from irrationality. Likewise the one who acts lawlessly offends against the law given in nature, because he lives without self-control. The Lord's disciple, then, did well to bring both to the same point. "And you know that he was revealed." So that you may no longer have room to sin, he says. For Christ came to take away sin, since he himself had no share in sin, and so nothing is left for you either to sin, you who have come to be in him and have been made firm by faith in him. This is what he means by "Everyone who abides in him." This is the one who pursues the virtues without letting up and never stops practising them. "And in him there is no sin. Everyone who abides in him does not sin." The "And" stands for "Because." "Everyone who sins," and so on. He has said that he was revealed, and the reason why he was revealed, namely that he, who had committed no sin, might take away our sins, that is, blot them out. He then adds: "Everyone who sins has not seen him." For if you, he says, who saw him when he was revealed, received this sign of having seen him, that you are not easily overcome by sin, since you are firmly settled in him, then surely those who sin have not seen him, and therefore have not known him either. By "having seen" and "having known" he does not mean the mere contact of the eyes, nor that they formed some ready impression of what is known. He means that they approached him with a certain judgment and understanding, as we said above. Having said this, he goes on to confirm it: "Let no one deceive you." For it is not otherwise than this: "The one who does righteousness has known the Righteous One, and is righteous as he is," that is, God. And as with this, so again with the opposite: "The one who commits sin is of the sinner." This is the devil, who has been sinning from the beginning. That is why God, caring for his own creature, and being himself righteousness and sanctification, was revealed, that is, appeared in the world, in order to destroy the works of the devil, which are sin.

"The one who commits sin is of the devil." Since the devil turned aside and came to be in sin, everyone who practises sin is called his. For he takes the lead in the sinner by suggesting evil thoughts, as in the case of Judas. But someone will say: "How does the devil come to be in those who sin, when they sinned before he did, by giving him room?" We must answer that committing sin is the same thing as sinning by giving room to the devil. The sinner, led on by desire, gives him room once he has received him, by carrying out the sin in practice. This is what "committing" sin means. He was right to say "the one who commits" and not "the one who committed," for the one who has repented is no longer of the devil, but only the one who is still doing it. This is how someone is a slave of sin: by committing it, not by having committed it. That is why he says, "Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin."

On love for one's neighbour and a disposition to share; including a good conscience in faith in Jesus Christ; on discerning spirits by their confession of the Lord's incarnation.

"Everyone who has been born of God does not commit sin, because his seed abides in him; and he cannot sin, because he has been born of God. By this the children of God and the children of the devil are made plain: everyone who does not do righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother. For this is the promise which you heard from the beginning, that we should love one another. We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and slaughtered his brother. And why did he slaughter him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother's were righteous. Do not be surprised, my brothers, if the world hates you. We know that we have passed from death into life, because we love the brothers. The one who does not love his brother remains in death. Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him. By this we have known love, that he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers. But whoever has the world's livelihood, and sees his brother in need, and shuts his heart against him, how does the love of God abide in him? My little children, let us not love in word or with the tongue, but in deed and in truth."

"Everyone who has been born of God." Everyone who commits sin is of the devil insofar as he sins, and is called a son of the devil, as blessed Paul says to Elymas: "You who are full of all deceit and all villainy, son of the devil, enemy of all righteousness!" So it is clear that the one born of God, as a son of God, does not sin. And the reason is that his seed, God's seed, that is, is in him. This is the Spirit, which we received through the gift. Abiding in us, that is,

settled in us, it makes our mind incapable of receiving sin [?]. Christ himself too, as he dwells in the faithful, makes them sons of God, just as in the seed of Abraham, which is Christ, all the nations are blessed. He has now advanced his argument in this way to confirm what he said above, namely that the faithful are children of God. And he makes it indisputable both from the fact itself, I mean from not sinning, and from its opposite, as we said a little before. For opposite is set against opposite, as in dialectical arguments. Notice how precise the saying is. He did not first say that one is born of God or of the devil before the works had come first, whether of righteousness or of lawlessness. For from these comes adoption, whether by God or by the devil. Even if we have been saved by grace, that is said because of the surpassing greatness of God's goodness: though we had offended past all cure, he bore no grudge against our salvation. But Paul confirms that he does not give his salvation to the idle when he cries out, "to those who are called according to purpose." Likewise, those who have been adopted by the devil are so called because of their great love of wickedness, even if they were estranged from the womb and had not yet committed sin by deliberate purpose. For no one can become the devil's own without doing evil. Rather, the one who commits sin is taken up by the devil, either as a son, because he does evil all the more and by his own choice, or as a slave, because he has been thrown in the wrestling by the evil one, subdued by him, and condemned to servitude. Notice this too: of the one born of God he did not say, "He does not sin," so as not to include infants as well, who do not sin because of their age. He said instead, "He does not commit sin." "He does not sin" amounts to a simple negation, whereas "he does not commit" shows that sin is not present in his disposition. That is why he also adds, "and he cannot sin." He does not mean a natural inability, as when we say that irrational animals cannot acquire knowledge, but a deliberately chosen inactivity in sin. He has gone through these things, and has declared that the mark of God's children is not committing sin, just as, conversely, the mark of the devil's sons is sinning. Having gone through them, then, he returns after much in between to love of neighbour, as if he had dealt with everything in between for its sake, since love is the fulfilment of all things. And he says: "The one who does not love his brother is not of God." For "is not of God" applies to this clause too. He means this: since the one who does righteousness has been born of God, it follows that one so born loves the brothers. But the one who does not do righteousness, and by not doing it hates his brothers, is not of God, and that in no other way than by not having been born of him. And he shows how such a one is not of God by saying, "This is the message

which you heard from the beginning." We have already said what this message is: that it is both natural and taught. It also comes with the commandment of the Law about loving one's neighbour, and with the Lord's commandment that says, "A new commandment I give you, that you love one another." Besides this, the natural bond with one's own kind also compels us to do this. Since, then, the commandments are of such a kind and so many, according to the Lord's declaration, the one who keeps his word and does it has eternal life and has passed from death into [?]

For these reasons, then, let us love the brothers. We are hated by the world, he says, but let this not harm us at all by provoking us to rivalry, so that we too should hate the brothers. Rather, let the Lord's word be more effective in us. For the one who hates his brothers is not only cast out of eternal life but is also a murderer; for it follows [?] for the murderer that he does not have eternal life either. Look at Cain, he says: he too hated his brother and killed him, though he was his brother. Since he had evil works, he was a son of the devil, while Abel, doing righteous works, was called a son of God. The devil is opposed to God, and evil works to good ones; that is why Cain too, being opposed to his brother, killed him. That would be the logical order of the argument. Blessed John, however, changed the order, as he always gives way to what is most urgent. Since he had mentioned the devil and those adopted by him through evil action, he felt it urgent to set forth as an example the one who, from the beginning of the world, ran off through evil works to become a child of the evil one. Having finished with Cain, and with those who emulate him and so are bound to inherit his lot, he runs back again to love and the good things that have come from it. He says that love persuaded the Lord to lay down his life for us, and that by this example we too ought to lay down our life for the brothers. And since this is rare and found among few, he begins his exhortation to brotherly love with more modest things, as if to shame them, and arranges his argument roughly like this: "Why do I speak of laying down one's life for the brothers, when we see some who do not even meet their brothers' need for the necessities of life? And I do not mean those who are short of a livelihood, but those whose wealth amounts almost to the whole world." Let them be shamed by this: if in these small matters they have shut their hearts, and so have shown themselves unworthy and empty of God's love, what would they show in the greater matter of dying for the brothers? Then he adds another rebuke, aimed at those who accept love in word and display it, but with the tongue alone, and says: "Let us not love in word and with the tongue, but in deed and in truth."

"And by this we know that we are of the truth, and we shall persuade our hearts before him. For if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows all things. Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have boldness toward God, and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what is pleasing in his sight. And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ."

"By this we know." By what? By loving not in word but in deed and in truth. And what do we know? That we are of the truth. How? Because the one who says one thing and does another, whose action does not agree with his word, is a liar and not truthful. "And we shall persuade our hearts before him." He means this: by this, by being truthful (and we shall be truthful when our deeds match our words), we shall persuade our conscience. This is what he means by "hearts." And how shall we persuade them? By settling it within ourselves that we speak our words with God as our witness. That is what "before" means. For if we do not act this way, he says, but our conscience, that is, our heart, condemns us, then our sinning does not go unnoticed. If, when we sin, we cannot escape the notice of our conscience, small as it is, belonging to a small creature, much less could we escape the notice of God, who is unbounded and present everywhere. So the whole saying runs like this: My little children, let us not lie to one another by loving with the tongue alone; let us show our love in deed as well. For by this we shall know that we are of the truth, that is, of God. And whatever we say, let us say it as though God were watching. No one would bring himself to lie with God as witness, not even someone more shameless than the demons. For if we do not act this way, but our heart convicts us of falsehood while we say that we love, we sin. How? We imagine that we can escape the notice of God, who is present everywhere, and we do not even grasp this: if we cannot escape the notice of our own heart, small as it is, how shall we escape the notice of him who is absent from nowhere? So, beloved, he says, if we have prepared ourselves to be beyond reproach in our own eyes, that is, by being truthful with one another, we shall have boldness toward God. And from that boldness we shall certainly receive from him whatever we ask. Why? Because we keep his commandments. Nothing does more to move the one who is asked to grant a request than the obedience of those who ask, when that obedience to the one asked is beyond dispute. Since, then, we too keep his commandments and do what pleases him, we are confident that we shall not fail in our requests. For when there is goodwill on both sides, it is readily repaid without delay to whichever comes in need of the other. And which of his commandments have we kept? The one that says, "Have love among one another." Since, then, we have a commandment that, by faith [?] in the name of his Son

Jesus Christ, we should love one another, and we have done this, we know from this that the grace of his Spirit, which he gave us, is settled in us. We should know that in many places in the New Scripture we find the phrase "to believe in the name of Jesus our Lord." What does this mean? Nothing other than his glory, his will, his renown. It means glory and renown, as in "Wonderful is your name in all the earth"; it means will, as here, and in "Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus," where it stands for "in the will." And what is the will of the Lord Jesus? To baptize all the nations into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

"And that we love one another, just as he gave us commandment. And the one who keeps his commandments abides in him, and he in him. And by this we know that he abides in us: by the Spirit which he gave us."

This stands for loving one another, he says, with a true disposition. And where is this commanded? Where he said, "Just as you wish people to do to you, do the same to them." If, then, we want our neighbours to be disposed toward us truly and without guile, we too should surely be disposed in the same way toward them. And if this is the Lord's commandment, much more, when we abide in him, that is, are settled in him, will he too give himself to us. For he cannot deny himself. That is, he would not be found to be giving us his commandments in empty words, but would first confirm them in himself. And if so, then surely, if we do what he commands, we too shall find him listening to us in whatever we ask, and his gift will remain firm in us. The whole sense of the passage is this: that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another truly, as his commandment says. For the one who keeps his commandments abides in him, and he in him. And from this we know that he abides in us: by the Spirit, that is, the gift, which he gave us. For as long as this remains inviolate, we can be sure beyond dispute that his gift will not be taken from us. And how will it remain inviolate? If we do not neglect, in any way, what he commanded us about love.

"Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are of God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world. By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh is of God. And every spirit that does not confess Jesus Christ come in the flesh is not of God. And this is the spirit of the Antichrist, of which you have heard that

it is coming, and now it is already in the world. You are of God, little children, and you have overcome them, because he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world. They are of the world; that is why they speak from the world, and the world listens to them. We are of God. The one who knows God listens to us. Whoever is not of God does not listen to us. By this we know the spirit of truth and the spirit of error."

He has gone through his discussion of love for one's neighbours, and has declared that this love is a mark that the Spirit we received abides in us. Now he adds a way of telling true brothers from their counterfeits. With this, we shall not fall in with false brothers, false apostles and false prophets because of the commandment about love, and so bring the greatest harm on ourselves. For if we cling to them as if they were like-minded, we shall first harm ourselves, by sharing the word of faith with the impious and setting holy things before dogs. Then we shall also harm those who look to us. For our love for them will persuade many to take them as teachers and to believe what they say without caution, beguiled by their association with us. And what is their mark? Only this, he says: "Every spirit that confesses." Every spirit, that is, every gift of prophecy or rank of apostleship, that confesses the Lord Jesus come in the flesh is of God. But whatever does not confess this is not of God; this rank comes from the Antichrist, of which you have heard. When? From what he said a little earlier: "Many antichrists are in the world," that is, the forerunners of the Antichrist. Confessing the Lord's coming in the flesh, he says, is done not with the tongue but with works. How? As blessed Paul says: "Always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body." So whoever has Jesus at work in him, and has died to the world, and no longer lives for the world but for Christ, and carries him about, not only in Christ's flesh but in his own as well, is of God. But whoever lives not for Christ but for the world, that is, for the world's luxuries, is not of God. That is why Paul too says: "Where there is strife and dissension among you, are you not fleshly, and walking in a merely human way?" The one who walks in a human way does not have the Spirit of Christ. And the one who does not have the Spirit of Christ, that is, who does not live according to Christ, having put himself to death to the world, does not belong to Christ. When he says the Antichrist is "already in the world," he means not bodily, but through those who prepare the way for his coming: false prophets, false apostles and heretics. This Antichrist will be a man who carries Satan within him, exalting himself above every so-called god or object of worship. So he will also reject the worship of idols, which is what he meant by "so-called gods." And by "every object of wor-

[?] and Christianity, and will attempt to declare himself alone to be God. Having made known by these marks the prophets and apostles of the Lord, he adds: “But you who are from God, little children, have overcome them [?] speaking [from the world].” That is, by teaching in accordance with fleshly desires they keep them as their obedient hearers, the perverse holding the perverse. But you, since you are from God and have become estranged from worldly desires, we are made unacceptable to them. Yet the one who lives soberly listens to us, and because of this, knowing God, he is ready to lend us his ear. That is why Christ too says, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear,” testifying that the one who is prepared to obey readily is the one who has ears. Having drawn these distinctions, he then adds, as a seal on what he has already said, that by this we know those who have the spirit of truth, that is, the true prophetic dignity, and the spirit of error, the spirit of false prophe[cy] [?]

On brotherly love leading to godliness. “Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God. And everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God. He who does not love has not known God, because God is love. In this the love of God was made manifest, that God has sent his only-begotten Son into the world, so that we might live through him. In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins. Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.” After this he takes up again the discourse about love. Having shown whom we must love, namely those of like character, he then holds to what he said at the beginning: that both love and the one who loves are from God, that only the one who loves has been born of God and knows God, and that the one who does not have love is also ignorant of God. He confirms opposites by opposites. And he establishes how the one who does not love has not known God in this way: “God is love.” How is this clear? From the fact that he sent his only-begotten Son into the world, so that he might grant us true life

and we might live through him. For just as he is called goodness, because out of goodness he established the intelligible world and the sensible world, so that he might have sharers in himself, who truly is, so too, out of his love for us, by giving his only-begotten Son into the world he showed through this as well that he is love. That is why the apostle himself adds, “In this is love,” in place of “In this it is shown that God is love.” Then, extolling the beauty of God's love, he says: God did not do this, giving his own Son for us, because we loved him. That would be what the beloved owe, to return an equal affection to those who love them. Rather, he took the initiative in his kindness toward us out of love and sent his Son. And he did not only send him, but sent him to make expiation for our sins by his own blood. If, then, he says, God so loved us, although we share nothing with him by nature, much more ought we to love those who share our nature, and, knowing the good that comes from love, to minister it to one another. For just as it brings reproach on someone not to choose what is worth choosing and not to love what is lovable, so it wins praise for those who love the ones worthy of love, because they are lovable. When we are so disposed, we have both: we are beloved, because we have been loved by God and taken to himself by him, and we are loving, through our love for our neighbors. But this must be sincere and pure love, not the passionate and filthy kind that could arise even among robbers and other evildoers. “No one has ever beheld God. If we love one another, God abides in us, and his love has been perfected in us. By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit. And we have beheld and testify that the Father has sent the Son as Savior of the world.” We said before this too that it is the custom of this blessed man to take up the same things about the same subjects, both because he wishes to give his disciples a settled habit of what is said, and because he leads the discourse to greater clarity and completeness. For by approaching it in one way and then another from what can be observed in the matter, and as it were filling up what was lacking in the discourse, he makes a most complete demonstration of what he says. Using this method now too, he says: “No one has ever beheld God.” In speaking about love toward the brothers he had put forward God as an example, who gave his only-begotten Son to death because of his love for us. It would be natural for someone to say, “And how can you say this about things unseen and unattainable, and assure us about things that no one has yet known?” So he goes along with those who speak this way and says himself that no one has ever seen God. “I agree as well,” he says. “But from our love for one another we know that God is in us.” And he is right to say this,

for we grasp that things invisible to us exist from their activities. Just as no one has seen [?], but perceives from its activities and movements that it is present, so too we know his love for us as from [?] movement and activity. And if this is not unreasonable, then neither does this divine man unreasonably show from his activity that God is also in us. And what is this activity? Pure and guileless love toward our neighbors. For this love is both active and unfailing, of course in being pure. This is the mark both of our abiding in him and of his abiding in us. And this, he says, he has given us from his Spirit, for the one who is pure bestows things that are pure and undefiled by any filth. Since, then, we share in him through pure love, from this we too, he says, who beheld him in the flesh, have known and testify that the Father has sent him as Savior of the world. Besides our knowledge, he himself also explained this, bringing us into such knowledge more perfectly. At one time he said, “I came forth from the Father and have come into the world,” speaking of the sending of his only-begotten Son down from heaven into the world for love of us. And again he said it more clearly in other words: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish,” and, “I did not come to judge the world, but to save the world.” So we know, he says, both from seeing him with our own eyes and from the exposition of the Only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, as is said in the Gospels, and from the activity of our love for one another, that God is in us, that he has given us of his Spirit, and that we share in him. “Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God. And we have known and believed the love that God has in us. God is love, and he who abides in love abides in God, and God in him. In this love has been perfected with us, so that we may have boldness on the day of judgment, because as he is, so are we in this world.” This refers back to what was said a little earlier, that every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh is from God. He has sufficiently shown that they are children of God and that God abides in them. He showed this through their love for one another, which confirms that the Holy Spirit, that is, spiritual gifts, has been given to them. So he brings the discourse back again to those matters and says, “Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him.” He means something like this: I said above that every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh

is from God. But as my discourse went on, he says, it also brought something else to light. So I put this forward as well: those who confess these things also have the Spirit abiding in themselves, that is, God and his spiritual gifts, and they themselves abide in God. And we do not say this at random, but with firm knowledge and faith, through our love for one another. Having mentioned love, he also adds again what he had said about love earlier, giving the discourse about love great credibility. “In this love has been perfected.” He wishes us, he says, to be perfected in love, so that we may have boldness on the day of judgment, clearly toward the one who became man, since he is the judge, according to his own declaration: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” And he made clear by what follows that our boldness will be toward the one who became man, saying, “As he is, so are we in this world.” He means this: since it has already been shown that God is in us and we in him, we also bear witness to ourselves, he says, of the perfection of love. As, then, he was blameless and pure in the world, which is why he said, “The ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me,” so we too shall be in the world, he says. For “is” and “are” are either used with one tense in place of another, as is the custom of Scripture, or they signify something deeper. For he has often said that [?] we are in God and God in us. If this is so, and he is in us purely, that is, as a guide and source of purity for us, then let us too carry him about in this world, carrying him purely and cleanly in the body. Living in this way, he says, we shall have boldness toward him, and then we shall be free of all fear. For when we have been perfected in love through good works, we shall be far from fear. And he adds [?] that “perfect love casts out fear.” [?] What kind of fear? He himself says: the fear of punishment. For some may love out of fear of being punished. But this fear has not been perfected, that is, it does not belong to perfect love. Having said these things about perfect love, he also shows compellingly that we ought to love God, because he, he says, first loved us. And we ought to hasten all the more eagerly to repay the one who took the initiative in doing us good, as has been said above at greater length. Some have asked how, when David says, “Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for those who fear him lack nothing,” this apostle now says, “Perfect love casts out fear.” Are we to suppose that the saints of God, who are commanded to fear, have not been perfected in love? We say, then, that fear is twofold. One is preliminary. It brings punishment with it as its companion, because of the terrible deeds a person has done, since the one who approaches God

is afraid, and for this reason approaches him so as not to be punished. This is the preliminary fear. The perfecting fear, on the other hand, is free from such dread. That is why it is called pure and enduring forever and ever: “For the fear of the Lord,” he says, “is pure, enduring forever and ever.” The preliminary fear is neither pure nor lasting, but fades away in perfect love. What, then, is the perfecting fear, and what is its cause? It is the fear of one who, having been taken up perfectly into love, is anxious not to fall short in anything that one who loves deeply would naturally do for the beloved. “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. And whoever fears has not been perfected in love. We love him, because he first loved us. If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar. For he who does not love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen? And this commandment we have from him, that he who loves God should love his brother also.”

The one who genuinely loves God does what pleases God not because of the threat of punishments, but out of the charm of virtue and love for God, though not without keeping himself safe through genuine fear, which is a passionate love of the good. Or again, there is the one who acts out of fear of falling into punishment, and this is the same as the first kind. That is why he adds, “Fear has punishment.” “If anyone says, ‘I love God.’” He has compellingly demonstrated that love passes across, both from God to us and from us to him, and he has added again that if God so loved us, we too ought to love one another. Now he brings the discourse back to this point once more. He says that it is laid upon us as a debt to love our brother, after the example of God's love toward us, and that by giving back and repaying God in this way we shall be discharging the debt. So we must, he says, love our brother without delay, as the most perfect mark of love toward God. For if we do not, neither could our love toward God be preserved, since the debt toward one another, which we have incurred from our love toward God, would collapse. “For he who does not love his brother.” To this he also adds a most vivid argument to refute those who try to counterfeit divine love, saying something like this: love truly arises from familiarity with one another. Familiarity brings with it seeing one's brother, and through this especially one is bound to love him, for sight draws one toward love. If this is so, the one who makes nothing of what draws more strongly to love and does not love the brother whom he has seen, how could he truthfully claim [?] to practice loving God whom he has not seen, who is neither familiar to him nor apprehensible by any sense? If, then, someone shamelessly says, [?]

that he loves God but hates his brother, does he not, besides counterfeiting divine love, also turn out to be a transgressor of his commandment? Which commandment? The one that says, “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another.” So the one who loves God and insists that he is his disciple also loves his brother, according to his commandment.
On the theology of the Son in the glory of the Father, and on the victory over the evil one through faith in Jesus Christ
“Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God. And everyone who loves the one who begot also loves the one begotten of him. By this we know that we love the

[children of God, when we love God and] keep his commandments. For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome. For everything that has been born of God overcomes the world, and this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith. Who is the one who overcomes the world, if not the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” Having said these things, he confirms the discourse once more with further arguments, building it up somewhat like this: if we received a commandment from the Teacher to love one another, then surely, if we believe that our teacher Jesus is the Christ (and he is Christ in this, that he is God and man), we shall also keep his commandments, as those of a teacher and as those of God. And believing him to be God, we shall be called his sons, as is said in the Gospels: “But as many as received him,” that is, as many as believed in him, “he gave them power to become children of God.” And if we have been born of him, we shall surely also show what is fitting toward the one who begot us. What is that? To love the one who begot us, since this follows naturally for children toward their fathers. Since this is so, he says, all of us who have believed have been born of him. (And if we have been born of him, we are debtors for this reason too to love one another, both as brothers and as born of him.) So he adds proof of this as well: that the one who loves the one who begot also loves the one begotten of him. Then he turns the argument around and says that love toward the brothers, that is, the children of God, confirms love toward the one who bore them. Above he said, “He who loves God loves his brother also”; but now, reversing it, he says that the one who loves the children of God also loves God. And he makes love toward one's brother the proof of love toward God. Then he says that love toward God also brings about the keeping of his commandments, and he is right to say so: “For he who loves me,” the Savior himself says, “keeps my commandments.” “For this is the love of God.” The passage before us is to be read as a hyperbaton, like this: “For this is love, that we keep his commandments, because everything that has been born of

675 OECUMENIUS [?] God.” The words “are not burdensome” have been inserted in between. “And his commandments are not burdensome.” He did not say, as Christ did, “My yoke is light,” that the commandments are light, but that they are not burdensome. For to one who is rising in virtue even very heavy things seem light, just as to one who has cast off the vigor that accomplishes all good things even very light things seem heavy. Since some thought that God's commandments were burdensome because they were God's, he says for this reason, “His commandments are not burdensome.” For what is burdensome about loving one's brother? Or what is burdensome about visiting someone in prison? He does not tell us to rescue the prisoner, which is difficult, but only to visit him. Nor does he tell us to rid the sick of their disease, but only to visit them. Nor does he command us to set a lavish table before the hungry, or to give the naked a garment made with excessive embroidery, but only what supplies the basic need that the hungry and the naked are seeking. Having dealt with these matters in this way, he adds to what has already been said another inducement to practice love. What is it? Victory. For he says: by your love toward your brother you show yourselves to be children of God, and you already have this as the consequence of that achievement: overcoming the world. For what has been born of God overcomes the world. Then he sets forth both the victory and the means of the victory, saying that both are faith, namely faith toward God. This faith, born of God, conquered and drove out all unbelief, and neither Jew, nor Greek, nor heretic can stand against it. And since faith does not conquer on its own, but together with the one who has it, he therefore adds: “And who is the one who overcomes the world, if not the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” And who is this Jesus? “Jesus the Christ, through water and blood. This is the one who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ, not in the water only, but in the water and the blood. And it is the Spirit who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth. For there are three that testify: the Spirit, and the water, and the blood, and the three agree as one. If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God which he has testified concerning his Son. He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. He who does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has testified concerning his Son. And this is the testimony: that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. He who has the Son has life; he who does not have the Son of God does not have life.” Since he has mentioned God's begetting and birth, [?]

[?]…saying, "Everything that is born of God"; and since these things come to us through holy baptism, he therefore says, "This is the one who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ." And for what purpose did he come? To give us new birth and make us sons of God. This is understood as following from what was said, so that the sense is: "And everything that is born of God conquers the world." And how was it born? "By water," he says, "and blood." For Jesus Christ, who came, gives new birth by water and blood. Then he adds, taking up the statement again, that he gives new birth not "by the water only," that is, "but by the water and the blood." For he wishes first to show how Christ, who adopts us as sons, was made manifest: that in him a man was first adopted as son by God, and through his own adoption granted such a dignity to us; and that he was revealed on three occasions. First at the baptism in the Jordan, when the Father bore witness from above that the one being baptized was the beloved Son. And who was it that went down into the water, if not the man united to God the Word, the visible one joined to the hidden one? For it was to him that the witness had to be given. By the water, then, that is, in the baptism of water, Jesus was revealed as Son of God through the Father's witness. By the blood, when, about to be crucified, he said, "Glorify me, Father," and the voice came, "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again," which those who heard it took for thunder. And by the Spirit, when as God he rose from the dead. For this belongs to God alone, to raise himself. By the word "Spirit" God is signified, since God too is Spirit. Since three, then, bear witness to Jesus' sonship, namely the baptism, the cross and the resurrection, the Lord's sonship is beyond dispute. Through this sonship, since he is the firstfruits of the whole lump of humanity, he has granted to us also to be sons of God. And these three point to the one Christ. This is what he means by saying, "The three are for the one," that is, for the witness about Christ. But it should be known that some of the Fathers said the Spirit stands not for the resurrection but for the Father, when at the Jordan he cried out, "This is my beloved Son," inasmuch as God too, as we said before, is called Spirit. Having said this, he goes on to make what he has said believable by arguing from the lesser, speaking thus: If we accept the witness of human beings about anything at all, should we not with much more justice accept the witness that comes from God, who is greater? For is not this witness about his Son, that is, Christ, from God? So the one who believes in the Son of God, that he is God as the Son of God, has the witness in him, that is, in himself, believing that he too is adopted as son through Jesus, who was adopted by God. But the one who does not believe is liable to two evils: to unbelief, since he makes God a liar, and to depriving himself of adoption, and through this also of the eternal life which he has promised to those he adopts [?]…

…Christ, which he himself also has in himself, as is written in the Gospel: "In him was life." So the one who has the Son through holy baptism also has life. For "as many of us as were baptized into Christ," that is, according to his commandment, "have put on Christ." But whoever does not have the Son of God through baptism does not have life either, and is dead. For he takes us when we are dead in our trespasses and raises us through holy baptism. As has been said many times, the one who has been buried with Christ through the immersion of baptism is dead to the world, that is, to worldly desires, and lives no longer for himself but for Christ, walking in newness of life according to his commandments and no longer giving sin any way in. "I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life, and so that you may believe in the name of the Son of God. And this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us. And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests from…"

Again, by way of epilogue, he sums up and says: I have written these things to you as heirs of eternal life. For these things would not be written to those who do not live in the hope of eternal life, since it is not commendable to give what is holy to the dogs, or to throw pearls before swine. Since he is writing these things, then, to heirs of eternal life, he goes back over them, as we have said, briefly reminding them of what has already been said. First, that one must believe without wavering in the name of the Son of God, that is, in the religion handed down to us by him; for this is what "the name of the Son of God" is meant to signify, as we have already said. To this, of course, the grace of holy baptism opens the way. Next, that the sign of this undoubting faith is nothing other than the confidence toward him which we find through blameless faith, as we also said above. And again, he has set down as the sign of such confidence that we do not fail to obtain anything we ask. But since not everyone obtains everything they ask, nor are they heard in what they ask, he adds "according to his will," since the one who asks against the will of the teacher will certainly not be heard. In this he declares the same as blessed James, who also says, "You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly," that is, for what is not good for you. Then, turning this sign around into a clearer mark, he says: "And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests we have asked of him." He means something like this: If we ask according to his will, he hears us. And if he hears us in whatever we ask, we know

that we are making our requests according to his will, and we have in ourselves the things we have asked for. These are his kingdom and his righteousness, which he himself commanded us to ask for. Having said this, he also sets out explicitly one of the things in accordance with God's will that he wants us to ask for. For since almost through the whole Epistle he has dwelt at length on extolling love for one's brother, and on the fact that God wills that love for one's brother be kept unadulterated, he now says that this is one of his wishes: that if anyone sees his brother sinning not unto death, he should ask, and God will give to him. And what will he give? Eternal life. To whom? To those who do not sin unto death.

On helping a brother who sins through prayer, and on not sinning; including abstaining from the worship of demons.

"If anyone sees his brother sinning a sin not unto death, he shall ask, and God will give him life—to those who sin not unto death. There is a sin unto death; I do not say that he should make request about that. All unrighteousness is sin, and there is sin that is not unto death. We know that everyone who is born of God does not sin, but the one born of God keeps himself, and the evil one does not touch him. We know that we are of God, and the whole world lies in the evil one. And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God. And we are in the true one, in his Son Jesus Christ."

"If anyone sees his brother sinning." This is one of his wishes. For it belongs to righteousness to grieve with a brother who has sinned and to work with him toward his salvation. "There is a sin unto death." The order of the sentence is: There is a sin unto death, and there is a sin not unto death; I do not say that he should ask about the sin unto death, but about the sin not unto death. Then he clarifies the statement by distinguishing between the sin unto death and the sin not unto death. For he makes the division as from the genus of sin in general, and says, "All unrighteousness is sin," that is, both the sin unto death and the sin [not] unto death. But about the sin unto death, he says, let no one make request, that is, ask. For he will not be heard, because he asks wrongly; he is speaking of the one who shows no sign of turning back. For this is [the sin] unto death [?]… [of those who do not] turn back, but cling to grudges and keep up their anger against their neighbor, and sin without repenting. Having made this clear, he then indicates whose part it is to sin unto death, and says that the one adopted by God would not

ever fall sick with either the sin unto death or the sin not unto death. For [?] having given himself over to Christ, who dwells in him through adoption, he will remain untouched by sin. However, so that no one should think that such a person has had his nature changed altogether, so as to be from then on beyond the reach of sin, he adds "keeps himself," implying that if he does not keep himself and guard himself from the evil one, he will certainly sin. So it is not by nature that he advances to sinlessness, he says, but by the bounty of God, who in adopting us deemed us worthy of this grace, so that by guarding and keeping what has been given

we may also have the power not to sin. For otherwise, he says, since the world lies in the evil one (by "world" he means those who have not transferred themselves by good works into God's adoption), nothing would prevent us from being counted among those who perish, since the mind of man is diligently set on evil from his youth, as God declared at the time of the flood. But since, he says, the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, that is, the discernment to recognize him by inward knowledge as true God, and to be in him, in his true Son Jesus Christ, we have come to know through this bounty that this is the true God and eternal life; and knowing it, we remain unharmed by the evil one and his snares. "This is the true God." Here too "this" stands in place of the relative article. "Guard yourselves from idols." Some have asked: if he is writing these things to perfect believers, why does he now give this charge, as if to someone rather sluggishly disposed toward

[Argument] of the Second Catholic Epistle of John

He writes this one as an elder to a lady and her children. The occasion of the Epistle is this: seeing that her children were conducting themselves well in the

faith, and that many deceivers were going about saying that Christ's coming was not in the flesh, he writes the Epistle. First he commends her children for walking well. Then, teaching that our mystery is nothing new, he again exhorts them about love, and urges them to remain in the teaching handed down to them. Next he teaches that whoever says that Christ has not come in the flesh is Antichrist. And he instructs them not to receive such people into their house, nor to greet them. And so he brings the Epistle to an end.

Chapters of the Second Catholic [Epistle] of John

1. After the preamble, on right living in the love of God through a devout and unshakeable faith; including that one must not take a heretic into one's house, or greet [him] on [?]…

The Second Catholic Epistle of John the Apostle

"The elder to the elect lady and her children, whom I love in truth, and not I alone but also all who have known the truth, because of the truth that remains in us (and it will be with us forever): grace, mercy and peace will be with you from God the Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, in truth and love."

Some have thought that this Epistle and the one after it are not by John the beloved but by another man of the same name, because in them he styles himself "elder," and writes to a woman and to another person, Gaius—a single individual, just as the woman is one—which is not the way of a catholic epistle. They also point out that he did not compose the heading as in the first Epistle, since he did not begin that one in this way. But we say that in the first Epistle he did not do this, writing a heading of this kind, because he was not writing to a particular person, nor to the Church of particular places, as blessed Peter did when he specified that he was writing to the Jews in the dispersion, and before him the divine James, who specified that he was writing to the twelve

tribes of the Jews. Rather, since he was addressing his discourse to all the faithful in common, both those who gather in church and those who do not, he left out the form of a heading. Here he styles himself "elder," and not "apostle" or "servant of Jesus Christ," as the other apostles do. He does not call himself an apostle perhaps because he was not the first to proclaim the word in Asia, but came after Paul; and he did not do so in passing, as Paul did while running the circuit of the Gospel, but stayed there and set forth the word in person to those who were present. Nor does he call himself "servant of Jesus Christ," for, because he was so greatly loved, he was confident that he was beyond the fear that belongs to servitude. He saw fit to call himself only "elder," either because he was already old when he wrote these letters, or because by "elder" he was calling himself a bishop, since at that time it was customary for the name "elder" to be applied to bishops as well, as is clear from the Acts written by blessed Luke and from the Epistle of Peter. In writing to a believing woman he held nothing back, because in Christ Jesus he recognizes neither male nor female. And in writing to Gaius, a single individual, he has the precedent of Paul writing to Titus and Timothy, and to Philemon, a private person. So much for the heading. The genuineness of the Epistles is shown by their style and by the rest of the way the discourse is arranged. For here too he often brings the discourse back, saying the same things about the same matters, with only a small occasion intervening, and in this way making the discourse secure. He testifies to two things in this Elect lady: first, that she walks in love; second, that she turns away from heretics. He calls her Elect either from her name or from her zeal for virtue. He says that he loves her in truth, and not only her but also all who are of like character with her, who have the truth that truly is firmly established within them. This is what he means by "which remains in us"; and this is faith in Christ. He says he loves "in truth" because it is also possible to love in pretence, with the mouth, as this same author showed in the first Epistle regarding certain sluggish believers. Having said "which remains in us," meaning the truth that is genuine and steadfast and not put on for show, he added "and will be with us forever," signifying that the gift cannot be lost. For it is possible even for those who are firmly established on something to be shaken again, if they do not make good use of their steadfastness. To this he adds, "Grace and mercy will be with us," showing the good things that blossom from perfect love. Having said "from God the Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ," he added "the Son of the Father." For he alone is properly Father. That is why Paul too says, "from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named." And again he adds "in truth and love," giving security to the statement and a mark of the love he speaks of.
After the preamble, on right living in the love of God through a devout and unshakeable faith; including that one must not take a heretic into one's house, [or] greet [him] on [?]…

"I rejoiced greatly that I have found some of your children walking in truth, just as we received a commandment from the Father. And now I ask you, lady, not as though I were writing you a new commandment, but the one we have had from the beginning, that we love one another. And this is love, that we walk according to his commandment. This is the commandment, just as you heard from the beginning, that you should walk in it. For many deceivers have gone out into the world, who do not confess Jesus Christ coming in the flesh."

"I rejoiced greatly." For it is truly a cause of the greatest joy to find someone travelling the course of faith in Christ without stumbling, according to his commandment. And what is the commandment? The one of which Christ says in the Gospels, "Whoever loves me will keep my commandments." Here he calls Christ "Father," since Christ is also father of the sons given to him by his own Father through the economy, as it is said: "Behold, I and the children whom God has given me." Notice also the genuineness of this Epistle, in that by these words it agrees with what was said in the first: "And we know that whoever loves God keeps his commandments." Walking according to the commandments is the same as keeping them. For the virtues are practical, and have their being in being exercised; so that whoever stops travelling by them neither keeps nor guards them. "Walking" is said with reference to progress. For the more someone acts in virtue, the further forward he presses, acquiring for himself a greater habit of [?]; for the road of virtue is boundless and never-ending. In this sense, I think, was also said, "Into which angels long to look." For so great is the splendour of the good things given to us by the one who became man that even for angels it is desirable to gain a brief glimpse of them; this is what "to look" hints at. A sensible person [desires?] not what will come to an end, but what goes on ever advancing and shines with undefiled glory. And since it is not possible to grasp the inexhaustible as a whole, one should be content to share in it at least in some measure.
