He said, "not as though I were writing you a new commandment," saying this too in agreement with the first Epistle, and at the same time showing that he is setting it before those who have already travelled it and have gained experience of it by acting in accordance with it, and not presenting strange and difficult things, which would wear her out through the unfamiliarity of the undertaking. "Not as though I were writing you a new commandment." He also adds what the commandment requires, that we love one another. And he explains love: that it has its being in walking according to the commandment; and again, that the commandment from the beginning was given for no other reason, he says, than "that you should walk in it," turning the same things

over and over. Through love he takes care that they remain undivided, and that they are not split off to follow the deceivers who are already going about in the world and rejecting the Lord's sojourn in the flesh. By [speaking of] walking according to the commandment from the beginning, he shows that the erroneous opinion of the heretics is recent, and urges them to hold fast to the commandment from the beginning and not be drawn away by their deceit. For Christ gave his disciples a command about these deceivers, saying: "Many will come in my name, saying, 'I am the Christ,' and they will deceive many. So do not go after them." Since they keep these commandments, then, he says, he bids them not to be deceived, but to regard the one who says such things as Antichrist. [Understand:] "So whoever does not confess these things," so that "This is the deceiver and the Antichrist" may follow fittingly; for without this the statement does not hang together, as it passes from plural to singular. This, he says, is the Antichrist and the deceiver. By saying "who do not confess Jesus Christ coming in the flesh," and not "having come," he indicates that he means those who reject the Lord's second coming. For the Lord himself, when he says, "Many will come in my name," is speaking not of his first coming but of his second. Yet by true reasoning those who reject the second coming cast off the first as well. For if the one who came in the flesh also promised the second coming, then whoever rejects the second certainly rejects the first too. If he believes that he came, he will also consider the promise of the one who came trustworthy; but if he rejects the promise, there is no reason why he should not disbelieve the first coming too. That, I think, is why the beloved disciple used this expression, saying "coming" and not "having come," so as to include those who deny both of the Lord's comings in the flesh. He charges them, then, to guard themselves against these people, and adds the reason: so that, he says, you do not lose through mixing with them what you have worked for, but receive your reward in full. But perhaps one of [?] will say: What if I do not believe in the coming of the

[?] ...Christ's [coming] in the flesh, yet I live by doing good; can I not, through these works, be counted among the godly and receive some reward for them?" The apostle heads off this objection in advance and speaks as follows. Let no one who rejects the Lord's sojourn in the flesh imagine that he can receive the full reward for his works, which is owed to believers, or be counted godly at all. Rather, "everyone who transgresses his commandment" (Christ's, that is, now that he has come) "and does not abide in his teaching does not have God." For if the one who came to teach human beings the perfect knowledge of God is plainly rejected, how could someone still be godly who drives away the guide to the divine [teachings] [?]? Such a person is therefore godless. On the other hand, the one who is grounded in the teaching of Christ is filled with God and dear to God, and has in himself the whole fullness of the Godhead, that is, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. For Christ himself teaches about the Father, saying, "All that the Father has is mine." In many places he teaches about himself and the Father, that the one is Father and the other Son. He teaches about the Spirit when he says, "The Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father." And he teaches more completely than in these passages when he says, "Baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." If the Lord's disciple speaks here only of the Father and the Son, and not also of the Holy Spirit, do not be scandalized. Here and now he needed to speak only of these, I mean the Father and the Son. That is enough on this for the present, so that we do not run on at length. A person abides in the teaching of Christ, that is, in the gospel teaching, when he thinks and acts in keeping with it, living a life of contemplation and of practice together. Whoever leads himself away from it is godless. Consider the one who makes himself God's own by an exact way of life, as Abraham did, and so heard from God, "I am your God." In the same way, the one who lives outside the commandment of the Gospel is godless, having cut himself off from having God. That person is godless, I mean the one who has estranged himself from divine instruction. But the one who abides in it has both the Father and the Son. Of such a person the Son also said, "We will come to him" (with the Father, that is) "and make our home with him." By keeping the commandments he has made himself a temple and dwelling place of God, and he has God dwelling within him. For "having God" is said in two senses. All created things are also said to have God, which is why Paul said, "For in him we live and move and have our being." That is said in the sense of being brought into existence. In another sense the one who serves God through goodness and virtue is again said to have God. In this sense God is called the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of all the God-loving Hebrews generally. With this in mind we must attend to what is now said: "He who has the Son has the Father also." For he who has seen the Son, as the Son himself says, "has seen the Father." And again: "I

am in the Father, and the Father in me," says the Savior himself. So from this, too, it is known that the Father and the Son are of one substance. Someone may say that on this reasoning anyone who receives the disciples also has both the Son and the Father, since the Savior says of them too, "Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me." Let him know that he speaks wrongly and does not argue as he should. These words are said about the teaching. Whoever received the apostles by assenting to their teaching received, through them, the Son and the Father, who taught through them. Or put another way: whoever abides in the teaching has both the Son and the Father, and the apostles abode in the teaching, so fully that they preached it. So whoever received them as temples of God has, by receiving them, the Son and the Father who are in them. "If anyone comes to you." He puts those to whom the Epistle is addressed on their guard. If anyone comes to you without this confession, not only must he not find shelter with you, he must not even be thought worthy of a greeting. He says this with precision, since such a greeting is owed only to those who share our way of life and our faith. For to whom do we offer the wish "Rejoice," if not to those who share our way of life and our faith? So if we were to offer such a greeting to the ungodly, we would certainly be offering it to them as people of like life and faith. Through it they would be taken as our partners, and they would drag us down into their own pit.

"Though I have many things to write to you, I did not want to do so with paper and ink. Instead I hope to come to you and speak face to face, so that our joy may be complete. The children of your elect sister greet you. Amen." He himself has explained why he set out the Epistle so briefly, both here and in the one after it: he hopes to come and to supply in person what is lacking. Because he adds "The children of your elect sister greet you," some want to establish that the Epistle is addressed not to a woman but to a church. On this I would not quarrel with anyone who wishes to think so. End, with God, of the Second Epistle of John.

OF THE THIRD CATHOLIC EPISTLE OF JOHN. The Epistle is about hospitality. First he commends Gaius, to whose hospitality everyone bears witness, and urges him to keep to the same purpose and to send the brothers on their way and welcome them. Then he accepts Gaius's gift, but he blames Diotrephes, who not only gives nothing to the poor himself but even prevents others from giving, and who talks a great deal of nonsense. He says that such people are strangers to the truth and do not even know God. He commends Demetrius, bearing him the finest witness.

ANOTHER ARGUMENT. He writes this Epistle too to commend certain brothers. He writes to Gaius and bears witness to his great hospitality, which he also judges worthy of great praise. For he says that the one who does good is of God. He spurs him on further by censuring Diotrephes, who has not learned to do this. He also praises Demetrius, who does the same, and gives him a trustworthy testimony. This Epistle is brief for the reason already given in the first Epistle.

CHAPTERS OF THE THIRD CATHOLIC EPISTLE OF JOHN. 1. A prayer for perfection, and thanksgiving for his acknowledged hospitality to the brothers for Christ's sake; in which he also speaks of the wickedness and misanthropy of Diotrephes. 2. On Demetrius, to whom he bears the finest witness. 3. On his coming to them soon, for their benefit.

THE CATHOLIC EPISTLE OF JOHN THE APOSTLE [?]. PROLOGUE. "The elder to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth." This was discussed in the preceding Epistle, and it would now be superfluous and redundant to go over the same points again. "Whom I love in truth." Whoever loves according to the Lord, with heartfelt love, loves in truth, as has often been said above. CHAPTER ONE. [A prayer for perfection, and thanksgiving for his acknowledged hospitality to the brothers for Christ's sake; in which he also speaks of the wickedness and misanthropy of Diotrephes.] "Beloved, I pray that in every way you may prosper and be in good health, just as your soul prospers. For I rejoiced greatly when brothers came and testified to your truth, just as you walk in truth. I have no greater joy than this, to hear that my children are walking in truth." "Just as your soul prospers." It prospers in the way of life that accords with the Gospel. "You walk in truth." Whoever walks in keeping with the simplicity of the Gospel walks in truth. By "walking" he does not mean movement on feet, for that kind of travel from place to place is the same for every animal with feet. He means the ordered and sober progress of the soul's impulses, which few attain, those who have knowledge. "Greater than this." By the strict standards of the Greek language the form "more greater" [?] is unacceptable, since it piles one intensifier on another beyond measure. "Beloved, you act faithfully in whatever you do for the brothers, strangers though they are, who have testified to your love before the church. You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God. For they went out for the sake of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. We ought therefore to welcome such people, so that we may become fellow workers with the truth." "You act faithfully." That is, "in a way worthy of a faithful man." "We ought to welcome." "To welcome" is used in place of

"They lay in wait for me like a lion ready for its prey." By this he teaches us not to wait until those in need come to us, but to run out to them ourselves and go after them, as Abraham and Lot did. "I wrote to the church, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, does not accept us. So if I come, I will call to mind the deeds he is doing, prating against us with wicked words. Not content with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers himself, and he hinders those who want to and expels them from the church. Beloved, do not imitate what is evil but what is good. Whoever does good is of God; whoever does evil has not seen

"I will call to mind the deeds he is doing." If we have been commanded not to repay evil for evil, how can he now make such threats? Our answer is that this commandment forbids retaliating against someone who sins only against ourselves. But if the sin against us also puts an obstacle in the way of the faith, such a person must be repaid, as Paul repaid Elymas, who was perverting the ways of the Lord. "Prating" means "reviling, speaking ill of." "Do not imitate what is evil." There is no fellowship between light and darkness, and no agreement between Christ and Belial. So the one who has been enlightened by the knowledge of Christ must not mix with the darkness by imitating the ungodly, that is, their licentious works. He says that the one who does good is of God. His spiritual eye has been made perfect by the light of the knowledge of God, and so, being wholly light, he both sees the true Light, God, and is seen by others as a light in the world, holding fast the word of life. In the same way the one who does evil walks in darkness. He is not able to see God himself, that is, to do the things of God, nor can others see him giving right guidance. Instead he is hated and loathed by all, as the oracle says: "I hated injustice and abhorred it [?]." On Demetrius, to whom he bears the finest witness. "Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also testify for him, and you know that our testimony is true." "From everyone." He has been attested by everyone, that is, by those who hold the truth. "And from the truth itself," that is, from the word put into action. For there are some to whom virtue is attributed, but falsely, on the strength of talk without deeds. If anyone takes "by everyone" to include unbelievers as well, because the word "every" is all-inclusive, he would not be found to have understood it wrongly. For Paul says that believers should

OF THE CATHOLIC EPISTLE OF JUDE. He writes this Epistle to those who already believe. The occasion is this. Certain people had come in, teaching that sin makes no difference and denying the Lord, so he found it necessary to write and to make the brothers secure. First he exhorts them to contend for the faith handed down to them and to remain in it. Then he denounces such people as deceivers and charges the brothers to have no fellowship with them, since they know that being called is not enough unless we also walk in a way worthy of our calling. For the Lord brought the former people out of Egypt and then destroyed them when they did not remain in the faith. And he did not spare the angels who did not keep their own rank. So one must withdraw from such people. For even Michael the archangel did not bring a charge of blasphemy against the devil. He teaches that their destruction will be like that of Sodom. Then he gives exhortations about conduct, prays that the Lord may give them firmness in the faith, and brings the Epistle to a close. [?] CHAPTERS OF THE CATHOLIC EPISTLE. "Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, to those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ: may mercy, peace and love be multiplied to you." To show his standing, it was enough for the present apostle, I mean, to call himself a servant of Christ and then to claim the dignity of James. James was praised by everyone for his virtue, and this made Jude more acceptable to his hearers as a teacher of the word. For one who shared James's birth and blood would hardly be seen as a stranger to the character of the man whose kinship he shared. This was all the more so because, serving under one Master, Christ, he was set to bear the yoke of servitude equally with his brother. "To those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ." The Lord said, "No one comes to me unless my Father draws him," and this blessed man now shows that saying proved true. For he says that those who are loved by the Father have been kept for Jesus Christ. That is why he also calls them "called." It is not from themselves but from the Father that, by being drawn, they also have their calling. He prays that mercy, peace and love may be multiplied to them. Mercy, because through the tender mercy of God we were called back and taken up to be his servants. Peace, because the same God the Father granted us this too, reconciling to himself through his Son Jesus Christ us who had offended him. Love, because through his love for us his only-begotten Son was handed over to death for our sake. These, then, he prays may be granted to them in overflowing measure, in harmony with the blessed

On watchfulness in faith in Christ, because of the uprising of ungodly and licentious men; in which he also speaks of their coming punishment, like that of those who sinned of old and the wicked. "Beloved, though I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write to you urging you to contend for the faith that was once for all handed down to the saints. For certain people have slipped in among you, who were long ago written down for this condemnation, ungodly people, who turn the grace of our God into licentiousness and deny our only Master, God, and our Lord Jesus Christ." With these words he indicates the subject of the Epistle. He sets out the present words out of concern for their salvation, so that they will not be caught through their simplicity by these most abominable heretics. By describing the heretics' licentious life he brands them, as it were, and makes them conspicuous to those who do not know them. Peter also spoke about these people, but Jude now does so more broadly and in more detail. He says they were "written down long ago" because both Peter and Paul said of them that such deceivers would come in the last times. Before them Christ himself said, "Many will come in my name and will lead many astray. So do not go after them." For they call themselves Christians and deceive many under this name. He means the followers of Nicolaus, Valentinus and Simon, who were most abominable and unclean. Being gluttonous and dissolute, they put on a show of the teaching so that through it they might find their way into households and take captive silly women weighed down with sins. They invented nocturnal rites and gave themselves over to debauchery and licentiousness. "Turning into licentiousness" means "debasing chastity into licentiousness, as one counterfeits coin." It follows from this that they also deny our Lord Jesus Christ. How could they not deny him? By the impurity of their lives they cut themselves off, as if with a loud and piercing cry, from the teacher of all chastity. For what fellowship has light with darkness? "Urging you to contend." He urges those who have once received Christ as Savior and believed in him to contend still further. That is, they must not let themselves grow slack, but must brace themselves and hold all the more firmly to their zeal for this. For we have received the Word made man. If we were to say that the one begotten of the Father before the ages is one person, and the one born of the Mother in the last times, with his own hypostasis, is another, how could we fail to deny the one Lord and Master? For

the Lord Jesus is one by the union of the incarnation. The Word of God, who is before the ages and is God, raised up into the glory of the Godhead the flesh that he assumed from the holy Virgin from the very moment of conception, and he is one and the same Master of all. "Changing grace." "Changing" means "transforming, perverting." "Now I want to remind you, though you once knew all this, that the Lord, after saving a people out of Egypt, later destroyed those who did not believe. And the angels who did not keep their own domain but abandoned their proper dwelling he has kept in eternal chains under gloom for the judgment of the great day. In the same way Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them, which [?] went after other flesh, are set forth as an example, undergoing the punishment of eternal fire. Yet in the same way these dreamers also defile the flesh, reject authority and blaspheme the glorious ones. But when Michael the archangel was contending with the devil and disputing about the body of Moses, he did not dare to bring a blasphemous judgment against him, but said, 'The Lord rebuke you.' But these people blaspheme whatever they do not understand, and by whatever they know by instinct, like irrational animals, they are destroyed." He has spoken of the licentiousness of the unclean Nicolaitans, Valentinians and Marcionites, and has made them notorious, as if with a brand, for the filth that clings to them. Now he adds this as well: "The Lord, [after saving] a people out of the land of Egypt," and so on. By this he shows that the same God is the author of the Old and the New Testament. These abominable people say otherwise: that the God of the Old is one God, punishing and cruel, and the God of the New another, gentle and kind [?]. At the same time he shows that the people of the present will not go unpunished either. Neither did those who came out of Egypt. Through his surpassing power, and because of his oath to their fathers, God delivered them from Egyptian oppression. Yet when they transgressed they did not remain unpunished but paid a fitting penalty. God's favor toward their fathers did not help them at all, nor did the overwhelming clarity of the miracles done for their sake. In the same way it did not help the fallen angels that they had come into being from God and been honored with an intellectual nature, nor did living alongside Lot help the Sodomites. Those who crossed the Red Sea on dry ground through faith later perished through unbelief. As for those who had been allotted the honor of angelic rank, they did not remain in their own domain because of their negligence, but rejected the heavenly way of life given them through God's goodness. These he has reserved for judgment, that is, for condemnation, on the great and unbearable day of punishment. That is what "he has kept" means here. As Christ also says: "which has been prepared for the devil and his angels." And indeed the Sodomites are evidence of the [?]

[?] And also in the case of the female: the woman taken according to the laws, one wife for one husband, is one's own proper flesh, but the woman who is poured out and public is other, alien flesh, and falls little short of the male kind in defilement. Having given these examples, he left the hearer to work out what follows from them. And what is that? It is to add: "If, then, he dealt with these in this way, without being put off at all by their earlier good fortune, will the fact that the Son of God came into the world for the sake of human beings and endured insults and sufferings on their behalf now rescue these men who live in licentiousness?" No one would say so. For even if he loves mankind, he is also truly just. Because of true justice he did not spare those who had sinned, and because of his love for mankind he brought harlots and tax collectors into the kingdom. Although this was the conclusion to be drawn, he passed over it himself, both for the reasons we gave earlier and because it had already been said by the blessed Peter when he wrote, "For if God did not spare the angels when they sinned," and so on. So much for that. As for "they defile the flesh while dreaming," the restraint of the expression is worth admiring. He testifies to their great licentiousness, saying that they are both impure in their life and utterly licentious in their tongue, but he veiled the extreme shamefulness of the deed with the word "dreaming." We will uncover this a little, as far as is fitting, taking our information on these matters from the work of the blessed Epiphanius of Cyprus, which he called the Panarion. For he says that these foul Borborites, when they shamefully have intercourse with women, do not let the seed remain in the womb. Instead, in an abomination left incomplete, they catch it in their own hands and at once bring it to their mouths, together with the women with whom they have corrupted themselves. Then the unclean ones part from one another, thinking they have accomplished something great. Because this unclean act is left incomplete, he calls it "dreaming," since that is how things are in dreams. So, he says, while they defile their own flesh through this filthy offering, they also rage against the divine nature, rejecting its lordship and its dominion over all things. The blessed Irenaeus of Lyons spoke about them at greater length in his refutation of knowledge falsely so called, and anyone who wishes can learn about them from him. Or else, by "lordship" he means that they reject the celebration of the mystery of Christ, performing their own licentious acts in the guise of angelic mysteries. By "glories" he means the Old and the New Covenant,

as Paul says: "[For if what was being done away with came] with glory, much more does what remains have glory." And again: "For if the ministry of condemnation was glory, much more is the ministry of righteousness glory." Or else by "glories" he means the authorities of the Church, whom they reviled, as can be learned from the Third Epistle of John the beloved, where he says that Diotrephes was prating against them with evil words. Since he has mentioned blasphemy, he corrects not only these men but all people, telling them to keep their tongues free of such an evil and not to use it even against those who deserve to be reviled. So he says, "But Michael the archangel," and so on. What does he mean by this? That these men use blasphemy readily and without restraint against everyone. But this must not be done, since it is not right to revile even those who deserve it, as is clear from the archangel Michael. When he was disputing with the devil about the body of Moses, he could have reviled the devil for his shamelessness, but he did not do so. He brought against him only the words "May God rebuke you, devil." If the archangel restrained himself in this way when a man was being slandered, how do these men dare to blaspheme the God of all? There is also another reading: "If the archangel acted so, it would not be right for us to bring blasphemies against a man who is our brother and of our own kind." So much for that. The dispute about the body of Moses was this. It is said that Michael the archangel ministered at the burial of Moses. The devil would not accept this, and brought a charge over the murder of the Egyptian, as though it made Moses guilty, claiming that for this reason he should not be allowed an honourable burial. Or else the apostle brings this up now because he wants to point by it to the reckoning that all people owe after their departure from the body, and to show that the same God is God of the Old and the New Covenant. For God wished to show the people of that time, who were of a grosser disposition, the invisible through the visible: that after our release from this life the devil with his evil demons opposes our souls, seeking to cut off their journey upward. He opposes them, but the good angels of God fight on their side, as the blessed Antony also saw. To show this, God allowed these things to happen then. Even so, Michael drove the devil off without rebuking him on his own authority. He left the judgment to the Lord of all and said, "May God rebuke you, devil." "But these men [blaspheme] what they do not know." Michael, he says, acted in this way and would not use blasphemy even on behalf of a man, namely Moses. But these men compose blasphemous words about doctrines they do not know, and the things they understand by natural impulse, without discernment, like irrational animals, those they chase after, like horses mad for mares, or swine. 2 Cor. 3:11. in licentiousness and blasphemy, and in feigned hypocrisy, taking bribes in order to deceive. "Woe to them! For they went the way of Cain, and abandoned themselves for gain to the error of Balaam, and perished in the rebellion of Korah. These are hidden reefs at your love feasts, feasting with you without fear, shepherding themselves; waterless clouds carried about by winds; autumn trees without fruit, twice dead, uprooted; wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the gloom of darkness has been kept forever." "The way of Cain": that is, by killing their brothers. For they too, by teaching such things, kill their brothers, that is, their fellow human beings, through their evil teachings. Or else, by eating seed, they kill the brother who existed in potential, whom the seed, carried to term, would have brought into life. "The way of Balaam," because they too, like him, do these things for the sake of gain. "That of Korah," because they too, like him, though unworthy, seized the rank of teacher. "These are at your love feasts." At that time tables were still being held in the churches, as Paul also says in his epistle to the Corinthians, and these they called love feasts. At these, he says, they come together, not for the need these meals served, but to find an opportunity to entice unstable souls, as Peter also says in his second epistle. As for "feasting without fear, shepherding themselves": "without fear" is to be construed either with "reefs," so that the sense is "reefs feasting with you without fear," that is, their fellow diners expect no danger from them, while they suddenly, like reefs, bring the destruction of souls upon them; or "without fear" is to be construed with "shepherding themselves." They do not fear, he says, the judgment that follows from not knowing how to shepherd, but, blind leading the blind, they fall into a pit, to use the Lord's words, together with those they shepherd. He compares them to reefs, waterless clouds, autumn trees, wild waves and wandering stars, for what belongs to those things by nature belongs to these men by choice. Reefs are deadly to sailors, rising up unexpectedly, just as these men spring an unlooked-for evil on those who dine with them. Waterless clouds driven by winds do not refresh with rain the places they are carried over (for they have none), but bring gloom upon them. In the same way these men do not water the souls of those they meet with a saving word, but darken them with their most foul suggestions, driven by the evil practices of the demons.

Then there are the autumn trees, which die twice, once in losing their fruit and again in shedding their leaves (for at that time they look dry, robbed of their beauty, both the splendour of their fruit and the blooming loveliness of their leaves). These men suffer something that matches this. They too are twice stripped: through their eating of seed, and by being robbed of the good order of a chaste way of life. That is why they are also uprooted from the paradise of the Lord, which is the Church, and, thrown out of it, they are gathered up for the eternal fire. For what standing or root will a man have who is cast out by everyone because of the filth of pleasure? They are also called wandering stars, not because they shine in the firmament of our faith and have Christ, the sun of righteousness, moving among them, bringing about the seasons of the virtues and giving life to the faithful who are ranked according to them. It is rather because, appearing to transform themselves into an angel of light like the evil demon who leads them, they simply move contrary to the doctrines of the Lord. With these they darken those who come near them, and win eternal gloom for themselves. And when they are compared to wild waves, they do not deny the likeness. For they too rage madly and uncontrollably in their blasphemies against God, driven by the spirits of wickedness, and foam up their own shame, ending in foam after the bluster of their blasphemy, because of the insubstantial and easily dissolved shamefulness of their life. Such is the foam of the [waves] to which they were compared. "Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied about these men, saying: Behold, the Lord came with his holy myriads to execute judgment on all, and to convict all the ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds that they committed in ungodliness, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him. These are grumblers, malcontents, walking according to their own desires, and their mouth speaks arrogant things, flattering people for the sake of advantage." Having said this, he also brings in Enoch, prophesying the affliction that God has stored up for them, namely at God's final just judgment. "And to convict all the ungodly." An ungodly man differs from a sinner in that the ungodly man's offence concerns God, while the sinner's lies in the things done in this life, some missing of the mark of righteousness. After this he leaves aside the comparisons for these licentious men and moves on to the substance of his charge against them, calling them grumblers and malcontents. A grumbler is one who finds fault with what displeases him under his breath and without speaking openly. A malcontent is one who makes a habit of mocking everything at all times. These foul men are grumblers and malcontents, 1 Pet. 3. 1 Tim. 2.

he says. They are grumblers because they cannot speak openly about their teaching on account of its shamefulness, since it is not without danger to make public a licentiousness joined with ungodliness and blasphemy. They are malcontents because they slander what belongs to others and what belongs to the truth, so as to establish their own supposed [?] licentious practices. What he said about Balaam, that these men, like him, abandoned themselves for gain, he now says more plainly: that they flatter people for the sake of advantage. By "flatter" he means that they treat those in authority with flattery, and by "advantage" he means gain. "But you, beloved, remember the words spoken beforehand by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ, how they told you that in the last time there will be scoffers, walking according to their own ungodly desires. These are the ones who cause divisions, worldly men, without the Spirit. But you, beloved, building yourselves up on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life. And some, who separate themselves, convict [?]; others save with fear, snatching them out of the fire, hating even the garment stained by the flesh. Now to him who is able to keep them from stumbling, and to present them blameless before his glory with rejoicing, to the only wise God our Saviour, be glory and majesty, dominion and authority, now and for all ages. Amen." "Remember the words spoken beforehand by the apostles": those spoken by Peter in his second Epistle, and by Paul in almost every Epistle. From this it is clear that he wrote these things last of all, after the apostles had passed away. "These are the ones who cause divisions." Here is another charge against these most foul men. Not only do they perish themselves, he says, but they also drag away the nurslings of the Church (this is what "cause divisions" is meant to signify), that is, they put them outside the boundaries of the Church, namely those of the faith and of the sacred tabernacle of the Church itself. For they turn their own assemblies into dens of robbers, leading people away from the Church and bringing them over to themselves. They do this because they are "soulish" men, that is, men who live by the ways of the world. We have already said that divine Scripture often uses "soul" for life, as in Job: "All that a man has he will give for his soul," that is, for his life. Paul too says that such men, being soulish, cannot receive the things of the Spirit of God. Being soulish, then, they also use a soulish teaching, Job 2:4.

About this teaching it is said: "This wisdom is not the kind that comes down from above, from the Father of lights, but is earthly, demonic," not having the divine Spirit speaking in it. "But you, beloved." Those men, then, he says, are like this, but you, building yourselves up on your most holy faith, that is, restoring yourselves in the Holy Spirit, which means holding your gatherings in your prayers according to the teaching of the Holy Spirit, "keep yourselves in the love of God." That is, guard yourselves, waiting for the mercy from the Lord, which is awarded to you on the last day as the prize of eternal life. As for those men, if they separate themselves from you (for this is what "separate" means), convict them, that is, make their ungodliness plain to everyone. But if they look toward healing, do not push them away; take them in with the mercy of your love, saving them from the fire with which they have been threatened. Take them in after convicting them, and with fear, taking care that receiving them, if you are careless in your attitude toward them, does not become a cause of harm to you, with those who are already firmly established being stolen away by them into the same flood of their ungodliness. For wickedness is easily imitated. So let them be received, he says, but admit them with fear, that is, with caution. Let your mercy toward them be accompanied by hatred of their foul works, as you hate and abhor even the garment stained, that is, defiled, by their flesh, since it too has become abominable by touching their flesh. Receiving them in this way, he says, lead them to repentance through fear of the punishment to come, so that they may be seen to be worthy of mercy. Having said this, he goes on to seal the Epistle with a prayer. The end, with God's help, of the Catholic Epistle of Jude.
